LII"TES ON THE DEATH OF MRS. JOHN OROSFIELD. abe following line* were composed by a yo,ng lady when she heard of Mrs. John Crosfield's death.]

" Such sad, sad news !" Yet Is it sad When one is cal el away To the bright glories of the eternal day? When one who suffered much Is called to see His face, And in the eternal place With Him to reign, Where there is no more But cloudless sky, And everlasting light? "Bach sad, sad news !" But is it sad To stand with those around the crystal sea, And with them share a glad eternity? To see the Ring, And never sin again, Or suffer grief or pain; Where troubles now have ceased, And where sad partings are no more? For sorrow never somes To that eternal shore. Is it so std to leave the battle field— To throw the weapon down, And to receive the crown From Christ's own hand? Is it so sad to V. ear the spotless dress Of His own righteousness— To see His gracious smile With which He welcomes to her rest "His poor tired child ?" Is it so sad to lean on Jesu's brea.t ? It is not sad for those who hear It's call, That tells the journey now is done, Ana bids them come and reign beyund the sun With Hun in glory. It is not sad to enter through the gates Where Christ our Lord now waits To welcome home His servants; It is not sad to hear the angels' song of joy: Because another comes To swell their throeg. But it is sad foe those who have b.-en left, They can no longer hear The voice so loved end dear That now for them is hushed. But it is only for a little white, For soon we, too, shalt meet the joyful smile That welcomes home; And soon we, too, upon the eternal shore Shall stand around the throne With those who went before.

CLEVER CRITICS. Tho mice, with courage in excess Of their inherent littleness, Were gazing just as critics do, Where Pussy's portrait stood on view. "'Tis very good, no doubt," said one; "So good I feel inclined to run; And yet there's something not quite true, Or something missing: what say you?" "You're right," his friend replied; "you miss The life that is net seen in this! You miss the love Miss Pussy shows In hunting us where'er she goes; "You miss the cruelty in her eyes, The greedy smile of glad surprise, That she would show to see us pause Close to her sharp and eager claws! Believe me, friend, the fault is this : "ris the expression that we miss! The cat that men love—that is here; But not the creature that we fear!" —Little Folk.? Magazine, for July.
G. W.

A "CI4CITLAI7." Saw.—A saying that cats all round. Woe to him whl has no court cf appeal against the world's judgment. —Carlyle. Occasions do not make a man frail, but they show what he is.—Thomas ci Keinpis. "It is generally the case with bad boys," philosophically remarks Mark Twain," that they look like their mother and act like their father."

"Sarah," said a teacher to cue of his pupils "Sarah, can you give the definition of a skipper ?" "No," answered Sarah, "but perhaps a cheese mite." "You must feel lonely since your husband went away," consolingly observed a neighbour to her lady friend. "Not at all. It is the first holiday I have had since I was a School girl." Steadfastly set your face against needless delays in doing any work for the good cf your fellow-men, or for your own edification. Do this very day and hour the duties which this hour and day demand. Beautiful it is to see and understand that no worth, known or unknown, can die, even on this earth. The work an un- known good man has done is like a vein of water flowing bidden, underground, secretly making the ground green. It flows and flows; it joins itself with other veins and veinlets ; and one day it will start forth as a visible perennial well. A schoolmistress asked one of her puoile, " What do you see above your head when you walk in the open air ?" "The sky," answered the little old. "But what do you see there in rainy weather?" "An umbrella," was the prompt reply. An officer of one of the ships at Spithead, having occasion to send to his country house in great haste, despatched a seller on horseback with a letter, who, after deny( ring it, and being refreshed, and the horse fed, went to the stable to rEtarro A bystander observed to him, "that he was putting the caddie on the hind part before." The sailor replied, " How do you know which way I am going to ride ?" A Broad•street merchant's wife gave him the following letter, with instructions that it should not be opened until he got to his place of business :—"I am forced to tell you something that I know will trouble you, but it is my duty to do so. lam determined you shall know it, let the result be what it may. I have known for a week that this trial was coming, but kept it to myself until to-day, when it has reached a crisis, and I cannot keep it any longer. You must not censure me too harshly, for you must reap the benefit as well as myself. Ido hope it won't crush you. The flour is all out. Please sand me some this afternoon. I thought by this method you would not forget it." The husband tele- phoned forthwith for a barrel of best flour in the market to be sent to his house instanter. A RAKING FOR TREE PEDLARS —When the Jester was travelling, recently, a nursery man got on the train. Why be should have selected the Jestex as a man pining away for a Norwegian stock pear tree, or an assortment of early green Lombardy apple scions, no one can tell; but he did., and he talked tree to that patient child of sorrow for fit ty- two miles. "I have tried this pear," the Jester said, his sad face lighting up with a gleam of pleased recogniGion as the tree man showed him a coloured lithograph of a pear as big as a football, with a neck like a champagne bottle, goiden-yellow on one side, scarlet-streaked on the other; "I have tried this pear. I planted four of these Hibernian Dutch-checked mongolia tricolours ten years ago." "She's the daisy," the tree man said ; "didn't they do splendidly ?" "Beautifully," said the Jester. "All died the first year, and I never had a particle of trouble with them." Then the tree man showed him a picture of an Oliver Gilsey open stone hybrid peach. "Oh," the Jester said, "I don't want any fruit trees this spring, anyhow." "But—" began the nursery man. "I never see a beautiful lithograph of a fruit tree, crowned and gemmed with luscious fruit," the Jester went on, "without being reminded of an eminent success I made with plums. I owned a beautiful home surrounded with charming grounds, and fruit trees were one of my pas- times. A tree man came along One year, and sold me a plum tree. I bad had little success with plum trees, on ac. count of the rapacious and never-satisfied curculio. But the tree man assured me the curculio would never touch this particularly beautiful variety ; the Alonzo du Belvidere, en Light of the Ha.reanscarum. I bought the tree. It grew as never plum tree grow before; a great swelling mass of foliage that wooed the sunbeams to play with the dancing shadows. And fruit! Everybody that went by the home- stead swore to himself there weren't enough dogs in the commonwealth to keep him on the roadway si .e of that fence a week longer. It never failed, not one single year. Season after season it put forth blooms until it looked like a springtime snow bank, and then in the season of its fruit it shone and gloried like a royal purple sunset in the back garden. One day Smith praised the tree, and I gave him of its fruit. He bit a piece of the plum, and then started borne for his gun. It was only a few steps, but twice before he got there he forgot what he had started after. He climbed over into the foundations of a new house and tried to die. Then he st :loped in a vacant lot and ate the tops off the tar weeds to take the taste out of his mouth. When he got borne he sent for Dr. Miller, and told him the Jester had ipoLsoned him to get some money he owed him, and he wanted him to take down his ante-mortem statement. But he lived, and forgave the man who had filled his young life with bitterness, and one day, standing under the swaying bongos cf this deadly upas plum tree, I told him all its woeful history. How at night the long-drawn howls and wails of terror-stricken boys lying, in the dew-sprinkled grass of the cow pasture, had filled the night with a weird, uncanny horror, and scared all the neighbours' dogs or so many of them as the:wails would go around, under the barn in the tree-bord'ered hollow. How thievish and road-weary tramps had eaten of this fruit, and had gone off down street shouting "Fire !" and had never been seen again. How one day a sandy pig, three and a half feet long, had .eaten a couple of these plums that somebody had thrown over the fence, and then eat down in the dust of the street, ,and cried and sobbed with pin and mortification, until the golden sun went down in a sea of roseate splendour in the distant west. How visit Ors, friends of the family and guests of the home, had plucked and bitten a plum before they Could be warned, and then, with ghastly countenances, We'd to look as though they liked it. The robins shunned that tree. The curculio never went near it. The wandering crows of the air wouldn't look at it. Nothing ever touched It except the English sparrows. They liked it, and grew fat upon it. Nothing," added the Jester ; "nothing that aver grew can kill an English sparrow." div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Dr. Ba.silskij has discovered some mammoth bones at 0 vidiopol. No less than 8,630 singers have been engaged for the Hamburg Masical Festival to be held in the coming August. Dr. Denis Dumont called the attention of the Paris Academy of Medicine recently to a case of hydrophobia which he had cured by the sub-cutaneous injection of nitrate of pilocarpine. The Atheneum says that Mr. Le Neve Foster, of Silver- town, has of late been studying the manufacture of perma- nent magnets. He has succeeded in producing some very powerful ones from steel containing from two to three per cent. of tungsten. Professor Marey, of the College de France, proposes to substitute for vivisection the use of apparatus for the regis- tration of the smallest details of the functions of the organs in animals. For these physiological studies the city of Paris has made a grant of land, and the Government will, it is said, bear the cost of constructing the necessary buildings, ' which will include a laboratory, stables, ctc. TEE ANEROID BAROMETER.— The sensitiveness and rapidity of action of the aneroid admirably illustrate the true principle upon which barometric indications for a rise or fall depend—viz., that the downward pressure of the atmosphere that surrounds our globe is as nearly as possible equal to 15 pounds on the squarelinch ; but that pressure is slightly in- creased or decreased by its rarefaction or densification, through ;varionsmeteorological influences, or the height above or; below the sea level. . . . By the aneroid, we can av ith facility not only measure the height of a mountain top, or the absolute ',height of an ',Egyptian pyramid above the plain on which it was built, or the variations of incline on a line of railway, even when the train is running at its utmost speed,!but even the difference in elevation between the basement:and attic of your house, as, aneroid in hand, you watch the gradual fall from "fair" to "change." Can any experiment better prove that:the barometer is in reality only a measurer of atmospheric pressure, and is but in- directly a weather-glass? For while making such a trial no change in the weather would take place, though the index passes from "fair" to "change," and so clearly proves the absurdity of the old-fashioned barometer indicationa.— " Cassell's Household Guide."

div.head: ASTRONOMICAL OCCURRENCES FOR JULY.
div.p: ASTRONOMICAL OCCURRENCES FOR JULY.

The moon is near Saturn during the morning hours of the 11th, she is near Jupiter during the morning hours of the 12th and 13ch, and near Mercury during the morning hours of the 13th; on the 18th, the day of New Moon, she is near Venue; and on the 19t.h she is near Mars. She is nearest the earth on the morning of the 4th, and again at midnight on the 21st, and farthest from it on the evening of the 19th. Mercury is a morning star, rising on the 3rd at about sunrise, on the 10th at 3h. ina., or 49 minutes before sun. rise; and on the 30th at 2h. 55m. a.m., or lb. 28m. before sunrise. He is stationary among the stars on the 9th, near the moon on the 13th, at his greatest western elongation (2) deg. 5 min.) on the 20th, and in his ascending node on the 30th. Venus is an evening star, setting on the Ist at 10h. 9m. p.m., or lh. 51ra. after sunset; on the last day at 9h. 13m. p.m or Ih. 26m. after sunset. She is near the moon on the 19th!

Mars is an evening star, setting on the Ist at 10h. 41m. p.m or 2b. 23m. after sunset; on the 20th at 9h. 46m. p.m., or iti. 42m. after the sun ;;and on the last day at 9h. 14m. p in. He is due south on the let at 3h. 34m. p.m., on the 15th at 313. 10m. p.m., and on the last day at 2h. 43m p.m. He is near the moon on the 19th. _ _ _

Jupiter is a morning :star, rising on the let at 2h. 16m. a.m., or lh. 32m. before sunrise; and on the last day at Ob. 42m. a.m. He is due south on the let at 10h. 23m. a.m., on the 15th at Pb. 41m. a.m., and on the last day at Bh. 52m. a.m. He is near the moon on the 12th. Saturn rises on the let at lh. 14m. a.m., and on the 29th at 11b. 23m. p.m. He is due south on the let at 811. 45m. a.m., on the 15th at 7b. 55m. a.m., and on the last day at 613. 57m. a.m. He is near the moon on the 11th.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &C. The damp weather has caused the spread of potato diseasa in South Wales. The latest census in Australasia placed the number of sheep in all the colonies at 75,242,936, or more than thrice the number in the United Kingdom, and nearly double the number in the United States. Panama Gowrs.—Mr. J. Watts, of South Carolina, re- ports having a female Angora goat that throughout the season gives four quarts of milk daily, and of a quality equal in richness to that of any Jersey cow on his farm. He says an Angora goat will thrive where a cow will starve, and six goats will subsist well in a pasture which would only afford sufficient nourishment for one cow.— Cultivator. _ _

A well-known north country gentleman and farmer has passed away in the person of Mr. Dickenson, of Thorncroft, Workington. Mr. Dickenson was a typical Cumberland man, and had published a glossary of the "oald farrant words of ty,ld Curnberlan'." Years ago he won various prizes for essays on agricultural subjects. He was the in. ventor of the Cumberland clod-crusher, and in his younger days had been a land surveyor. THE DONCASTER AGRICULTURAL SIIOW.—The .11th an- nual exhibition in connection with the Doncaster Agrical- tur d Society was held on the 28th ult. The entries of horses numbered 283, cattle 81. sheep 51, and pigs 72. In the class for cart stallions Mr. Forshaw's Benefactor took the first prize. Among the agricultural brood mares with foal at foot, Stout, owned by Mr. W. Johnson, was placed first, Messrs. Crowther's 11 year old Cyprus coming next, and a four year old bay named Bessie, the property of Mr. T. H. Miller, of Singleton Park, was commended. Wild geese have been inflicting heavy losses upon wheat growers in California. According to the an Francisco Call, Dr. J. H. Glenn, who owns the greater portion of Colusa County, is so much troubled with geese that he purchased for the ptesent season 230,000 cartridges, and employed 40 mounted men, armed with rifles, to patrol his property during day and on moonlight nights, to protect his wheat fields. It is estimated that 8,000 cartridges are used in a day, and 20.000 geese are put to flight. The cost is said to be 10,000 dollars a year, the value of the wheat crop being 100,000 dollars. The geese shot are plucked, but the reve- nue derived from them is small. _ _ _

SELLING GREEN FODDER —The other day, a tradesman asked a neighbour to sell him a bit of green fodder, offering 23/4d. per stone. He opened out in a field of seed grass, next the gate. cut 10 yards square, which weighed Bcwt., and realised 13s. 4d. This led him to do a sum in arithmetic, and he found he was realising £32 ss. 4d. per acre, so he advertised, and now one half of the field is dawn. He has to deliver it in the town, about two miles distant, but he can well afford that. Last ,year he had an unusual acreage under the plough, and as a consequence he has this year more seed grass than he will need for home consumption; but he has full liberty to sell, and to farm as he thinks best. EXTERMINATING CHARLOCIC.—" If you intend to 30W with oats, plough the land early—not later than January—and be sure not to sow the oats until you see the charlock springing out of the ground; then,by harrowing your seed in on a sunny day, you are sure to kill one crop of char- lock. Some will come after, but:nothing like the original quantity. This you will have to allow to grow with the oats, and as soon as the latter are taken from the field, give the land a good harrowing. The seed that has been left on the field will grow immediately, and you can either pasture it with sheep or plough it down. You have thus killed two crops. Next clean the land well for turnips,and allow what charlock seed has been left in the ground to just begin to grow, and clean the turnips in the usual way, and so pre- vent any charlock seeding. If the land is for barley after the turnips, plough it a month before you intend sowing your barley. After sowing the barley, harrow with seed and chain harrows, and you will not be much troubled with charlock when you again plough the land for oats after it has lain the usual time." The process is se simple and so effectual that it is surprising so many "cloth of gold" fields are now seen in the country, unless on the hypothesis that the bulk of agriculturists do not care to read. .

RAILWAY RATES AND FARES.—The Select Committee of the House of Commons on the sabject of railway rates and fares met yesterday week to consider their report. Four clauses of the draft report by Mr. Barclay—adopted as a basis at the last meeting in preference to that of the Chair- man, Mr. Ashley—were gone through and passed with some amendments. The most material of the alterations made was one advocated by Sir E. W. Watkin and other members, by which railway companies will be allowed to make ter- minal charges for storage, station room, delivery, dm., in- stead of simply being allowed the actual tariff for carriager as propocaqd by Mr. BArelay_ The amendment was decided on by the casting vote of the Chairman. It was agreed that the Committee should devote a day especially to a clause:in which Mr. O'Sullivan proposes that the Irish railways should be purchased by the State. In case this should not be carried, Mr. O'Sullivan will bring forward an alternative proposal to have all the Irish railways amalgamated under one board of 15 dirtctors.—Another meeting of the Com- miltee was held on Tuesday to further consider their report, which, however, has not yet been completed or finally ap- proved. The Committee have now confirmed and put into form, again by the casting vote of the Chairman, their re- commendation that railway companies should be entitled not only to mileage rates for the carriage of goods, but should also be allowed to made moderate terminal charges for stor- age, station expenses, &c. ENGLAND'S NEW SHEEP FARM (LONDON, E. STANFORD), BY MICHAEL G. Mumama., Mulhall, in this pamphlet, shows that it is necessary Great Britain should look for farther sources from which she may draw the residua of her supply of meat beyond what she is able to produce at home, which is not more than seven•twelfths of her consumption at the present time. Seeing that her popu- lation is increasing at the rate of 1,000 per diem, whilst her means of increasing her flocks and herds are extremely limited, and the supply at present forwarded by the United Statea must eventually be required by America for her own population, the question is a pressing one. Mr. Malhall naturally turns his eyes to New Zealand, and is able by the statistics to show that this colony is capable of supplying no less than 30,000 tons of meat per annum, or 106,000 sheep monthly, without dimishing her flocks. Already the frozen carcas?es of 5,000 sheep have been delivered here in splendid condition, at a cost of 5. per lb. for the mutton. In twenty years her flocks have multiplied ninefold, and in t,/enty more years her sheep will equal in number those of Great Britain. For weight of fleece and size of sheep she la untouched by the Australian colonies, and since one of her sheep farms has been recently sold for £480,000, after yielding for some years a net profit of £53,000 per annum, she may fairly claim to be considered as England's new cheep farm; The material prosperity of the cal '^y in other

HAY DRYING IN STACIL—I think it might interest your readers to have an account of the way in which I am drying my clover stacks with an ordinary corn-winnowing fan. At the cost of a day's wage to the village carpenter, and a few boards, I have made a fan which I believe to be quite as efficient as those for which my neighbours are paying from £6 to £l4. I first remove the crank that drives the riddles, &c., so that the handle has nothing to turn but the blades of the blower (if the riddles and hopper can be readily taken out, so much the better). I then, on the side next the handles Aboard up the circular hole which admits air to the blower, and over the opposite hole, on the other side, by means of screws and angle irons, I fix a wooden shoot sloping downwards to within 18 inches of the ground, and termin- ating in a mouthpiece nine inches sivare, with the edges bevelled off to fit accurately on the wooden trough project- ing from the stack. This shoot must have the corners and edges well fitted, and made good with paint and putty, so that it is air-tight. Then close the mouth of the fan where the wind comes upon the corn, leaving an aperture Of about five inches high, but of course leaving it open the fall width of the blades. This, in ordinary fans, will much increase the draught. Finally, as the fan alone requires but very slight power to turn it, I find that by shortening the handle about three inches, so that the man's arm will describe a small circle, it can be turned much quicker and easier. This fan I have applied to two large stacks, 40 feet long and 14 feet wide. The first stack was carried in so green a state that the next morning it had sunk considerably, and was smoking at the top, so that I applied the fan directly, and , in a few minutes a dense vapour was issuing from its month like the steam from a large cauldron. It- reduced the heat of the stack about nine degrees in less than an hour, and now, after using it occasionally whenever a man or boy had ten or fifteen minutes to spare, at the end of 48 hours we can only extract a dry air, many degrees cooler than at first. can confidently say that a fan made in this way is suffi- ,• ciently powerful for any ordinary sized stack, and that with I a little ingenuity in fixing the mouthpiece, the fan will be \none the worse for being so used.—Jso. WARD, Ramsdale House near Nottingham, June 30.—The following is from , a glebe farm, Northampton It may interest you and I your readers to hear of my experiments with a new fan, of Imy own devising, for working on the Neilson system. The I fan, of entirely novel design, is 14 inches in diameter, ex-, I hanging from the centre through a 7in. hole. The width ' of the fan is five inches only, the catch of the wings 3i inches ; but the wings are five inches long. I bolt it on the , tube (9in. square—deal with lin. elm flange) which goes I into an old cask placed in the centre of the rick bored fall of ls holes. The power is applied from the fly wheel of a I turnip cutter by a strap to the 4in. pulley on the fan shaft. I Now for results. I tried it in a rick of half dried hay, put up with many doleful prognostications from my rick man. Of coarse it heated rapidly. as the rick bottom is 20 feet ; square, and" have about 15 tons of hay in the rick. I set a boy of 13 to work the fan yesterday, when the tempera- ture of the rick was 90dee. In twenty-five minutes I took the temperature; it was 79,1eg. The fan made only MO revolutions per minute, bat so little power is required to drive it that the fly wheel 'raced away' from the boy [l] and it is probable that 650 revolutions were often made. 1 can increase the revolutions of my fan to 1,000 per minute, Ibut it is not necessary to do so, as it is waste of power. I am working out an experiment for doing away with the fan 'altogether, and one man can cause a vacuum in a 7in. tube 'four times greater than by a fan driven by steam power. This system will make the exhausting of hot-air from ricks as simple and easy as cutting turnips for the sheep. My !experiments are quite successful on a small scale ; this week I I try them on a large scale, and when I have done so, I will again report to you."

with the revolted Colonies the voice of Shelburne was raised with that of Chatham and other true patriots in denouncing the war. In 1784, he was created Marquis of Lansdowne, and withdrew from political life. At the outbreak of the French Revolution, he emerged from his retirement to denounce the war made by England upon the new Republic Faithful in his maintenance of the Whig policy of peace and retrenchment, he continued to oppose the great war with France down to his death, soon after the opening of the pre- sent century. The career of the second Marquis was, happily, a short one; and he was succeeded, in 1809, by his younger brother, Lord Henry Petty, who was already looked upon as one of the rising statesmen of the Whig party. It was the third Marquis who inherited the Kerry estates and title, and ho thereupon reassumed the ancient family name of itzmaurice in addition to that of etty. A supporter Catholic Emancipation twenty years before that measure ,fas carried; an avowed Free-Trader a quarter of a century before Peel abolished the Bread Tax; a member of the Reform Cabinet of Earl Grey; and, in later years, the lted and confidential adviser of the Queen, the Marquis Lansdowne fairly earned the gratitude of his country- in during his long and useful life. His grandson is the )resent Marquis. The name of Fitzmaurice is also borne by the Earl of Orkney, who owns 11,489 acres in Tipperary, Queen's County, and Kerry, with a rent-roll of £5,789. He is descended from Lord George Hamilton, afterwards Earl of Orkney, who was a prominent figure in the Irish War of William 111. One of his descendants, the third Countess of Orkney, married a Fitzmaurice, the brother of the first Marquis of Lansdowne. *The work from which this article is taken has been pub- lished by Mr. Kibblewhite in two volumes. The first volume is out of print; but a few copies of the second may be had, price 2s. 6. each.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,"
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,"
[Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-street, London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] TIIE FITZ MAURIC ES.

The Fitzmaurices have been for more than a century !among the most distinguished of the great Whig houses. Politically, the house is now represented by Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice, M.P. for the little family borough of Caine, who is certainly something more than a Whig, and who occasionally contributes political articles to the magazines. In Wiltshire he is a tower of strength to the Liberal party. On the rare occasions when he addresses the House, though he is not the man to command a large audience, he shows a thorough knowledge of his subject, and possibly in the -future, with the family advantages which he possesses, he may become a much more prominent politician than he is now. His elder brother, the Marquis of Lansdowne, does not take a very active part in public affairs, but fulfils the duties of a liberal and enlightened landowner. I know something of the condition of Wiltshire, where for the most part the agricultural labourers are in a low condition, and if I were asked to point out the district in which they obtain the highest wages and occupy the best cottages, I should certainly give the palm to the estates of the Marquis of Lansdowne. Indeed, sometime back, when there was a dis- pute between the farmers and the men, in which the Marquis endeavoured to pay the part of a mediator, the men were divided, because a considerable number of them lived in the - - cottages of the. Marquis, and had a very strong sense of the advantage of being his tenants. The Marquis- of Lansdowne owns in Wilts 11,145 acres, and in Hants four acres. The greater part of his property is in Ireland, where he owns in Dublin, Kerry, Kilkenny, King's County, Meath, Limerick, and Queen's County 124,368 acres, making a total in England and Ireland of 135,517 acres, with a rent-roll of £5a,405. Besides this, the Dowager Marchioness, his mother, who claims the Barony of Nairne, has 9,070 acres in Perth and 134 in Kinross, with a rental of £8,812. The Fitzmaurices derive their ancient lineage from the family by whose name they are now known, but most of their wealth from the Pettys, whose name they used to bear alone. The third Marquis, who for some years before his death was the Nestor of the Whig party, was prominent in the politics of the opening years of the present century as Lord Henry Petty. Petty is certainly not so pretty as Fitzmaurice, but it happens that Sir William Petty is one of the most distinguished of the ancestors which the family can boast.

Sir William Petty was the son of a Hampshire clothier, ' and as a boy giving evidence of great ability, he•was sent to Oxford, where he made the best use of his advantages, Sub- ' sequently he went on the Continent, and continued his studies at Leyden, Paris, and other Universities. Returning to,Eng- land about the close of the Civil War, he took up his resi- dence at Oxford as a Physician, and became a Professor at the University. The mats who had studied under Thomas Hobbes, and who was associated in university work with ' John Owen, though he had made a great reputation, had yet to make a great fortune. The opportunity, however, arrived in 1651, when he was appointed Physician-General' to the Irish Army. The allowance was bat £1 per day, but Ireland was then to adventurous spirits what India became a hundred years later. He practised as a physician in Ireland for a time, but he also obtained the offices of Clerk of the Council and Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant. The division of con- fiscated lands among the English soldiers afforded a fine opportunity for using his scientific attainments, and he was appointed to make a careful survey of the island. He was paid by a per-centage on the redistributed lands, and his profits were so enormous that he acquired.about 50,000. acres of land in Kerry, his Irish estates being estimated at a value of nearly £6,000 per annum. Though high in office under Cromwell, he had not taken such a decided part in political affairs as to preclude him from making his submission to Charles 11. at the Restoration' and having his newly-acquired property settled upon him by special order of the ICing, together. with considerable additions thereto. He was I knighted by Charles 11., was one of the founders of the !Royal Society, and in his old age still pursued his career of invention and scientific research. Of all the men who pro- fited by the Cromwellian confiscations, he was apparently the worthiest. He is said to have expended £lo,ooa in planting an English colony at Kenmare, in the county of Kerry, where he established fisheries and ironworks. In 1685, the colonists were driven away by the natives' but they returned when William 111. had accomplished the subjection of Ireland. In modern times the Fitzmaurices have liberally expended their money in roads and piers in the neighbourhood. Sir William lived almost till- the Re- ; voluoon of 1688, and was succeeded by his son, was was created Baron Shelbnrne, and, agreeably with family tratli- ; ditions, sided with William. His younger brother suc- ceeded, and obtained a re-grant of the Kerry estates"' then ' &0,000 acres, and two steps in the Peerage as Earl of Shel- burne. He purchased an estate at Wycombe, Bucks, which !included that pocket borough, which was afterwards sold (shall we not say borough as well as estate?) to the Car- -1 ringtons. He died without issue, and bequeathed his estates to John Fitzmaurice, his nephew (second son of the Earl of !Kerry), one of whose descendants ultimately succeeded to the title and estates of the latter nobleman. The second Earl of Shelburne obtained by purchase the estate of Bowood, We must now turn to the Fitzmaurices. It is probable that the first of this family who set foot in England was one of the foreign favourites of Edward the Confessor. From him are descended the Fitzgeralds and the Fitzmaurices. 1 One of his descendants, William Fitzwalter by name, assisted Earl Strongbow in the conquest of Ireland in the reign of Henry 11. He returned to England; but his second son, Raymond, remained, and obtained as his reward a con- siderable grant of land in Kerry. His ,eldest son (illegiti- mate) succeeded him, and from him the name of Fitzmaurice is probably derived. Xis unnecessary to go into details as to the part played by the Fitarmaurices in the stormy history of Ireland; suffice it to say that they largely profited by the confiscation of the Abbey lands in the reign of Henry VIII., though these did not long remain in the possession of the family. In the reign of Elizabeth, the Fitzmaurices had, by repeated tebelliDns, forfeited their lands; but from James I. the head of tile house obtained pardon and restora- tion. The twenty-first Lord Kerry married the daughter of Sir William Petty above mentioned, and at the death of the twenty-fourth Lord Kerry the estates of both families became united. The first Marquis of Lansdowne is . better known' to, fame as the Earl of Shelburne, the friend of Chatham, Fax, and Lord Holland.. Few statesmen of his time had mare liberal and enlightg::ned views. When all the Jingoism of that age supported the Tory Government in the diS:lctraiii 9try,..!;?),,

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.

The Daily News announces that it is the intention of the Conservative leaders on an early day to bring forward in both houses a resolution raising the question of the foreign policy of the Government. It is expected that, unless a conflict should arise between the two homes on the Arrears Bill, the ordinary business of Parliament may be wound up the first week in August. It is denied on the part of the Liberal members who divided against the Government on Friday night that their vote was the result of a combination. The majority of them, it is said, had no knowledge of the Liberal members who would vote with them until they got into the division lobby. The Daily News learns that if the Land League members had left the gallery to support the Government, about a dozen more Liberals would have voted with the Conservatives. As it was, these malcontents abstained from taking part in the division. The Earl of Northbrook and Mr. Fawcett, M.P., have ac- cepted an invitation of Mr. Arthur Earle, the chairman of the Committee of the Liverpool Reform Club, to a banquet to be held at the Clubhouse, in Dale-street, on the 12th of October. Should all go well, according to Mr. Gladstone's programme announced last night, this date will be imme- diately anterior to the Autumn Session of Parliament, as well as that point of the year at which Cabinet Councils are accustomed to be resumed. The expected banquet, therefore, will take place at a juncture of very special interest, and may be expected to be one of the most notable public events of the recess.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

From a Parliamentary return, issued on Saturday, the number of agrarian outrages reported to the Royal Irish Constabulary during the last month was 283, of which 155 were acts of intimidation by threatening letters or notices, and 18 other acts of like offence. Of murders there were five, of firing at the person eight, of aggravated assault five, of assault endangering life three, and one case of assault on a bailiff. There were also 18 incendiary fires, 24 cases of killing, maiming, and wounding cattle, and 30 cases of injury to property. A desperate attempt at murder occurred on Sunday, near Ennis, county Clare. As a man named Deloughty was returning home from mass at Ennis, about two p.m, he was fired at. His injuries are very serious. He has lost the sight of both eyes. A party of police proceeded at once from Ennis, and found the unfortunate man lying on the road in a pool of blood. In consequence of a statement he made, the police arrested Francis Hynes, the previous occupant of a farm the injured man has been some time in possession of. A COURAGEOUS WOMAN.—Mrs. Kenny, widow of the man who was murdered in the streets of Dublin a few nights ago, is a courageous woman. After the funeral several persons went to her house, and with fearful menaces and oaths threatened her with the fate of her husband if she attempted to give any information on the subject of the murder. This, however, did not silence her, and when three men—named Ward, Grundy, and Richmond—were on Wednesday charged with threatening Mrs. Kenny, she appeared and boldly gave evidence against them. Public sympathy will be on the side of Mrs. Kenny, both for the loss she has sustained and for her courage in the terrible circumstances in which she finds herself; and it is to be hoped that the Dublin police will be able to protect her from the vengeance of the cowardly assassins whom she is doing her best to bring to justice. Eleven men have been arrested in connection with the murder of her husband—the difficulty, however, is to find evidence on which any of them could be convicted.

div.head: TEIE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS
div.p: TEIE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS

A telegram from Liatowel states that two brothers, named Flaherty, who recently reeurty,:d from America, were arrested in Ballvduff, North Kerry, on suspicion of being concerned in the Phenix Park murders. One of the prisoners is said to correspond in every particular with the description of one of the murderers. They have been brought More Captain Massey, and remanded.

div.head: ATTEMPTING THE LIFE OF A CARETAKER.
div.p: ATTEMPTING THE LIFE OF A CARETAKER.

A daring attempt on the life of a caretaker in the employ of the E irl of Kenmare is reported. The man, whose name is Murtv Fernane, had charge of a farm from which a tenant named Crowley had been evicted. He was returning from mass on Sunday morning when he saw three men, with blackened faces, lying in wait for him, and he started to run. Then one of the assassins fired at him 4 but missed him ; a second shot, and then a third, followed; and the result was that Fernane was shot in the hack. He managed to reach the police barrack at Killarney, and gave informa- tion there, and the police shortly afterwards arrested three persons on suspicion, among them being Crowley. John Deloughty, the herd who was shoe near Clarecastle, died on Monday. The deceased was conscious to the last, though both his eyes were destroyed, and be gave his evidence in the clearest manner as to the identity of the prisoner in custody, who was the former tenant of the lands of which Deloughty Was in charge. CONVICTION FOR MURDER. At the Kilkenny Assizes, on Saturday, Thomas Pembroke was indicted before Mr. Baron Dowse for the wilful murder of James Dunne, at Ennisnag, Kilkenny. The prisoner and the deceased were small farmers living close to each other. About eight o'clock on the morning of the 6th May the deceased left his house to go to work on a neighbouring farm, and had to pass the prisoner's house. The prisoner was seen sitting outside the house on a stone with a gun in his hand. A shot was heard, and the deceased was seen by his brother, who was following, lying on the ground. He got up, came towards his brother, with his face bleeding, and shouted, "Tom Pembroke shot me." The prisoner at this time was seen going away from the deceased with a gun in his hand. The gun was found a few moments after- wards, having the appearance of having been recently dis- charged. The deceased died on the 30th May from the effects of the wounds. The defence was that it was an accident, and evidence of good character was given. The judge charged the jury, and said there were no circumatances in the case to warrant them finding it was an accident. The jury retired, and, after an absence of three-quarters of an hour, returned a verdict of guilty, with a recommendation to mercy. His Lordship said he would take care to have it forwarded to the proper quarter. He sentenced the prisoner to be hanged on the Bth of August, 1882, at Kilkenrry Gaol.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. THE CRISIS AT ALEXANDRIA : HOSTILITIES IMMINENT,— Earl GRANVILLE stated that the British Admiral reported that guns were being mounted on forts five miles from the harbour, and on Sunday the Government were informed by the Admiral that there was a certainty that preparations were going on and that guns were being mounted, and he proposed to issue an ultimatum to the local authorities. The noble Earl added that he had no doubt such a step had been taken that morning, ard that the Admiral had inti- mated that unless there was a temporary surrender of the fortresses for the purpose of disarmament he would open fire at daybreak on Tuesday. It was painful for a powerful and great nation to have to exercise force against those who are weaker, but he believed that in this case there was no other alternative. The hostile preparations had been going on in defiance of the wish of the Ktiedive, of the orders of the Sultan, and in spite of the assurances given by the local authorities themselves, and the action proposed to be taken would be simply one of legitimate defence. PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELA.ND) BILL.—The second reading of this Bill was moved by Lord CARLINGFORD, who described its provisions in detail, and expressed his convic- tion that the great powers of the Bill would be exercised by the Lord Lieutenant and the Irish Government with prudence, though at the same time with firmness.—Lord Cranrnore and Brown and Lord Lansdowne approved of the Bill.—The Marquis of SALISBURY contended that much of the difficulty in the way of dealing with Ireland had arisen from the dislike of the Government to look the existing state of things in that country boldly in the face and deal with it accordingly. He trusted that nothing that had occurred elsewhere would be allowed to affect the zeal and firmness with which they would administer the Bill when passed.—The Bill was read a second time without a division. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

THE Clams IN EGYPT.—In reply to questions, Sir C. DILKE stated that Admiral Sir B. Seymour had intimated to Ourabi Pasha that unless the work in the fortifications be discontinued he would open fire against the works. On Sunday the Admiral informed the foreign Consols that at daylight on Monday morning he would give twenty-four hours' notice that unless the forts on the isthmus and those commanding the entrance to the harbour were temporarily surrendered for the purpose of being disarmed he would open fire. Nearly all the Europeans resident at Alexandria had now left.—At a subsequent period of the evening Mr. C. SEELY asked if the bombardment by the fleet would not be an act of war and an infringement of the Treaty of Berlin and several other treaties.—Mr. GLADSTONE declined to answer the question, remarking that no answer he could give would influence the policy of the Government, and he was by no means prepared to admit that the assumptions on the ques- tion were correct assumptions. THE RECENT DIVISTON.—The PRIME MINISTER referred to the occurrence of Friday, which, he said, was without precedent in the annals of the House. The House had placed in the hands of the Government a power restrictive of liberty which the Government deeme& unnecessary, but the powers of the bill were discretionary, and it would be the duty of the Government to exercise only such powers as they might find necessary. He cherished the hope that no such neces- sity would arise for their use, but if the necessity did arise the Government would be under the same obligation and responsibility as they were under with respect to the other powers in the bill. As to the future of the session, his statement would be upon the assumption that the two Irish bills before the House would become law. The Government abandoned all hope of passing any of the bills announced at the commencement of the session except the Corrupt Prac- tices Bill. It would be impossible to lay before the House any proposal for the amendment of the Irish Land Act dur- ing the present session. He proposed after the Irish bills became law to wind up the ordinary business of the session and then adjourn until some day in the second part of October' and then meet to discuss the subject of procedure. He should propose to give precedence daily to that subject. When that business was concluded the session would be wound up by prorogation in the usual manner. THE ARREARS BILL. In committee on the Arrears of Rent Bill, Sir S. NORTHCOTE criticised the bill generally, which, be said, would tend to degrade the tenant, and moved an amendment on clause 1, which relates to the settlement by the Land Commission of arrears of rent. The right hon. Baronet's proposal was to the effect that application to the Court under the clause should be made jointly by the land- lord and tenant. Mr. GLADSTONE entered his protest against the leader of the Opposition taking the opportunity upon an amendment of a limited scope to speak not only upon the whole bill but also upon subjects that were entirely outside it. He pointed omit that arrears of rent had long been used in Ireland for purpeses totally unknown to English landlords, and were used to place power in the bands of landlords to establish control over their tenants, to compel them to agree to an increase of rent, or Co comply with any other condi- tion. These arrears, as long as they continued, would be the I fountain of disturbance and disorder, and would make it difficult to obtain that peace and quietness for which they were makine; so many struggles. Mr. BRAITD opposed the amendment, as fatal to the bill. —The continued debate gave no indication of any renewal of the split in the Liberal ranks, and the division was no surprise. Sir Stafford's amendment was lost by a majority of 78, 170 members voting for it and 248 against it.—Mr. JANES LOWTHER then proposed to transfer the administra- tion of the bill from the Land Commissioners to the County Court Judges, and this amendment was rejected by a majority of 72. • A discussion took place between twelve and one o'clock upon amendments in reference to the period in respect of which rent must be paid under the Bill, which were proposed by Lord G. Hamilton and Mr. Brodrick and resisted by the Government. The former was withdrawn and the second negatived by 187 to 124. Progress was then reported at 25 minutes past one. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXANDRIA. The exciting news from Egypt formed the subject of comment. A ques- tion was put by the Marquis of Salisbury, to which Lord Ncarriinnom replied by reading the telegrams relating to the bombardment of Alexandria.--The Earl of CARNARVON desired to know if the Khedive was safe' and was told that no information at all on the subject had been received from Alexandria. The telegrams were from the Admiral's secre- tary, and he was close to the ship to which the cable was attached; whifth was now lying four miles from Alex- andria.—Earl Dr LA WARE asked if any formal declaration of war had been made, and for what reason a bombardment of forts had taken place in a country with which we were in close alliance. Earl GRANVILLE denied that we were in alliance with the military despotism which was at this moment the facqa Government of Egypt. THE PREVENTION OF CRIME (IRELAND) BILL. Their Lordships, after a few words from Lord STANLEY of Alder- -1?y, went into committee on this bill. The measure was at once reported, and the Standing Orders having been suspended it was passed through all its stages. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.

THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXANDRIA.—In the House Of Commons, Mr. W. H. SMITH, asking for information, wished to know if any of Her Majesty's ships had been injured, and whether any casualties had occurred among the crews Mr. CAMPICELL-BANNERMAN read the telegrams which ap- pear in another column.—The PRIME MINISTER informed Mr. H. Richard that there was a 'general understanding among the members of the Conference at Constantinople to the effect that no step should be taken by any one Power pending the deliberations of the Conference, but from that understanding was excluded the class of cases under which bombardment,falls.. There could therefore be no question in this matter of a departure from that under- standing. —Mt. COWEN asked if any communica- tion had been received from Turkey as to the bornbardment,.and Sir C. DILKE replied that notice had better be given of the question, but, he added, that certain communications had passed in view of the bombardment.— Sir W. LAWSON was anxious to know what opportunity would be given for the discussion of Egyptian matters, to which Mr. GLADSTONE answered that the only specific promise he had given was that about the middle of Jnly the Government would think it their duty to ask tor Supply, and that was apart from any general discussion founded on any motion in regard to the Egyptian policy of the govern- ment.--Before the suspension of the sitting Mr. Campbell- Bannerman was able to read to the House a telegram announeing that the action ended at half-past fine o'clock in the afternoon. At the evening sitting of the Commons Mr. Campbell-Bannerman announced that the total British caseaalties during the operations were five killed, and 27 wounded. THE ARREARS, BlLL.—There was an intereeting discus- aim upon an amendment proposed by Mr. H. Allen, stipu- lating that inability to pay arrears entitling a tenant to relief should be "by reason of failure of cropaor disaster to stock, and without any fault on his own part.-" Mr. GIBSON urged that nothing could be more demoralising than to allow the tenants who had withheld their rents at the instigation of the Land League to participate equally with poor and innocent tenants in the national lcovesse.—Mr. GLADSTONE inferred that the intention of the amendment was to exclude from the benefits of the Act those tenantswho, although unable to pay rent now. were at one time able to pay, but did not pay at the instigation of the Land League. He was. ready to condemn the conduct of those who "held tha- harvest," and should be prepared' to go a long way with the right lion. geeetlemart if he could draw a distinction between those who acted under terror and those who proceeded, wilfully.—Mr. Goscemer suggested the insertion of words excluding those who were in arrear by wilful default of their own, aneaSir M. H. BEAM moved an amendment to that effect.—Mr. Gileansrome, remarked that the proposal raised a question of considerable importance and the utmoet delicacy, ana".as he wished to discuss it with his colleagues he asked that it might ho*postponed until "report."—Sir M. H. 131..,ae3.1 in- sisted upon going to a divie;ion unless a definite prol'aise was given by the Governmente—Sir S. NORTHCOTE pressed for a full explanation, but Ma Goscreze; thought aftee the state- meat of the Government it was not desirable to ga to a div.. sion.—Mr. FORSTER saw great difficulties in ezabarking on an enquiry of this character. The action of the Land Leagne commenced long aftee the time to which the bill app:ned, and he believed that now most persons who could pay their rent had paid.—On a division the amendment of Sir M. H. Beach was defeated by 261 to 184, and Mr. Allen's amend- ment was negatived without a 'division.—At the evening sitting Mr. CHILDERS moved Mr. Gladstone's promised amendment requiring it to be proved that the tenant could not pay antecedent arrears without the loas.of 1 his holding or being deprived of tho necessary means for its cultivation. Mr. Goschen wished for a Ministerial ex- planation as to the part which the tenant-right was to pay in Cal.anhating tta tenant's a2isets, and thought it fionid not

be left entirely to the ,Commissioners to decide; but Mr Gladstone stood to his p 05111.1114 maintaining that the amend- ment was conceived not for PA.*, exclusive benefit of either tenant or landlord, but was mean: to exprass the meeting point of those conflicting interests'. The Government, how- ever, could not consent to the tenote bet:lg deprived of his holding, or of the necessary plant a' StM),. with which to etso work it. Mr. FORSTER pointed out t iffeJence between the value of tenant-right in Ulster and hr othr parts of Ireland, and showed that it must be left' to t,l'e Com- missioners to deal with this matter. The Royal Assent was given by commission to'tbe Pre- vention of Crime (Ireland), the Boiler Explosions, and nearly fifty other bills. The only peers present were the three Royal Commissioners. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXANDRIA.—The latest news from Alexandria communicated to the House was that yes- terday morning the Inflexible and Temeraire fired three shells into the Moncrieff battery, that there was no response from the shore, and that further operations were suspended at noon.—Sir C. DILKE stated that since the bombardment no remonstrance had been received from any of the Powers. The hon. baronet also stated that it was not true that Admiral Seymour had prohibited merchant vessels from passing through the Suez Canal. He had cautioned vessels that if they passed through it must be at their own risk.— Mr. GOURLEY wished to know what was the present policy of the Government, and whether the action taken at Alexan- dria had been for the purpose of protecting the bondholders. —Sir W. LAWSON said that for weeks past we had been drifting into war, and he declared that what took place on Tuesday was an act of international atrocity, cowardly, cruel, and criminal. He asked, What had become of the concert of Europe? If the Government pursued their present policy of "gunpowder and glory" they would lose the confidence of the working men of England, though they might gain that of the "Cot- ton Jingoes." He implored the Government to reconsider their position, and to attempt to carry out a policy more in accordance with common sense, common justice, and com- mon humanity.—The PRIME MINISTER replied that it was almost wholly without reference to the bondholders that the bombardment had taken place. The French, by the course they had taken, were acting within their own rights, and it would be a mistake to suppose that the difference of action implied any unfriendly change in the actions of the Govern- ments of England and France. He had never been un- friendly to intervention, and his complaint against the late Government was not that they interfered, but that they did not interfere at the right time. He did not admit that we were at war with Egypt, and he asserted that the concert of Europe had not been departed from. What had been done was for the protection of the fleet. The right hon. gentlemen, who declined to go into a full discussion of the question, mentioned that a telegram had been received stating that a flag of truce had been sent from Alexandria, and was on its way to the fleet. As to the damage done to the town the humanity and skill of the officers of the fleet might be relied upon to secure that on this occasion the least possible injury was done to the town. The government in the course they had taken had no selfish object or purpose in view, hnd it was not the people of Egypt, but their oppressors who would be sufferers by the operations conducted so successfully by British arms. In conclusion, the right hon. gentleman maintained that the bombardment was not an act of hostility against the people of Egypt, but strictly and solely a measure of self-defence. —Mr. RYLANDS was of opinion that those who entertained the views expressed by the member for Carlisle were bound to take the first opportunity of protesting against the conduct on the part of the Government which they believed to be in dirett violation of those principles of policy which brought the Liberal party into power. He felt that thoughtful men would now be asking in what respect the policy of the chief of the Liberal party differed from that of Lord Beaconsfield. He looked upon the business as the old story of the wolf and the lamb. He saw nothing to justify the wicked act of opening fire upon Alexandria, and he feared we lead created ill-feeling in Europe, and mieht possibly have endangered the peace of the world.—Mr. ILLINGWORTH, as an independent member, regarded the events of the previous 24 hoers with great anxiety.—Sir S. NORTRUOTE desired to impress upon the Government the importance of taking advantage of the flag of truce to arrange measures for the protection of the Khedive.—Mr. SLAGG hoped the country would recognise the distinction between the action now taken solely for the honour of the country, and measures of aggression entered upon solely for the sake of power or prestige. The hon. member warmly resented the insinuation of Sir W. Lawson that the portion of the commercial community interested in the cotton trade were for their own personal advantage prepared to aid and abet the hostilities in Egypt.—Sir C. DILKE assured the House that every possible step would be taken to secure the safety of the Khedive. He denied that there had been any violation of the principles of policy which members of the Government proclaimed-before they entered upon office. What had been done was absolutely necessary for the safety of the British fleet, and reparation would have to be made for the massacres at Alexandria, otherwise the lives of Europeans throughout the East would be in danger. He submitted that long-suffering had been pushed to its utmost limits. If the massacre was allowed to re- main without redress the lives or Europeans throughout the East would be absolutely at the mercy of fanatical mobs. He could not think that any regard to peace principles would make the workmen of this country look with indifference on a state of things under which all English interests would be sacrificed and the whole of our trade brought to an end. As to the Powers, Austria and Ger- many, the only two that had referred to the action taken by this country, had both declared it to be perfectly legitimate and justifiable.—Mr. FORSTER thought the Government could not have acted otherwise than they had done without disregarding its duty of protecting not merely British in- terests but the lives of Europeans.—Mr. RICHARD was unable to see how the bombardment, if not an act of war, could be anything else than murder.

. - TIIE ARREARS BlLL.—Little time was left to the com- mittee on the Arrears Bill, but one impirtant point was dis- posed of satisfactorily.—Mr. EcnoYD proposed an amend- ment to make the sum advanced by the Government a loan, to bear interest at the rate of 1 per cent, per annum, and be repayable by fifteen annual instalments.—The committee, however, by a majority of 101, supported the Government's proposal to make the advance a gift.

div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TEURSDAY.

THE SITUATION AT ALEXANDRIA.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, in the House of Lords, asked for information as to the terrible events now taking place at Alexandria, and the First LORD of the ADMIRALTY read in consecutive order the telegrams received at the Admiralty since Tuesday. The story of the dig of truce was then communicated to their Lordships. The terms demanded by the Admiral were that the fort on the Isthmus as well as those command- ing the entrance to the harbour should be temporarily sur- rendered for the purpose of disarmament—which, however, had been partically effected by the fleet. These terms were refused, and the flag of truce struck. Upon a shot being fired the flag was hoisted again, and fire ceased, and had not "since been renewed. That morning information had been received of a terrible conflagration, the abandonment of the forts, and the withdrawal of the entire garrison under flag of truce, leaving convicts to pillage and fire the town. There was no reason to suppose that the con- flagration arose from the tire of our ships. The Secretary to the Admiral had telegraphed that the wounded were doing well, and that nothing certain was known as to the Khedive, but it was believed that he was at Ramleh, six miles to the east of Alexandria.—The Marquis of SAMS- EurRY inquired if the Government were prevented by any diplomatic arrangement from landing troops for the purpose of occupying and maintaining order in Alexandria, and was told by Earl GRANVILLE that he did not think we should be debarred from taking eteps•in that direction, and that in- structioaa bad been given as to the landing of troops.—The FOREIGN SECRETARY added that the exceptional measures taken by the Admiral in self-defence were quite separate from the general question of restoring order in Egypt, which was the subject of the Conference. 4

'Reams alleged on the part of the plaintiff that he had sustained' permanent injury to the hip, and would never again be able to work at his trade. The Company paid £l2O into Courtaand called several medical men practising at Carnarvorefeettiniog, and Portmadoc to prove that the plaintiff, a young man 24 years old, was merely shamming, and that irelaad sustained no permanent or serious injury. His late' landlady, with whom he had quarrelled,nwore that when in the house he could walk well, and that be told her he wan-putting it on to get more money. The jury eeturned a verdiot for the company. ANOTHER CHARGE OF MIIIDER ON A FISHING SMACK.— On Wednesday, at Hull, Edward Wheatfield, second hand on board the fishing smack:Gleaner, was charged with the murder of the cook, a boy named Peter Huge, on the high seas, on the 24th of Febreary last. The evidence of William Charles Leake, one of the smack bands, showed that on the voyage of the Gleaner from the 11th to the 24th February, the prisoner systematically ill-used the boy in a most oar- barons manner, frequently beating him unmercifully, knock- ing him down, and jumping on him, and also prevented him getting proper food. On two occasions, one of which was in the middle of the night, he made the lad strip naked on the deck and carry a bucket of water on his head, back- wards and forwards until he was exhausted. Between four and five on the morning of tbe 24th he dragged the lad out of his bunk, and shortly afterwards called up the crew,' saying he had fallen overboard. He was remanded for eight days. POLITICS UNDEL DIFFICULTIES.—A great :meeting at which 10,000 people were present, was held on Tuesday in Paradise-square, Sheffield. The Conservatives called the meeting to protest against the action of the Government in Ireland and Egypt, but the 'Liberals were also present in great force and proposed an amendment. Mr. H. E. Watson presided, and on one side of the platform were the leading, members of the Conservative party, and on the other the more prominent 'Liberals of the town. Mr. A. Thomas moved: "That this meeting expresses its indignation at the demoralising policy of her 'Majesty's Ministers in relation to Irelarri, and calls on the Houses of Parliament to reject the clauses in the Irish Arrears Bill which would 'impose upon British taxpayers the payment of the rents dishonestly withheld by Irish tenants and rendered irrecoverable by the weakness of the Government." The resolution was seconded bee Mr. Tandy. Alderman Leader moved an amendment "That this meeting declares its unswerving confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and calls upon all Liberal members of Parlia- ment to persevere in the policy approved by the country at the last election." The amendment was seconded by Mrell. J. Wilson. The vote was then taken, and the chairman de- clared Ole resolution against the Government carried. FATAL Botts': ExeLosioN.—On Wednesday afternoon, about ten minutes to one, while a young man named Prince Saunders was minding a* engine and boiler at the quarry of Messrs. Henry Heys and Co., which is situated on the 'kill side above Facit, Rochdale, the boiler exploded, and the shed in which it stood was thrown into ruins. Saunders was found buried' in the debris, and on being removed to -his home, Heys Buildings, Millgate, it was seen that there'seas no hope of his recovery. One of his ankles was broken and his foot severely-crushed. His face and arms were -scalded and he had received a dangerous wound under one of his arms. He died in about an hour after the accident. The boiler was a small horizontal one, which worked an engine used for dragging-up rock from the quarry. Messrs. 'Hayes had worked the boiler for the last five or six years, and they purchased it from a firm in Oldham when it was compara- tively new. In November last it was examined and repairedo and was thought to be in a good condition. The force of ; the explosion tore it right in two, and threw one half a tance of about 50 yards. About 20 men were working in the quarry at the time, about 20 yards from the shed, but for- tunately escaped injury. SPENDING THE HONEYMOON IN PRlSON.—Fortimately, it is not oftsn that a newly-married couple have the mis- fortune to spend the first night of the honeymoon in a ;police cell, or rather in separate police cells, but this was the unhappy lot of Mr. Henry Glainster and his young wife, who got married on Monday, and subsequently adjourned to the house of the bride's mother in Prince's-terrace, Aigburtinstreet, Liverpool, where uproarious festivities were indulged in. The mother partook too freely of drink, and in the fulness of her joy smashed a neighbour's windows and blackened his eye, and rumour even says that the bride's conduct was not beyond reproach. The rejoicings were suddenly interrupted by the appearance of a constable on the scene to convey the mother to the police station:; but the newly-wedded pair could not permit such an out- rage upon their joy, and by a well directed simultaneous attack they succeeded in rescuing the lady from the officer's grasp. Subsequently, however, the bride and bridegroom were themselves arrested, and conveyed to bridewell, where regardless of the injunction against putting man and wife asunder, they were placed in generate cells, there to remain until they could be brought before Mr. Clarke Aspinall. The genial coroner's good nature would not permit him to inflict further penalty upon the bride, who was discharged, but the groom was ordered to pay ,103. and costs on pain of the terrible alternative of seven day's imprisonment. Let no hope that the rine was paid. ATTEMPT TO SWINDLE LORD DALHOUSIE : A BEGGING- LETTER IMPOSTER.--AI the Bow-street (London) Police• court, on Saturday, John Smith, aNase Black, was charged •with obtaining charitable contributions by means of false pretences. It appeared that in March last the prisoner wrote to Lord Dalhousie, in Carlton-gardens,-representing himself as a relative of a family named Black, residing atßrechin, Forfarshire. He signed the letter "Alexander Black." He was seen by his lordship, to whom he repeated the represen- tations made, and believing them to be true Lord Dalhousie advanced tim a sovereiga. The next day his lordship went to Scotland, saw a member of the Black family, and received a positive denial of all letowledge of the prisoner. His lordship at once communicated with his private secretary, Mr.Taylor,whe subsequently had an interview with the pri- soner in the preeence of Detective-Inspector Langrish, of Scotlandevard. The prisoner was arrested by that officer, and upon being searched a paper with a list of the names of several noblemen was foetid in his possession. In- quiries' reeulted in the discovery of other victims, one being the Earl of Strathmore, to whom he wrote in the name of Armstrong. To Lord Aberdeen he represented that he was a native of Stonehaven, Scotland, and had coma to London some months ago in search of work. Lord Aber- deen advanced him a sovereign to pay his rent, and also gave him the desired letter. A few days afterwards he called again, and represented that the Scottish Corporation had favourably entertained his application, and would sub- sequently make some provision for his return, but, as he had been unable to redeem his tools, as the sovereign had been used for the rent, he applied to his lordship for a further sum of 103. This was given to him. He was now sen- tenced to a term of three months' imprieenment as a rogue and yagabond. THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW AT READING. The Royal Agricultural Society's show at Reading openeA on Monday in fine weather, the implement department havieg been opened on Saturday. The yard stands on seven acres of high and very gravelly soil, about a mile from the rail- way station, with good roads to it, and easy communication from the town. The town is gaily decorated for the occa- sion. The entries are more numerous than at any show since 1879, there being 239 for horses, 598 for cattle, 442 for sheep, and 188 for pigs. A novel feature in this year's show will be the awarding of prizes for market gardens and for garden produce. Amongst the visitors were the Nawah of Hyderabad, the Dukes of Richmond, of Bedford, and of Manchester, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, dic. There was a good show of horses, especially in the agricultural classes. In the cattle classes the Channel Island breeds were notably fine, and shorthorn bulls made a very fair display. Sheep formed a very excellent section, especially Southdowns and Shrop- shire.—The second day of the show was (like the first day) as regards the number of visitors a failure. The day was very wet and the attendance was only about half of that at the Derby show. At the meeting of the Council the Duke of Richmond and Gordon was elected President for the en- suing year. The Prince of Wales paid a visit on 'Wednes- day to the show, His Royal Highness was presented on his arrival with an address from the Mayor and Corporation. In reply, the Prince expressed his pleasure at revisiting that ancient and loyal borough. Following the example ef his father, he had taken a great interest in the progress of agri- culture, and lost no opportunity of encouraging its pursuit both by his example and presence. The Prince afterwards inspected the show ground and exhibits, and was every- where received in the most enthusiastic manner. He subse- quently lunched with the Council. During the day a num- ber of the Society's medals were awarded in the implement classes, The weather being fine, there was an enormous attendanee of the public.

div.head: L7XAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 15, 1882. THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXANDRIA.
div.p: THE L7XAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 15, 1882. THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALEXANDRIA.
War Oflice order were issue a on ThursdAl' for the whole of the First Army Corps to at.,,nce complAtTheir equipment and to make all the arrangeraents nctevAry for moving at the shortest notice.

At the Stoke-upon-Trent Ilcatkl of Guardians on Wednes- day afternoon the )vorkhouse master reported that he had been compelled tr., birch seven of the workhouse school boys for their incoalgible condect. Their offence was that in order to escape school ,daties they filled their eyes full of soap, thus almost blinding themselves for some hours and by that ineans accompilished their idle purposes. About half-rtiast three on Wednesday morning the body of Watson Buckley, a boy sixteen years old, was found in a pit of water off Sholver-lane, Oldham. The deceased has been subje,A to fits, and it is conjectured that when playing near the pat he AWLS seized with a fit and fell in. He was eoen near the vine about nine o'clock on Wednesday night. On Wednesday night an important question was intro- duced at the meeting of the Industrial Co-operative Society, Oldham. in the early days of limited companies, the society took out shares and lent money, but it appears that limited,companies deny the right of the representatives of the sockty to act as ordinary shareholders. In one large concern the society holds a large number of shares, and it was resolved to sell them.

At Bolton, on Thursday, Robert Stewart, draper, Deans- gate, was charged with a breach of the Workshops' Act. On the' inspector of factories, Mr. H. Brewer, visiting the defen- dant's shop on two or three occasions he found a girl em- ployed without a school certificate, and other assistants working at illegal hours. The defendant refused to answer 'the questions of the inspector, and advised the hands not to sign the usual declarations. He was convicted of obstruc- tion, drc., and fined £6 1,65. At Oldham, on Thursday, James Duff was committed for trial for tenderinc, counterfeit coin. The prisoner went to a beerhouse and tendered a base half-sovereign. At Victoria Station, Manchester, he tendered a bad half-sovereign, an& on other cocasiens had tendered a base lorin and a bane half-crown in Oldham. A silversmith stated that the whole of the coins were Britannia metal. John Marr, charged with being implicated, was discharged. On Wednesday night, John Rydall, a student, was on duty at the Rotunda ,Hospital, Dublin, when Dr. Horne, who was turning to leave the room, heard a muffled report and saw Mr. Rydall fall, exclaiming, "I am shot." It was found that a bullet had entered the right groin, death ensuing from hemorrhage in half-an-hour. A pistol was discovered in deceased's waistcoat pocket, having, it is sup- posed, gone off accidentally, and so caused his death. Robert Marshall, who was killed at the bombardment of Alexandria, en Tuesday, is a native of Darwen, where his widowed mother now resides. He joined the Royal Navy in 1870, and was sent on the training ship Impregnable, at Devonport. In 1876, he went on board the Imogene, a gunboat, and afterwards on Sir John Hay's flagship Mino- t tur. Lc the Russo-Turkish war he went upthe Dardanelles with the British fleet, and took part in planting the British flag on the island of Cyprus on the acquisition of that island by England. His last letter is dated June 4th, from Alexandria. Singular to relate it arrived on the morning subsequent to his death. Deceased was twenty-four years O age. SHOCKING A CCIDENT.—On Tuesday evening Miss E. Ell- wood, an assistant in Mr. tireenall's music .warehouse at Lancaster, was about to visit Morecambe, after business holm, with a friend. They arrived on the Midland plat- form ijust as the 7-20 train was moving out of the station, and deceased, in attempting to enter a carriage, missed her hold of the door handle, and fell on the line. The wheels passed over her neck and one arm, causing instantaneous death, and nearly severing her head from her body. Her friend-was trying to get tickets at the booking office when the accident occurred. Deceased was about 2I years of age, and not long ago she lost a brother by drowning.

WANTING TO HANG HIMSELF: SCENE IN A POLICE Comm—At the Chester County Police-court, on Saturday, a tramp named George Fidler, who had been at the Chester Union Workhouse, was charged with having torn up his clothes, at that institution on the 3rd inst. The prisoner, it appeared, had acted like a maniac, shouting, cutting •oaperand tearing his clothes to pieces. fie,was sentenced to seventeen days' imprisonment, with hard labour. On hearing the sentence he called wildly for- " a rope that he might harg himself," and as he was bang removed from the dock he kept shouting "Let me hang 'myself." The magistrates ordered that the attention of the, medical officer of the prison should be called to the state of the prisoner's rosind.

THE TETON COLLIERY ACCIDENT: TEC ONE.RGE AGAINST THE HON. G. E. TREVOR—At Oswestry dr-once Court, on Thursday, the Hon. George Edwin Hill Trevor and John Williams were charged with manslaughter—the former as agent, and the latter as manager, of Ifton Colliery. A boy named JohE Kynaston was killed by a fall of roof while working in the mine. It was stated in evidence that the manager was not cerficated, and that no person was left in charge at the top of the pit. The magistrates dismissed the charge, holding the accused were not ,directly culpable. They both stand committed upon the toroner's,watrant to the next Shropshire Assiza.
