O. 176 of te32, specially issued June '2B, is cancelled, and the manmuvres therein referred to will not take,place. 2. The battalions of militia under orders for 'Aldershot in connection with the manoeuvres, will proceed to the caturras previously arranged. 3. All arrangements for the attendance of volunteers at.Aldershot between August Mand 19 twerill with the regular, troops will hold good if they still,wish to attend. If any volunteer corps wishes to withdraw its appli- cation to attend, a notification to that effect should be at once made to thecAdjutant-General. SUPPOSED SUICIDE OF A CLERGTMiN.—.OI Thursday morning the hody.of the Rev. Abraham Smith, aged fifty- ,five years, principal .of the Collegiate School, Huddersfield; and curate-in-charge of St. Thomas's, Bradley,'Euddersfield,, was found in a lock of the canal at Fieldhouse, near Messrs.' Edward Brooke arnieCon's Pottery Works. Two men saw 'Mr. Smith welkin t about on the canal bank, and,he seemed Leo be watching them; and, thinking that he was about to eio something, they .concealed themselves. On looking ngain in a few minutes they missed him, and on .feoing to tile lock they saw that he was in it. They opened the lock, let him through, and got him out, but he was quite dead. 'His body was remove.d. to his home. He had been depeassed and troubled with sleepleeeness for some time past. THE QUEEN'S REFUSAL OF A BOUQUET.—The Middlesex District Council of Juvenile GoodTemplars having thanked Her Majesty for having reftesed to accept a bouquet from Ihe Monte Carl gambling-house while she was staying at 'Men- tone, the following reply has been received : Windsor Castle, June 26,.1-SB'2.—Sir,—l have to acknowledge the receipt of your letter audits enclosure, which I would have had much pleasure in laving-hcfsre the Queen, but regret that I am unable to do so in its present form, as anacceptance of 'the memorial would be an acknowledgment that the statements were accurate. Although the :„Qpeen would have •refused a bouquet had it been sent by tile manager of the Casino at Monaco, no such b iuquet was se,nt. and no such refusal was therefore ever given. While the Queen was at Mentonc, the gardener :at the Casino Gardens did send Her Majesty a bouquet, as it turned out afterwards, without the knowledge of his employers. The Queen considers it advisable to decline to accept any present from any of the officials connected with the establishment, for fear that such an .r.cceptance might be mis- understood: consequently the bouquet was refused —I am, sir, your obedient servant, HENRY F. Pomoracr. About ten clays ago a Presbyterian minister diseppeared from a town in Ireland, without giving any satisfactory reason for his absence. At the same time a young lady of his acquaintance, daughter of a well-to-do gentleman in the , district, was tniesed from home, and though there is a wide ' disparity between their ages, the clergyman having seen considerable more than seventy summers, and the lady only twenty-one, the 'friends had too good a reason to suppose that they had left together with a purpose of marriage. They were traced to Glasgow, and the case was put into the bands of a privata detective, Knowles. The officer dis- covered that the couple had taken lodgings in a.quiet street in the west-end of Glasgow, and that they proposed getting married. On Wednesday, a friend of the family, a well- known clergyman in the city, had an, interview with the old gentleman and his fair inamorata, and endeavoured to dissuade them from their purpose. But the young lady was not to be convinced, and declared she would marry her venerable admirer in spite of all opposition. STRANGE BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—Sheriff Lees' Glasgow, has just issued an interlocutor in an action raised by Eliztbeth Allan, Old Basin House, Possil-road, against Robert Aitkin, clerk, 19, Windsor-street, Glasgow. in which pursuer claimed £5OO as damtges for breach of promise of marriage. His lordship finds that the defendant promised to marry the pursuer, but that he has broken that Promise vlithout adequate cause, and now refuses to marry her; that in these circumstances she is entitled to a solatium and damages from the defendant. He assessed the sum to be paid to her at £5O, and decerns accordingly. In a note the sheriff-substitute says the question is solely and purely, was the defender justified in receding from his promise to marry the pursuer on finding that she Was illegitimate? On this Point his lordship can find no authority in Scotch or Eng- lish law. As a rule, the cases that a court would sustain as justifying a man in breaking a promise of marriage were faults or the woman's own, and not faults of her parents. There might be circumstances in which such a cause would be held sufficient, and there might occur cases in which one intending spouse would be held to have sufficient cause to break an engagement to marry on discovering that the other contracting party was of illegitimate birth; but in the circumstances of the present case Sheriff Lees could not say he saw such cause, and he thought it would be cruel to hold otherwise.

THE COPES OF DURHAM CATHEDRAL.—The copes be- longing to the Church are still preserved at Durham. Mr. Ornsby says in his "Sketches of Durham" (1846) that they are kept in a closet with glass doors which faces the entrances to the Cathedral Library. " They were used," he continues, "in the Cathedral Of Durham, in accordance with the XXIV. Canon, at the administration of the Holy Communion within the last seventy years. Bishop War- burton, who held a prebendal stall here until his death in 1799, was the first who laid them aside. His temper, which was none of the best, was wont to get uncommonly ruffled by the high collar of the cope getting between his neck and his full-bottomed wig. At last, in a fit of more than ordinary irritation, he threw aside the cope, and vowed he would never wear it again. After this they were gradually laid aside by the other prebendaries, and at last fell into total disuetude. They are curious specimens of the loom and needle of former days, some of them, in all , probability, having been in existence two centuries before I the Dissolution. The one of crimson silk, on which is worked David holding the head of Goliath, was presented to the Church by Charles L"

THE FORTS DESTROYED. Tut SUEZ CANAL SAVED. GREAT CONFLAGRATIONS. Since our last issue the seaward defences of Alexandria have been destroyed by the British fleet under Admiral Sey- mour. On Friday it was announced that the Egyptians had discontinued the arming of the forts, but on Sunday one of the light vessels which had been reconnoitering the coast discovered that more guns were being mounted. Incensed at this deliberate breach of faith, Sir Beauchamp Seymour prepared an ultimatum, in which he gave the Egyptians 12 hours in which to evacuate the forts. If, the ultimatum stated, the demand was not complied with, the fleet would open fire ()lithe defences after a further period of twenty- four hours had elapsed. The French representative in com- mon with the Consuls General of other European Powers protested against the resort.to force. Sir B. Seymour in his reply suggested that the Consuls General should use their influence with the Commandant to induce him to act with sincerity, and pointed out that if they succeeded there would be no bombardment. "Mere written assurances," he said, "in whatever terms they may be expressed, are of little value in view of the interests cnnfided to me." He added: "I must point out that I do not propose and have never ex• pressed the intention of bombarding the town of Alexandria. Any operations, if rendered necessary, will be directed against the fortifications, and I therefore see no reason to fear the injury to private property of which you are appre- hensive. I must strictly adhere to the terms of my com- munication sent to the Mililary Commandant should the slightest attempt be made to renew offensive works. In any case twenty-four clear hours' notice shall be given." As the forts were not dismantled nor surrendered, Admiral Seymour intimated at four o'clock on Monday morning that in 24 hours he would bombard the fortifications, and the threat being still disregarded the following morning the British ironclads commenced to open fire. In a few hours most of the forts and earthworks were reduced to ruins through the effect of the shot or the explosion of their magazines. During the day a large number of telegrams were received from the Admiralty, the Foreign Office, the Eastern Tele- graph Company, and other sources, and from these tele- grams the materials for the following connected narrative of the bombardment were gathered : THE BRITISH FLEET. The first important operation of war in which the Eng- lish Fleet has been engaged for more than 25 years, and in- deed the first occasion on which the famous British ironzlads broadside, and turret ships have been put to the test of actual fighting, occurred on Tuesday at Alexandria. Eight iron- clads, supported by five gunboats, represented the effective English force. The ironclads were :—The Inflexible, 11,400 tons, turret ship, mounting four guns of 81 tons each, and carrying armour of from 16 to 24 inches; the Temeraire, 8,540 tons, mounting eight heavy guns, four of 25 tons each and four of 18 tons each, and carrying 8 and 10 inch armour; the Superb, "9,100 tons, mounting four 25 ton guns, and being protected by 10 to 12 inch armour; and the Sultan, 9290 tons, mounting eight 18 ton guns and four 12 ton guns, and carrying armour of from six to eight inches in thickness; the Alexandra (Admiral Beauchamp Seymour's flag ship), 9,490 tons, mounting two guns of 25 tons each and ten of 18 tons each, and bearing armour of eight to twelve inches; the Monarch, 8,320 tons, mounting four 25 ton guns and two of 61 tons each, and being armoured with from eight to ten inches of iron; the invincible, 6,010 tons, mounting ten 12 ton guns, and carrying eight to ten inches of armour; the Penelope, 4,470 tons, also mounting ten 12 ton guns, and carrying five to six inch armour. These eight powerful fighting ships were supported by the gunboats Beacon, Bittern, Cygnet, Condor, and Decoy. All the 13 vessels were fully manned, and ln addition to their heavy-armament most of them were fitted with torpedoes and machine guns of the modern Nor- denfeldt and Gaffing patterns. The whole fleet was under the command of Vice-Admiral Sir F. Beauchamp Paget Seymour, G.C.8., the flag-officer of the Mediterranean station,

there was not a single casualty on board any one of the five. Thus ended the first naval fight in which England has been engaged since the time of the Crimean War. Though we are not yet masters of Alexandria, and though the state- ment that the guns of the fleet command the railroad to Cairo requires confirmation, yet, with all its outer defences destroyed, Alexandria can scarcely be called a fortified town.

div.head: EGYPTIAN FORTS.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN FORTS.

The forts against which this naval force was -brought to bear have been to recently strengthened and enlarged that no precise idea cif the Egyptian strength can yet be formed. The fortifications, however, extend from Pharos Castle on the extreme east, to Marsa-el-Kanat and Marabout Island on the west. The chief fortifications between these two extreme points were Fort Ada on the northern point of the town, a long line of batteries extending from the east of the Ras-el-Tin Palate to the Lighthouse at the shore end of the great breakwater, and the row of forts bearing upon the outer harbour, and covering the road by which vessels must steam after passing the shore by way of either the Corvette Pass, the Bogiaaz'(Central) Pass,or the Marabout or Western Pass, to get inside the breakwater. The forts pre- sented an almost unbroken line of defences from Fort Tsale to the south-west of the landing- place to the fort and battery of Marsa-el-Kanat, situated just where the shore reaches away to the north. Then come the long stretch of low sandhills terminating in Chersonese Point, which was protected by Fort Adjemi and the guns of Marabout Island, covering more or less effectually the Man- bout Pass, with itstve or six fathoms of water. Besides these fortifications, the town was protected byFort Caffarelli or Napoleon, Fort. Cretin, and the fort which, from its posi- tion in the front of the ruins of Ptolemy's Palace, commands the east harbour or new port. There were, therefore, two distinct systems of defence—those which protected the new port and eastern town, and of which Forts Pharos and Ada were the principal:; and those which protected the entrance to the outer westem harbour.

div.head: ATTACK.
div.p: THE ATTACK.

Admiral Seymoue-s plan of attack consisted in dividing hi 3 vessels so as practicallrto simultaneously bombard the wiole of the Egyptian positions. The British seen-of-war stezmed into their allotted positions at five o'clock on Tues- day morning, all neutral vessels anchoring out of range. The, Alexandra, Sultan, and Superb steamed to the east. The first-named vessel opened ,fire on Fort Ras-el-Tin ; the Are was returned by the fort, and then in rapid .suc- cessien the British irenclads joined in the bombardment. The Manarch, Penelope, and Invincible engaged the forts guarding the western harbour. They went right inside aad fought close quarters, being supported by the Temeraire in their Leavy cannonade ipon Fort Meks. The Inflexible, from the great range of her 81-ton guns, was able to assist both the eastern and the western squadrons of the British Fleet; and, meantime, the gunboats were on the extreme: west engaging the Adjerni Fort and Marabout Island. From: the first thezttack was successful. The great power of the 1 4:aval guns, and the skilful way those guns were worked, .son took effect.

div.head: DEETRUCTIO3I OF THE FORTS.
div.p: DEETRUCTIO3I OF THE FORTS.

The Alexandka, Sultan, and Superb were continuously engaged with the forts along the northern front of the town from Fort Pharos to the Lighthouse, but the first Egyptian disaster occurred at the other end of the line of operations, Fort Mersa-el-Kanat being destroyed by the fire of the Mon- arch and Invincible about half-past eight in the morning, and blowing ,cp with a tremendous explosion. The gunboats were able to silence the Marabout Fort soon after eleven o'clock. It was evide at that great damage was being done to all the attacked positions, and when the Temeraire, anchoring in the Central Pass, aided in the direct .eanonade upon Fort Aides at a distance of 1 miles, the fate of the defensive work was sealed. The Temeraire did great execu- tion, while the Inflexible, from a longer range, kept up a good fire, assisting the closer bombard nent by the batteries of the Monarch, Invincible, and Penelope. On the other band, the reply from the forts was feeble and ill-directed, the missiles either failing short of the ships or flying above the mast heads.

div.head: LANDING A PARTY OF SAILORS.
div.p: LANDING A PARTY OF SAILORS.

Fort Meks was unable to withstasd the combined attack from the gunboats. After silencing the Marabout, the gun- boats ran close in and shelled l‘leks, which was captured by a landing party and thrown into ruins. On the west the fleet had thus completely succeeded, and on the east the force assaulting Fort Ada was now strengthened by the In- flexible. This vessel brought the heavy guns to bear upon the fort, the whole face of which was blown away by the shot from the 81-tonners. About 1-15 the magazine of Fort Ada blew up, and no further danger was to be apprehended from that part of the defences. Fort Pharos and the ad- Sicent batteries, however, still held out, so the Inflexible and the Temeraire, the most powerful vessels in the fleet, turned the full force of their fire upon these positions, and by four o'clock in the afternoon the fort and batteries were silenced and laid in ruins. Of the positions attacked and still capable of fighting there only remained the harbour forts, and upon these the Monarch and other vessels of the fleet directed their batteries, until at balf-past five in the afternoon the firing ceased for the day. The Admiralty telegram conveying thie la4t inti illation says the forte were silenced.

div.head: LOSSES.
div.p: THE LOSSES.

The Egyptian losses C-at-trnoT,-o-f-c-Oti-rse, be yet estimated, but they must have been heavy. The English losses were five men killed and twenty-seven wounded. The five men killed belonged—two to the Sultan, and one each to the Alexandra, Superb, and Inflexible. The twenty-seven wounded belonged—eight to the Penelope, seven to the Sultan, six to the Invincible, three to the Alexandra, two to the Inflexible, and oae to the Superb. RESULTS OF THE FIGHTING.

The general result of the first day's fighting seems to be that the whole of the outer defences of Alexandria were rendered useless, and that, in fact, the fortifications protecting the approaches to the town were laid in ruins. The great fact in connection with Tuesday's ergagement is that, though there were several hours' continuous firing, and many forts were blown in pieces, no injury of any impor- tance was received by any one of the English ships. This fact is virtually certain, for Admiral Seymour, tele- graphing at twenty minutes t eight o'clock, and giving the list of killed and wounded, does not in any way refer to injuries to his ships. A few other facts in connection with the engagement deserve to be mentioned. Not one of the telegrams says anything about torpedoes, and it may almost be taken for granted that the Egyptians had neither the means nor the opportunity of using these deadly engines of modern war- fare. Fire gunboats were engaged, not merely as supports, but actually in serious fighting at Marabout and Meks, yet

div.head: ANOTHER ACCOUNT.
div.p: ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

Another account of the bombardment says :—ln the first half-hour many of the more exposed guns were dismounted and others were abandoned by the native gunners, but from the more protected forts the artillery duel was kept up with little diminution of spirit. Just one hour after the time of opening fire a well-directed shell from the Invincible caused the magazine in the newly-eonstructed fort of Marsa-el- Kanat to explode with a mighty roar, scattering death and destruction in all directions. From this time the fire of the enemy perceptibly slackened as gun after gun was dis- mounted. The Monarch, with her well-directed 25-ton guns, pitched shell after shell into the Lighthouse Fort until the work seemed a ruin. Then, turning her attention to Fort Napoleon, the Monarch gave the native gunners little respite, the return fire becoming more and more inter- mittent, while the guns from Her Majesty's ships rendered it too hot to live near the forts unless well protected. The Monarch formed the advance of the Fleet on the west, the ships lying around Alexandria in the shape of a horse shoe, and on the extreme east the Superb and the Sultan were hotly engaged with Forts Pharos and Ada. Fort Pharos soon exhibited signs of the heavy cannonade, breaches in the walls and dismounted guns being observable. Fort Ada maintained an obstinate fire for hours, having one fairly well-handled gun until about one o'clock, when the Inflexible having come into position, the magazine exploded, and the guns on the penin- sula were all silenced. Fort Pharos, however, maintained the fight. _ Then the gunboats boldly pushed forward into the shallow waters, planting a shot wheresoever the enemy continued to reply, until only the shattered forts kept up the fire. The smoke over the shore defences cleared away and revealed the fearful execution our guns had wrought. Some works were just a heap of ruins, Lilt still the British ironclads planted shot and shell wherever a shelter remained for an Egyptian gun, and it appears as though the admiral has determined to destroy every vestige of a defensive work.

div.head: DETAILS OF CASUALTIES.
div.p: DETAILS OF CASUALTIES.

The following is a list of the casualties in the fleet : KILLED: William Shannon, carpenter, Inflexible; Walter Fisher, A.B. Alexandra; Charles Collins, A. 8., and Robert Marshall, A. 8., Sultan; George M'Claine, gunner, R.M.A., Superb: DANGEROUSLY WOUNDED: Henry Dawson, leading sea- man, Levi bides, boy, and 41fred Jackson, boy, Penelope. SEVERELY WOUNDED: Lieutenant Jackson, Inflexible ; John Myers, A. 8., Alexandra; James Dexter' boy, Sultan; Redmond M`Guire, boy, Invincible ; John Wheadon, leading seaman, and William Woon, captain of the mast, Penelope WOUNDED SLIGHrLY: William Houghton, private, R.M., Inflexible; Thomas Palmer, captain of forecastle, and George Talbot, private R. 111., Alexandra; Albert Jutson, A. 8., James M'Carthy, A. 8., Robert Pacey, A. 8., James Tussell, A. 8., Thomas Poigndestre, A. 8., Joseph Gomes, boatswain's mate, Samuel Fuller, leading seaman, and Geo. Webb, ship's corporal, Sultan; Mr. William Lumsden, mid- shipman, Chaseira, stoker, John Yolland, A. 8., John Gill, ordinary seaman, and J. W. Moore private R.M., In- vincible; Lieutenant Davies, William Lee, A. 8., and Wm. M. Canalley, A. 8., Penelope. WEDNESDAY'S OPERATIONS. BURIAL OF THE

div.head: DEAD.
div.p: DEAD.

After the fierce fighting and terrible havoc of Tuesday, Alexandria and its shattered defences were quiet enough on Wednesday. In place of the continuous cannonade, there were only at the most half-a-dozen shots. The brisk rattle of the Nordenfeldts and Gatlings, the sharp reports of the light ordnance and the bursting shells, the appalling din of the electric broadsides, and the grandly sullen thunder of the gigantic Woolwich guns, gave place to an almost un- natural quietude; and the great British ironclads that had on Tuesday proved so sternly their immense power lay peacefully rolling in the heavy ground swell, half obscured from each other and the shore by the heavy mist that hung over the wounded and still menaced the maritime capital of Egypt. -I.Co doubt the British captains were glad of an op- portunity to rest and repair damages after an engagement which Mr. Gladstone has called a measure of safety and security to British Subjects and Europeans throughout the whole of the East; a measure rendered necessary by the unavenged massacre at Alexandria, and by the threatened safety of our fleet; a measure unselfishly carried out with so much honour to England and the British arms. The solemn ceremony of burying the men killed in action was performed early on Wednesday morning, the ensigns of the entire fleet flying half-mast high as the bodies were com- mitted to the sea. Fortunately, the damage to the vessels proves to have been very slight, and not to have in any way interfered with their fighting powers. The Sultan and Superb were both shot through the funnel, and the former's mainmast was also pierced by a cannon ball. The hulls of the Alexandra and Superb showed traces of having been under fire, while the swinging boats of the turret ram In- flexible were damaged. In no case, however, was an English vessel a whit less formidable as a destructive engine of war, or less safe for a home for a crew, after the fight than she was before going into action. This was surprising; for not only did the giants of the fleet expose themselves to the fire of the forts and shore batteries, but the unarmoured and lightly armoured runboats were also continually within ran. The Inflexible, while she was demolishing the northern forts, was for hours the object at which the gun- ners of Ras-el-Tin and the Harbette batteries directed their fire. It was upon these particular batteries that the only shots fired on Wednesday were directed. They were built in front of the Harem Palace, which was burning all night, and was still on fire when the morning broke. The Inflexible and Temeraire each fired three shells into the batteries, but there was no respense. Some accounts say a gun, which had during the night been mounted or remounted on a Moncreiffe carriage, was dismantled by the fire of the guns, but, whether that be so or not, the batteries did not reply, and indeed, all through the day, no act of hostility was committed by the defenders of the town. No doubt but for the wind and the puzzling haze Admiral Seymour would have completed the demoli- tion of the ruined forts and batteries, and rendered them not only incapable of present mischief but beyond repair, the earthworks levelled, and the cannon either fully spiked or blown to pieces. A telegram I furnished to the Press Asso- ciation, as many other telegrams were furnished on Wednes- day, by the courtesy of the Eastern Telegraph Company, states that just as the British man-of-war Achilles, 9,521 tons, armour-plated, and mounting 16 guns, was sighted steaming towards the 'fleet to reinforce it, the signal was given " cease firing." The cause of the cessation of the operations of the Inflexible and Terneraire against the northern forts was the hoisting of a flag of truce over the Egyptian Arsenal, which is situated just inside the western :harbour, E.N.E. of the Mole Lighthouse. A Eritish Admiralty despatch says that when this dig of truce was discerned one of the gunboats of the fleet proceeded, also under a white flags to communicate. The gunboat remained some time, and returned to Amin! Seymour, brit the result of the negotiations was not known. The Turkish ships, as the swell' increased, were got under weigh for safety. A late telegram from the Eastern Telegraph Company says that the Turkish despatch boat which brought the last envoy from Stamboul was anchored off the Viceroy's palace at Ramleh. This message goes on to say that several large fires have broken out in several parts of Alexandria, that the flag of truce was still flying, that there had been no communication between the steamer Chiltern and the fleet, and that there was a heavy sea on, but no fears of the cables parting. These facts were the latest known at London at the time this report was written—nine p.m. To sum up the day's proceedings is not a difficult task. There has been no , firing, and no further attempt at resistance has been made by the Egyptians. It meet not, however, be concluded that , the flag of truce necessarily means the surrender of the ' enemy—which enemy we are told by the Prime Minister is not the people of Egypt, but those who have established a system of military violence against the will, not less than against the interest, of the people of Egypt. A Standard telegram announces that Her Majesty the Queen has telegraphed for news as to the progress of her wounded sailors. The storeship Humber had arrived with ammunition for the fleet.

THE CONFERENCE AND THE BOMBARDMENT. The Vienna Presse says :—We learn from the best in- formed diplomatic sources that the Powers are agreed that the bombardment of the forts at Alexandria should be re- garded as an incident provoked by the local situation and particularly by considerations for the safety of the British fleet, and that this incident is not calculated to disturb the European entente or interrupt the labours of the Conferene6. If England remains faithful to her declarations, regards her action as terminated with the disarming of the forts, and beyond this takes no further step, the Conference will shortly resume its labours, and address to the Porte the collective invitation already resolved upon to take part in the delibera- tions. At present all the Powers have not given their assent to this step, but it is pretty confidently expected to be re- ceived within the next few days.

The Khedive's yacht was sunk in the harbour, and a por- tion of his Palace is in ruins from the bombardment. Of His Highness's fate no news has been received. A considerable sensation was excited by the news that Admiral Seymour had prohibited merchant vessels from entering the Suez Canal during the bombardment of the Alexandria Forts. M. Victor de Lesseps has sent in a formal protest against the order. The Porte has also pro- tested against the bombardment, on the ground that " order " had been re-established in Egypt. The War Office and the Admiralty are both putting much pressure for immediate consignments upon hardware manu- facturers in the Birmingham and Wolverhampton districts, I who are under contract to supply Government stores. On Tuesday telegrams were received by certain of the firms asking for all urgency to be used in execution because of , the crisis in the East. Additional orders have likewise been received this week from both departments for culinary utensils, and shipping tackle for despatch to Woolwich and to Malta. Manufacturers are doing their best to comply with the demands. In the Parliamentary Lobby, as well as in the clubs, hotels, and other resorts of a more or less public character, the bombardment formed the chief topic of conversation. In the House of Commons itself the committee discussion upon the Irish Arrears Bill continued, but the interest of that sub- ject was for the time eclipsed by the stirring events at Alexandria. Several of the telegrams read by Mr. Camp- bell-Bannerman had already been published. Copies of each official telegram were instantly despatched by Royal corn-

mind to the Queen and the Prince of Wales. Duplicates were also placed in the waiting-room at the Admiralty, Whitehall, for the inspection of visitors, in order to save tFie time of the already occupied officials from being unduly taken "up in answering enquiries. As early as half past four on Tuesday morning the resi- dent officers at the Admiralty,Whitehall, received a telegram from the fleet at Alexandria, but it was merely a prelimi- nary announcement that the time of grace bad expired, and the bombardment of the forts was about to commence. The news that the opening shot had been fired reached Sir A. Cooper Air, the First Sea-Lord, before seven o'clock (Eng- lish time), and within an hour messengers were despatched with the intelligence to the members of the Government, to the various public offices, and to the "usual channels of in- formation." Lord Northbrook arrived early, and before the regular hour for business was in consultation with the other Lords of the Admiralty, Vice-Admiral Lord John Hay, Rear-Admiral Anthony Hiley Hoskins, Sir Thomas Brassey, M.P., Admiral Brandreth (Controller of the Navy), and Mr. Stuart Rendel, being all present. There were likewise in attendance Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, M.P., Secretary to the Admiralty; Captain George Tryon, Naval Secretary; Ad- miral Sir William Mends, Director of Transports; Mr. Willis, Accountant-General; Mr. J. Collert, Director of Contracts ; Mr. M. L. M‘Hardy, Director of Stores; Mr. S. S. Lewes, Director of Victualing ; Mr. John Watt Reid, Director- General of the Medical Department; Major-General Charles Pasley, Royal Engineers, Director of Naval Engineering; and other officers.

In some quarters a little disappointment was expressed that the action of the fleet, sharp and decisive as it had been, was not so short as had been anticipated. Many per- sons seemed to suppose that when once fire was opened from the British Squadron, the destruction of all the forts would be the work of only half an hour. Over sanguine as was this view, there was no misgiving whatever in any quarter as to the early and complete success of the imme- diate object with which the naval preparations have been undertaken. The bombardment excited the more interest on account of the long period which had passed since the British fleet was engaged in warfare. Except the casual and comparatively unimportant encounter between the Shah and the Peruvian ram Huascar, in the Pacific, two or three years ago, the British war vessels have not been engaged as they are now since the Crimea, when they had, as on the present occasion, the task of bombarding forts.

LATER DETAILS. A telegram from the-harbour of Alexandria, at 9-48 a.m. on Thursday, says:—The Egyptian army is greatly de- moralised, and in full retreat towards the interior. The European quarter of the town, including the Exchange and Telegraph Office, is utterly destroyed. The city has been set on fire by released convicts, who have committed horrible atrocities. The Egyptians made use of the flag of truce merely to enable the troops to withdraw from the town. The Helicon is now alongstde the Chiltern, which is crowded with survivors who fought their way to the beach, whence they were taken off by the boats of the fleet. They repor having passed a dreadful night, defending themselves des- perately. One hundred Europeans and other Christians in the Ottoman Bank and adjoining buildings were brutally massacred. Part of the fleet is now leaving for Port Said. The Turkish despatch boat is still anchored off the Ramleh Palace. The whereabouts of the Khedive is unknown. The telegraph ship Chiltern has been ordered to take up a posi- tion nearer shore. Communication is still kept up with Malta and Cyprus. Telegraphing at 8-20 on Thursday morning, the Daily News correspondent says :—Although the detached portion of the Ras-el-Tin Palace is still burning, it is thought that the main building will not be destroyed. Two large fires are raging in Alexandria, and it is feared that this is the com- mencement of incendiarism, which may be accompanied by loot and pillage. There is no communication whatever with the town, and it is thus impossible to know what is going on; but the Arabs probably mistake the silence of the big guns to-day, and are committing all manner of excesses. Although the negotiations which the flag of truce gate rise to yesterday morning fell through, and notice was given that the bombardment would recommence, the flag of truce was kept flying all day, and no operations were begun. At five o'clock the Helicon sent to Ras-el-Tin for explanations, and the flag is now down. The Superb, Temeraire, Achilles, and Inflexible are in position, and ready to recommence bombardment this morning. The fires alluded to are burning and spreading fearfully, and it seems that nothing will prevent a large portion of the city being reduced to cinders. The Bedouins in thousands are looting. The soldiers have evacuated the town. There are no Ministers or officials to be found. The in-shore squadron will proceed up the harbour at dawn. At half-past four orders came from the Invincible for the ships to remain where they are, and not to move to Alexandria. The Consul-General and Sir Auckland Colvin are going off to the Invincible to consult with Admiral Seymour on the situation.

The St2nclard's special correspondent on board H.M.S.. Invincible, telegraphed at eight a.m., on Thursday morning: —Alexandria is abandoned by the Egyptians, the whole population, civil and military, having withdrawn. The entire European quarter, including the Grand Square, has been burnt. Last evening the Helicon, which had gone in to inquire the meaning of the fltg of truce, found no one on board the Mahroussa or in the Arsenal. Unable to open communicotion with the enemy the Helicon returned with the news to the Admiral. The great fires in the city con- tinued to extend. The Admiral determined to discover what was passing there. First-Lieutenant Forsyth took the steam pinnance on shore. I received permission to accom- pany the reconnoitring party. Upon reaching the shore, Mr Ross, purveyor to the fleet, who was well acquainted with the town, landed, and with great courage proceeded for a considerable distance. He found that all was perfectly silent save the roar and crackle of the flames and the sound of falling beams and walls, and that Alexandria was wholly destroyed. It is clear that Arabi withdrew his troops under cover of the flag of truce, and is no doubt con- centrated in the neighbourhood—to oppose our advance— with the troops and the entire male popnlation of Alexan- dria. The Invincible is now going inside the harbour to make a complete reconnaissance. The work of the ships is over and any further action must be on shore. The whole of the forts were found to be abandoned at daylight. The Admiral telegraphed to the fleet not to open fire, as the place was evacuated by the enemy. Half the town is wrapped in flames, and a dense cloud of smoke hangs over it. The fate of the Europeans and Christiana who had remained in the city is unknown. A landing force will take place to in- vestigate the general condition, and render aid if possible. The Chiltern has received orders to prepare to change her position and come in nearer. Telegraphic communication will therefore probably be suspended for three or four hours. OFFICIAL REPORT. The following has been received by the Admiralty from Sir Beauchamp Seymour:— ALEX iNDRIA, Thursday Morning, 9-21—Immense con- flagration in Alexandria last night. Forts apparently abandoned, and entire garrison withdrawn under flag of truce., leaving Bedouins to pillage and fire the town. The Invincible, Monarch, Penelope, and the gunboats are inside the harbour; the other ironclads are under weigh off New Port. The Decoy has gone to Port Said for information. The weather is bad. Comnkunication difficult.
LANDING OF MARINES AND BLUEJACKET'S.

The course of events in Alexandria since \Wednesday morning may be summarised as follows: The flag of truce which was hoisted on Wednesday morning was acknowledged by the British Commander in Chief, who sent a gunboat to communicate with the Egyptian authorities. Lieutenant Lambton, who was sent on this duty, had an interview with an officer of the rank of Pasha who had commanded in the forts, but he had no proposals to make, and no trace could be found of the men who were really at the head of affairs. After a con- siderable lapse of time the British gunboat returned to the flagship and riported that the negotiations, if such an imposing title could be given to the purposeless and abortive conversation on shore, had failed. The forts con- tinued silent, and no troops could be seen. It soon be- came clear that the Egyptians had Made use of the flag of truce to cover their withdrawal from the forts, where their loss had been very great. A shell was fired at Fort Meks, and a portion of that work set on fire, but the only reply of the Egyptians was to hoist another white fl ig, and again a fruitless mission was sent in. Meantime the fires which were seen in the city had continued to spread, and as darkness fell a scene "awful but grand," was presented to the fleet. On Thursday morning the Admiral sent a party of men en shore, and then it was found that the city was "abandoned and in flames." A body of Europeans, 100 strong, who had " fought their way down to the beach," were taken off by the boats of the fleet. These fugitives reported that terrible scenes of massac:e and pillage had been going on in the city throughout the night, and that great numbers of Christians had been slain. No one made the least effort to stay the progress of the flames. Ourabi and his troops had marched out, and were posted, it was believed, in a position where they could dispute the passage of any troops debouching from Alexandria on the road to Cairo. For many hours great anxiety was felt as to the position of the Khedive, but the last account from the Admiral affords much reason for believing that his High- ness, with Dervish Pasha, is safe on board ship in the harbour. On Thursday eveuing Admiral Seymour landed 600 marines and bluejackets. There was reason to fear that the forts were mined, and no doubt the greatest caution would be used in approaching them. The Latest telegram from Constantinople states that a " Grand Council " of present and former Ministers was thes bitting to consider the advisableness of despatching a Turkish force to Alexandria.

TRINITY WESLF.-YAN SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT. - The managers of this school had arranged to take the children t.o Sutton Hall, but the unsettled state of the weather necess:- tated an afteration in the programme, and after a march out between the showers. headed by the drum and fife band, t.A was provided in the school-room, and an adjournment afteri wards took place to Victoria Hall for indoor recreation ath amusement.

div.head: STATE OF THE CROPS.
div.p: STATE OF THE CROPS.

Through the courtesy of farmers we are able to publish the following details as to the state of the crops in the districts mentioned, but we ought to state that some of the reports were'written prior to the recent heavy rains : ANTROBTTS.—Corn, grass, and root crops good; better than they have been for the last three years. ACTON GriANGß.—Early potatoes are being raised, hut are a very light crop. Late potatoes, such as magnum bonnme and champions, are looking fairly well and promising, though magnums are a very poor braid. In a good many cases mangolds are a failure. Swedes, though they have grown very indifferently up to now, are looking fairly well, and with an average season may prove a fair crop. Clovers and ryegrass are average crops; but meadow grasses are not quite an average. Wheat is in most fields looking well, and with fine, su nmer-like weather, might prove a fair yield; but all depends upon the weather just now. Oats are thick upon the ground, but it is feared they will, through the unseasonableness of the weather, turn out very deficient as regards the bulk of straw. APPLETON. Grass is good this year as a rule, but our correspondent is very much afraid there will be a large quantity spoiled by the weather before stacking. Pastures are good. Wheat will be short in the straw; the weather has been too cold and wet for it. Oats will be short on most soils where sown after wheat. On ley land after gate they are better. On the whole he thinks straw crops will be light, they are so short in the straw. Early potatoes are very light crops,and late ones are not doing well on cold soils. Swede turnips (late) have been very !much troubled with fly. Mangolds are not very good, as it has been too wet and cold for them. We have had too much wet and cold for all crops on strong land, and shows very much where the land is not well farmed.

CLuerow, NEAR RUNCORN.—Wheat is very much im- proved with the late fine weather, and with plenty of sun- shine will be a full average crop. Oats are very good, and above average. Barley and beans are not much grown in this district. There is a good crop of clover, most of which is cat, but very little is carried. Fine weather is very much needed. Meadow grass and pastures are above average, being very full of herbige; better than for some years past. Early potatoes have turned up well, with steadier markete and better prices than last year. Late sorts are looking well. Magnums are very irregular in some fields, owing to the cut sets rotting in the ground. Those which have come up are now looking well, and growing vigorously. Turnips are a good braid, and look very well. Of marigolds very few sown except for planting purposes; and plants have been much plagued with the maggot. With good harvest weather farmers have not much to complain of as regards crops this season. CRONTON.—Naturally rreat anxiety for farmers just new is the weather. There is certainly in this neighbourhood a very small proportion of the hay crops secured, and what is worse, there are many acres lying broadcast. No damage has been done as yet, but unless things improve it will be- come serious. Wheat never looked better, and if it is true that the bloom has only to remain on for 24 hours to secure a good crop, we should have heavy returns, because during the fine days of last week it was in full flower, Oats as a rule are not doing well; they are short in the straw. GRAPPENHALL.—Wheat is looking well, and has shot into ears, which are to all appearance of good size, and promises, if the blooming season be favourable, to be quite an average crop. Oats are doing exceedingly well. Potatoes have im- proved very much in appearance during the last few days. The early ones, which are now being dug up, are small in size; they want hot weather. Mangolds and turnips have not made much progress; insects are attacking the leaves of the former.

GREAT BUDWORTII DISTRICT.— The prospect for the farmer is not very bright here, owing chiefly to the want of sunshine which is very much required for all crops now. Wheat, on sound land especially, is looking well, and being now in flower, its future productiveness will in a great measure depend upon fine weather. Oats are looking re- markably well on all high and dry land, and promises to be a very heavy crop on such; but they are suffering very much on cold and wet land where they have never been able to get away from the greund, and will neither be productivo in grain nor straw. Hay, about half of which is cut, will prove an average on clover soils. Some very heavy crops have been cut, and in many cases secured. Fine weather is very much wanted for the remain&r. Potatoes: Farmers are busy harvesting the earlies, which vary much in quality and quantity according, as they escaped the late spring frosts. On strong land this crop is suffering from oold and wet. Our correspondent has not seen anything of the disease yet, but such weather as they are experiencing, he says, is very conducive to it. Turnips, first crop, come up very irregu- larly, but have got away lately, and are beyond the reach of the fly, and promising well for a crop. HALEWOOD.—M e crops are exceedingly good.

HALE.—In Hale and neighbourhood there are good average crops. Wheat, oats, and barley are good, except small patches; they have plenty of straw, and every- appearance of a good yield of grain. The hay crop is yield- ing well, especially first year's clover and good second year's lay. The root crops have been backward in growth, there having been too much wet weather, but they have been filling up well since the week of fine hot weather, and if the weather be favourable a good yield, above the average, may be expected this year. KINGSLEY AND NErannounnoon.—Wheat, good. Oats, about an average crop, excepting those growing on heavy land, which will prove under. The grass crop is very good all rorind, and the same may be said of beans. Turnips and mangolds are in a late, poor, and backward state. Potatoes are good upon dry, sound, well-formed land, but are likely to be a poor crop upon medium and heavy soils, where they are showing signs of disease. As to fruit, it is the worst crop our correspondent ever knew; pears and. plums not being more tipn 1-100th of a crop. HAINFORD.—Wheat is very good, but there is not so much sown as formerly. Oats a fair crop, but rather short of straw. Barley is not very good: the straw is yellow, and there is a want of sunshine. Rye a very good crop, the straw being long and healthy. Beans are looking very well—not many sown. Ist year's pass very thick and heavy ; and 2nd year's very fair. With regard to potatoes, all the early sorts are doing very well, and are sound and healthy. The later sorts are very fair, but wanting sun. All kinds of turnips are doing very well. SPEKE AND NEIGHBOURTIOOD.—MOSt Of the hay in this district is cut, and very little in stack. Clover, good crop, but very badly weathered, and will be of inferior qoallt7 ; second and third years lay very thin, and much weathered. Wheat would have been an average crop to all appearance before this week's rain and wind, but now much beaten down, and rust appears to have set in. Oats in some places are thin, and where good, are very much laid as if they had been rolled. Barley, good, but down. Potatoes have much improved in s:ze since the rain, and now want sun, or the disease will set in.

WHEATIIILL, GATEACRE, NEAR LIVERPOOL —The crops in this neighbourhood are anything that could be desired. Clover and meadow grass are quite a full average. Wheat is looking most promising; oats, as though they would yield a good average, but are rather short in the straw. Turnips and mangold3 are also looking well. Potatoes, having re- covered from the rec,mt stronz gales and cold weather, are looking well; but complaints are general at many of the sets having missed, through a sort of rot, no doubt through the inclement weather during setting time.

WIGAN. WIGAN 'CRICKET CLIM ATHLETIC FESTITAL.—It will be seen from ow advertising columns that the Seventh Annual Athletic Festival of the Wigan Cricket Club will be held on Saturday, the 22nd instant, and all lovers of such gather- ings should avail themselves of the opportunity of being present, the Wigan people having gained an enviable I reputation for the completeness of their arrangements. The last day for receiving entries is Saturday, the 15th instant, and nothing save fine weather is wanting to make the meet- ing as successful as its predecessors. CHARGE pF KILLING A GRANDFATHER.—At Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, a collier named James Ashcroft, living at Orrell, near Wigan, was charged with causing the death of his grandfather, George Winstanley, aged 79. The two were drinking together at the prisoner's house, when Ashcroft bean breaking the furniture, and his wife went out leaving Winstanley nursing a child three years old. On a daughter oi the deceased entering shortly afterwards, she found her father lying on the floor with the child still in his arms, and bleeding profusely from a wound in the leg. He died a few hours afterwards without having made any statement, but it is supposed he was struck by the prisoner.—A remand was granted.

Figures remained without much alteration on the news of the bombardment of A.lexanchia arriving, and yesterday afternoon some strength was given to values on the announcement of tie appearance of a'4 flag of truce." have since Mr. Bright has expressed himself somewhat in favour of it; but unless the tenant-right is preserved intact it seems to me the whole object of the bill will be defeated. If these destructive amendments are not rejected by large majorities, the Peers will undoubtedly throw out the bill; but if their lordships find that the Commoners are pretty well at one upon the measure, then they will quietly accept the inevitable and pass it. At the same time a combination of Whigs and Tories, such as took place on Friday last, on a vital clause, would do all the mischief. The Primo Minister's announcement that an autumn session has been finally decided upon will, I think, be hailed with general satisfaction. The object of the session is, of course, to pass the procedure rules, and the further semi- official announcement that it is the intention of the Govern- ment to go on with the first rule of procedure in the exact form in which it has been approved by a large majority of the House of Commons will be received with equal satisfac- tion. That rule, if I mistake not, provides that the cldlure may be applied by a bare majority of the Home, reccent events in which lead me to suppose that it is the only safe and judicious course to adopt. The autumn session is to be taken by adjournment instead of prorogation, and the gain to the Government will be a substantial one. The progress already made with the first rule will, under adjournment, stand to the credit of the Government, whereas if Parliament were prorogued in August the work accomplished on the rules would have to be recommenced from the beginning, It is a consolation to know that we shall not have such another protracted debate as was main- tained over the first rule repeated, a debate which I think went a very far way indeed to prove the ntcessity for the adoption of the rule as originally submitted. FLACCUS.
WIDNES SEWERAGE SCHEME.—We understand the Widnes Local Board have decided to re-let the contract for the sewerage works.

Colonel I. Blaekburne, in the House of Commons on Monday, presented a petition from the Prescot Board of Guardians in favour of Sunday closing in Lancashire. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.—The librarian, Mr. Jones, attended the library on Saturday for the purpose of issuing ratepayers' youchera, and up to Tuesday n;ght 186 had been given. On Tuesday night 155 volumes were issued, classified as follows :—Theology 6, political economy 1, science and art 12, history, arc., 33, poe:ry and the drama 3, prose fiction 95, miscellaneous 5. MUSIC ON THE WIDNES PROMENADE.—OR Friday On the promenade, the Widnes Star of Temperance Brass Band, performed the following selections of music :—Niarch, "We've swept the seas ;" fantasia, "La Bouquetere," Euschel ; valse' "Cordelia," R. Smith; sel eption, "Patience," Charles and Albert; lancers, "Merry England," H. Round; polka, " Leontine," J. Arnaud ; schottische, "Rainbow," H. Aleber ; National Anthem. ACCIDENT AT RUNConan—Whilst he was painting a flag- staff at Trinity schools, Runcorn, on Wednesday, a young man named John Oliver, who lives in Parker-street, was precipitated to the ground in consequence of the ladder upon which he was standing breaking. No bones we understand, were broken, but he was seriously bruised, and be was carried home. Under the care of Dr. Robinson he is pro- gressing favourably. PAVILION THEATRE, WIDNES.—The pieces performed at this theatre this week have been of great variety and attrac- tiveness, and the result has been well-filled houses each night. Mr. Charles Quayle has sustained the chief char- acters with much ability, and has nightly received the plaudits of the audience. On Wednesday evening, Mr. Tom Greenwood and Miss Annie Coveney took their benefit. The Irish drama, "Shamus na Leena," was given, Mr. Quayle taking the character of Shamus. "Colleen Bawn " was presented on Thursday and last night. On the occasion of his benefit, Mr. Quayle took the part of the Prince of Denmark in "Hamlet." A fresh programme of novelties, with a new company, is announced for next week. THREATENING A WITNESS AT WIDNES. A ease arising out of the recent outrage perpetrated on a man on the Old Marsh, Widnes, was heard at Widnes Police-court on Thursday, before Mr. John Brock. Mary McDermott, a married woman, apprehended under warrant, was charged with threatening to assault and illtreat Ann Keogh and James Smith on the Widnes Old Marsh. The complain- ants were witnesses in the case mentioned, and McDer- mott is the mother of one of the prisoners. On Monday Mc Dermott came out of gaol, where she had been undergoing a term of imprisonment, and went to Keogh's house and threatened she " would do" for her. She said Keogh was going to the assizes to obtain money for her coming child's clothes' and made use of certain obscene expressions. After- wards she saw Smith, who she said she would fight though she was only a woman, and used threats which complainants said put them in bodily fear.—lt appeared the daughter of the defendant was also " wanted " for a like offence, and the magistrates remanded the prisoner, who pleaded guilty, in custody until Wednesday. WIDNES PRISONERS AT KIRIDALE SESSIONS.—At these sessions this week the following prisoners from Widnes were dealt with es under :—Bridget Oates, 36, of no occupa tion, for having, at Widnes, on the 22nd May, attempted to commit suicide by throwing herself into a pond, three months' imprisonment ; Catherine Bowden, 27, of no occu- pation, for stealing £1 from John Grady, at Widnes, on the 29th May, six months' imprisonment; Thomas Kendrick, 23, labourer, and Elizabeth Ann Read, 28, for having robbed James M`Quaid of a purse and tie sum of £2 10s., at Widnes, on the 25th April, six months' imprisonment each ; John Nash, 30, sailor, iltary Nash, 55, and Annie Nash, 13, were charged with having, at Widnes, on the 27th April, broken into the flats Carrie and Garston, lying in the Widnes canal, and stolen a quantity of wearing apparel. The male prisoner was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude and seven years' police supervision. The female prisoners were acquitted.—Hannah Maria Adams, 16, charwoman, was ac- quitted of a charge of having, at Widnes, in February last, broken into the dwelling-house of John O'Donnell, and stolen an alarum clock ; George Walker, charged with steal- ing a waistcoat and a watch, at Widnes, on the 15th ult., the property of Robert Forster, has also been acquitted. THE WESLETAN CONFERENCE: STATIONS OF MINISTERS. —The Stationary Committee did not complete its work until nearly eight o'clock on Thursday evening. The fol- lowing are the stations in this neighbourhood :—Warring- ton: John Eglinton, Joseph Agar Beet, and thomas Rip- pon. Runcorn: George Mather, George Hack, and Sidney Mess. Frodsham : John M. Bainford, and Frederick F. Edmunds (sup.) Widnes: Richard Harper and John Tesseyman. St. Helens: John M. Wamsley, George Smith, Joshua Fairburn, and Samuel Taylor (sup.) Wigan: Joseph Bacon, George King Pryor, and G. Heathcote Barker. Liverpool: Brunswick, William F. Slater, George S. Weston, Albert Clayton, Joshua Haigh, and Henry W. Shrewsbury; Cranmer, Robert W. Starr, James C. Fowler, J. C. W. Gostick, Elijah Sholl, and Henry Dodds (sup.) ; Grove-street, Frederick W. Briggs, M.A., Zadok Robinson, , John Aldred, Robert Ordely, and John Malvern (sup.) ; I Wesley, Thomas McCullagh, Ashton Jones, Gregory Renton, i and John Tucker (sup.) ; Mission, Charles Garrett and John W. Simister ; Pitt-street, George Byron; 'St. John's Jobs Jaker and T. B. Nicholson. Chester: John S. Workman, Alfred Sargent.: John M. Budden (sup.) Crewe: William Lees, Ebenezer Cole, and Cresar Caine. LOCAL VOLUNTEERS AT THE WIMBLEDON RIFLE MEETING.—The 23rd annual meeting of the National Rifle Association commenced on Monday morning on Wimbledon Common, under most advantageous circumstances as far as fair weather and the attendance of volunteers were con- cerned. The principal competitions on Monday were those for the Gregory, the Halford, the Heath, the Willa', and the St. Leger prizes • the prize of the Secretary of State for War, and the Alexandra prizes. In the latter competition, which is one at 500 yards, the following scores were made by members of the St. Helens L.R.V., viz. :—Sergeant Junor, 21st Lancashire, 27; Private Foster, ditto, 30 ; Sergeant West, ditto, 28; Sergeant White, ditto, 28; Private Taylor (who was winner of the Queen's prize in 1879), ditto, 27. On Tuesday the competitions opened were the Queen's first stage, 200 yards, and the Alfred, also 200 yards. This latter, a prize of £4OO, divided into 118 prizes, ranging from £2O to £2, came in for considerable competition. div.p: DISILTILBrNG TIC 3 SALTA.TIOR ARXY r WIDNEO.—A young woman named Catherine Neiland Was brought before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Holbrook Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court on Monday, charged with committing a breach of the peace by shouting and creating a disturbance.—P.C. Savory stated that while on the Market Ground on Sunday, he saw the prisoner throw a stone into the middle of the Salvation Army as they were proceeding through the streets. He was unable to say whether the stone struck anybody.— Mr. Inspector Barnett said this conduct had been very pre- valent in the town for the past two Sundays, and wanted putting down.—The Bench bound the prisoner over to keep the peace for three months in two sureties of £lO each, or in default 14 days' imprisonment.

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT WIDNES.—At the Millfield Recreation Grounds, Widncs, on Saturday, athletic sports organised by Mr. T. Brown, the proprietor, were held. The weather was very unfavourable, but a considerable number of spectators nevertheless assembled. There were only two events, 120 yards handicap flat race and a half-mile handi- cap. The first was run off in six heats, the first in each heat to compete in the final. At the conclusion of the heats the names of the competitors were J. Tarpey, (Cuerdley), D. Harding (Widnes), W. Pearse (Widnes), R. Valentine (St. Helens), J. Smith and W. Wareing (Widnes). The result of the final was first (£2), Tarpey ; second (10s.), Pearse ; third (55.), Smith. For the half-mile handicap there were 27 entries, and the following were successful in gaining a place in the heats:—First heat: 1, 11. Broome (Ditton); 2, T. Fitzpatrick; 3, R. Broome (Appleton). The result of the second heat was: 1, W. Wareing (Widnes); 2, S. Morris (Widnes); 3, E. M. Harrison (Appleton). In the final W. Wareing came in first, S. Morris second, and H. Broome third. The prizes were respectively £2, 10s., and ss. Messrs. W. Smith and T. Edwardson mere the judges, and Mr. W. Tilley the starter.

INHUMAN ATTA.CIZ UPON A WIFE AT WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. Helbrook Gaskell, jun., Patrick Ward, a chemical labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Mary, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. From the evidence of the prosecutrix it seemed that she went to bed between 7 and 8 o'clock, on Sunday night. She lay down without undressing. Towards 10 o'clock she heard her husband enter the house. 119 walked straight up stairs and asked her where she had been, and she replied that she had not been out of the house. He then dragged her from off the bed, knocked her to the floor, and proceeded to kick her with the clogs produced on the head and body. She raised her hand to ward off the blows from her head, and the prisoner kicked the middle finger on her left hand hurt- ing it very badly. • She screamed loudly for assistance, and she heard somebody attempting to open the street door. Her husband, however, had locked the door, and they were unable to gain admittance. At last she became insensible, and only knew that someone came to her assistance and carried her downstairs. Afterwards she recovered some- what, and went to Dr. McLennan, who attended to her wounds.—The prisoner asked his wife if there had not been four quarts of beer drank between them that night, and if she had not had her "share." She denied this.—Mr. Urquahart McLennan, physician and surgeon, practising in Widnes, said that on Sunday night, about 11 o'clock, he saw the prosecutrix. She had an incised wound, about two inches long, on her head, and discoloured bruises on various parts of her body. The middle finger on her left hand was much injured, and he thought it quite possible she might lose it altogether. The injuries were such as might have been caused by kicking with the clogs produced.---P.S. Robinson deposed to apprehending the prisoner at an early hour, on Monday morning. He charged the prisoner with the Offence upon which he was being tried that morning, and he replied "I know all about it." Having been cautioned in the usual way the prisoner made a statement in which he acknowledged kicking his wife, but denied having locked the street door as alleged by her.—He was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. BREACH OF THE LICENSING ACT AT WESTON. —At the Runcorn Police Court on Monday, before the Rev. E.& P. Campbell and Mr. C. W. Hanlehurst, William Hulse, landlord of the Village Inn, Weston, was charged with having on the 2nd inst., kept open his premises for the sale of in- toxicating liqaor to persons not being bona Ale travellers, during prohibited hours. The defendant pleaded guilty. —P.C. Cooper said at five minutes to three on Sunday after- noon the 2nd inst., he was on duty in the village of Weston. He saw two men come from the house of the defendant, and in consequence went round to the back door, where he effected an entrance. Entering an inner room he found sitting there three men. He asked the landlady what kind of business she called that, and she replied that she had told them to go out at closing time. Afterwards she went to look at the pigs, and•the men must have remained. There were glasses and jugs on the table, but they contained no been—The defendant stated that he was away from home on the day in question, but his wife had informed him that the clock had stopped at 2-20, and she did not know it was after closing time. The offence was not committed intentionally.—lu answer to Mr. Superintendent Williamson, the constable said the clock was not pointed out to him.—The defendant was fined 20s. and Os. 6d. costs.—Three young men named Wm. Johnson, Edward Onions, and John Hallows were then charged with being on the premises during prohibited hours, and after hearing the evidence, the Bench fined them ss. and 9s. 6(1. costs each.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday, Colonel Ireland Blackburne presented 'a petition from St. Helens in favour of repealing the Contagious Diseases Acts. In the House of Commons, on Monday, a petition in favour of Sunday closing in Lancashire was presented by Mr. McMinnies, from Warrrington Board of Guardians. The following night the hon. member presented two petitions also in favour of the Sanday Closing Bill, from Warrington, and one from Stockton Heath. ACTING LIRE A. MADMAN AT WARIZINGTON.-A.rthut Warburton, blacksmith, 29, Nicholson-street, was summoned at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and ex-Mayor, for having, on the 3rd inst., as- saulted William Finch.—The complainant said that on the day named he was walking quietly down Nicholson-street, when be saw the defendant running about the street like a madman. Defendant hit witness on the head with a loaded stick and a poker, although he said nothing to the defen- dant. The latter ;lad been "on to" a man who was wearing a blue ribbon in his coat; and there was a great crowd in the street. Witness's head bled fearfully, and he had to go to the Infirmary to get the wound dressed. He was knocked senseless. Defendant afterwards brought out an axe.—De- fendant said he got the axe to frighten away a great crowd from his door.—Finch's father, on being asked what was the defendant's condition, said he could not say that he was sober, but he was "more of a fool than anything else."—De- fendant said Ile took the "blue ribbon" some two or three months ago, but on the day in question he got some beer which "took hold" of him. He met several young fellows who "were on to him" for getting drunk, as they knew he had taken the blue ribbon. Finch challenged him to hit him, and he did so. There was a great crowd, and they " punched " his front door in.—The Bench bad no doubt defendant was much annoyed by the crowd kicking in his door, but he had no right to take the law in his own hands. However, taking everything in consideration, the defendant would be fined ss. and costs, which were rather heavy.

ST. HELENS AND DISTRICT TRAISMATS.—On Monday at the St. Helens Borough Court, Mr. J. C. Swift, solicitor made an application on behalf of the St. Helens and District Tramways Company for a justices certificate to empower the company to borrow the sum of £17,500.—Mr. Swift said be applied under section 12 of the "St. Helens and District Tiamways Act, 1879," and of section 40 of the "Companies Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845." Section 12 of the "St. Helens and District Tramways Act" provided that the company might from time to time borrow any sum not exceeding £17,500. Mr. Swift having read the clauses bearing on the application, said that they had been com- plied with, in proof of which he produced the books, and Mr. Hainmil, the secretary to the Tramways Company, would be sworn and would give the required evidence. Mr. Swift also read the copy of the resolution passed at the meeting of the shareholders of the company held at 19 and 21, Queen Victoria-street, London, on the sth inst., as re- ported in our last issue.—Mr. Hammil, secretary to the Tramways Company, deposed to the whole of the shares of the company having been issued, and at least £2 having been paid on each share, so that each holder of a share had became legally liable. The forfeited shares had been re- alloted and transmitted to other people. Two pound had tbeen paid on each of them before they were forfeited.—The certificate was granted.

HALTON LADIES CLID3.—In very favourable weather, the members of this club celebrated its 66th anniversary on Monday afternoon. They walked in procession to the church, where an appropriate sermon was preached. Tea was afterwards provided at the castle. A brass band was in attendance, and played for dancing, until dark, when the proceedings were brought to a conclusion.

EXCURSION rßom WIDNES.—The workmen of Messrs. Mort, Liddell, & Co., Widnts, had their annual excursion to Southport, on Saturday last. The tiain, which conyeyed about 500 persons, left Widnes at seven o'clock, and arrived at its destination shortly before nine. A pleasant day was passed in viewing the many attractions of this fashionable watering place, notwithstanding the boisterous nature of the weather. The return journey was accomplished in good time.

MASONIC FUNERAL AT RUNCORN. On Monday after- noon the remains of the late Mr. John Forrest Williams only son of Mi. Joseph Williams, were interred at Runcorn Cemetery. The funeral was attended by members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons, who -rh:ire the sprig of acacia. The Rev. John Nowell performed the service. General regret was expressed at the early death of the deceased, who had only completed his 32nd year. THE SALVATION ARMY AT WIDNES.—Under the command of Captain Gibbs, "the devil defeater," the Runcorn con- tingent of the Salvation Army paid another visit to Widnes, on Suinday. The attack of the previous Sunday was instru- mental, we were informed, in rescuing many of the "perishing," and the services are to be held weekly. The services on Sunday commenced at seven o'clock with "an hour's knee drill together upon armour for an attack on old smutty face." During the day they walked in procession through the streets' (Newtown being visited), headed by the brass band, but no disturbance took place. After the morn- ing services in the Volunteer Hall. the army marched.to West Bank, where" hot work against Old Nutcracker" was announced to be performed. Returning to the hall "a host of hallelujah lasses, and blood and fire boys," sang and spoke of Jesus; and in the. evening the "Salvation tiger" gave his aid in the attack on "the powers of darkness." The army returned to Runcorn about 9-30 p.m.

BRI7NSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN..— On Wednesday, the teachers attending this school, accom- panied by their friends, had a trip to Eastham. One portion of the party, numbering about 30 persons, departed from Runcorn in the morning for the ancient city of Chester, where they had a stay of several hours. The queer nooks of the magnificent cathedral were explored, and its many interesting objects inspected; admirers of scenery found pleasure in a stroll in the park; and a walk round the walls was enjoyed by all, the view there obtained insensibly con- juring up in the mind visions of the stirring events of which it had been the scene in olden time. In the afternoon the second contingent of the party, consisting of about 20 per- sons, were met at Chester station, and the entire party then proceeded by train to Hooton. To reach their final destina- tion a distance of three miles had to be traversed, but the way lay throng a most beautiful country, and the excur- sionists arrived at Eastham, the Richmond of the Mersey, without fatigue. The weather was delightfully fine, and a most enjoyable excursion was brought to a termination about nine o'clock, when the party arrived at Runcorn, having returned via Helsby. WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—The returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery, during the week ending Friday, July 14th, 1882, were :—Adults, 7; children, 12; total 19.

At the Present Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Evans, John McGlove and Miry Ann McDermott were each tined ss. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly. Mr. J. G. McMinnies, the Member for Warrington, we are glad to find, supported the Government in the adverse and accidental division which they sustained on Friday evening.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF ,WARRINGTON.—For week ending Bth July.—The mean temperature was 55.2 Fahrenheit, and therefore about the same as the preceeding week. The maximum temperature 72 F. was re- corded on the 3rd inst., and the minimum temperature 41 F. on the Bth inst. The rainfall measured 2.61 inches. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 27th of the current year, 35 births and 22 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was eqnal to 27 Der 1,000, against 25.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 6 2 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from measles, 2 from scarlet fever, 1 from erysipelas, 1 from diarrhoet. 13 cases of scarlet fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.--JonN H. GonNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday. at the Werkbou,e, Whiston, when there were present—Messrs. Marsh (in the chair), Leatherbarrow, Fidler, Penketb, Paris, Sadler, Garrard, Jackson, Buckley, Agnew, Tyrer, Dobell, Meadows, P. Longton, W. B. Long- ton, Birch, Birchall, Tuson, and tile Revs. T. Chambers, and Barnacle.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.-FmDAY.

The Earl of MAIL and KELLIE moved that their lordships do insist on their amendments to the London Riverside Fishmarket Bill.—Earl CAMPERDOWN, as an amendment, moved that their lordships do not insist on their amend- ments.—A long discussion ended in its being resolved their lordships should not insist on their amendments.—On the motion for the second reading of the Public Offices Sites Bill, Lord STRATHEDEN moved that the Bill be read a second time that day six montlis.—After a discussion the Bill was read a second time.—Several bills were forwarded a stage, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY. THE RIOTS AT TREDEOAR. —Sir W. HARCOURT, replying to Mr. T. O'Connor, said an inquiry into the disgraceful riot at Tredegar would commence on Monday. He would not, therefore-, enter into details on that occasion. Tran- quility and order had been restored. Ile would make i enquiry into delay n the arrival of the military. AFFAIRS AT ALEXANDRIA.—Mr. CAMPBELL—BANNER- MANN decided not to answer questions relative to the report al the splitting of two of the Alexandra's guns during the action of the 11th.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to a ques- tion as to the present position of the Khedive, said the Khedive had returned to his palace from Ram Dab, that he had won the confidence of his guards, and had called the pashas together with the view of restoring order in Alexandria.—Mr. MITCHELL HENRY wished to know whether 700 Marines guarding the Khedive were English or Egyptians. Mr. GLADSTONE said the Marines were English. There were, however, not only English Marines with the Khedive, but he had the guards, soldiers, and cavalry left by Arabi net for the purpose of guarding but watching him. —Mr. MAclvEu wished to know whether it was true the ships were being looted in the Suez Canal.—Mr. CANPRELI - BANNERMAN said the information they had was that the canal was open. The latest telegram stated that a number of vessels were waiting to pass the canal and the English gunboats had been ordered to accompany the vessels if i necessary. The ship Glenlyon was not on shore n the canal, and being looted she had passed through in safety.— Sir C. DICKE said he had not information as to the present position of Arabi.—Lord ErSTACE CECIL said there was no truth in the report of the purchase of 5,000 mules in Spain for £lOO,OOO. Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. A. O'Connor, said Mr. Cartwright, who had sent a telegram stating the Khedive had won over the guards Arabi has left for watching him, had hitherto sent authentic informa- tion, and he had no reason to doubt the accuracy of his statements in the present instance. Tun ARREARS BILL.—The House went into committee on the Arrrears of Rent (Ireland) Bill.—Mr. GIBSON moved an amendment to the clause, which be finally altered so that it stood that no remission of rent for the previous year should be credited to the year 1871.—The 'ATTOIINEY-GENERAL for IRELAND opposed the amendment, and it was negatived

by 213 to 31.—Mr. LABOITHERE moved an amendment to his sub-section empowering the tenant to make certain de- ductions from the rent prior to application to court.—An angry discussion ensued.—Mr. HEALEY called the Irish landlords a set of extortionate thieves.—Mr. FITZPARICL moved that the words should be taken down.—The Chair- man of the Committee interfered, and the matter passed over by Mr. Healey being asked to withdraw the observation, but he made no reply.—The amendment was rejected by 231 to 50.-Several amendments were ruled out of order.-Mr. W. H.
