div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. Darbyshire. Present : Revs. J. Lcckwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. H. Jackson, John Highfiekl, U. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).
MR. DUTTON'S 'EXECUTORS AND THE. SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The CLERK said that he had received a letter from Messrs. Robert Davies & Co.' of Warrington, re James Dutton's executors, and the Frodsham sewer, in which they wished to know whether they were to infer from a report of a discus- sion which took place at the Board whether the Board had any idea ot repudiating the arrangements. If so the Board would be put to the serious and unnecessary expense of an arbitration. They could hardly imagine that this was intended, but if it was not, they were instructed by Mr. Dutton's executors to say that the £35 must be paid at once.
~..--- The BOAIID, after some discussion, decided to pay the money at once. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The DEPUTY CLEWS read the medical officer's report, which was as follows have to report that during the quarter ending June 8)t , 1882, the registrar's re'urns record 167 births and 78 deaths in the three districts comprised in the rural sanitary district of the Runcoen Union. Of the births 84 were males, and 83 females ; birth rate, 86 per 1,000. Of the deaths 39 were males, and 39 females; death rate, 4'o per 1,009, as against 153 births; birth rate, 7•9 per 1,000, and 92 deaths ; death rate 4'T per 1,000 during the corresponding quarter of 1831. Of the diaths 23 were under 5 years of age, 22 of these being under 1 'rear; and 50 were 5 years and upwards. In consequence of the county analyst's unfavourable certificate of analysis of the drinking water obtained from a well situated on Quiesty Farm premises oecupled by Mrs. Beecroft, in Halton township, I pro- ceeded to inspect the farm, at which time 1 had the opportunity of conferring with Mrs. Beecroit's medical attendant, who favoured me with a history of the sickness at the farm during ,the past few years, most of which, I /save little doubt, had its origin in the polluted drinking water. The plgstyes being on apiece higher than, and in close contiguity o, the water well and farmhouse, it is quite clear that they re con- tributing largely to the impurities contained in the water, which is of very bad quality. The privy is on the same high level, and some of its more fluid contents must find its way Into the well in question. lam of opini,sn that a nuisance dan- gerous to health exists, and have accordingly prohibited the use of the water for dunking put poses. It will be necessary to cause the immediate removal of the pigstyes some distance to the rear of the dwelling-house, where the ground slopes away from the dwelling and well. The privy should be removed some distance, at least 18 feet from its present position, to the rear of the house for the same reason and object, otherwise to be converted to the " Pail System." The well should be emptied so far as is pos sible and thor tughly cleansed. The cattle pond from its low lying situation must receive a large quantity of liquid manure from the caw sheds and farm yard, rtc., whila are all placed on higher levels than the pond from which the cattle obtain their drinking water. I think it quite impossible for the milk to be pure under such conditions. Scarlet fever has attacked a child at Sutton. Fever also exists at Halton, Overton, and Aston Heath. The usual measures have been taken. lam glad to state the disease is not epidemic in any part of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary district; the cases herein reported are, of a sporadic nature. NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT. Mr. JAMES FARRINGTON, inspector of nuisances, reported as follows:

Having received various complaints as to the unsani- tary condition of that portion of Frodshana called Newtown, I have made a thorough inspection of the same, and beg to re- port an follows :—At the time of inspection Newtown contained 61 occupied houses, with a population of about 329; 19 of the houses belonged to the Runcorn Property Inve-tment Com- pany, 29 belong to the Lancashire and Cheshire Building Society, 8 are under the agency of Mr. Robert Andrews, jun , and 5 are owned by Mr. Wm. Fletcher, of Frodsharn. The sewage, Ac., from 48 houses is conveyed by drainage to a small receptacle, with an overflow into a running stream. The out- let of the drainage to 8 houses is into an open ditch, where the sewage is stagnant and fast becoming a nuisance Five are drained into a covered cesspool, with an overflow into stream. Each house is supplied with a sewage inlet In back yard; of snch inlets 41 are untrapped and 17 are trapped. The drainage to two of the yards to houses be- longing to the Runcorn Property Investment Company is in a defective condition, and requires opening , also three of the yards to houses owned by the same conspany require relaying, seven yards to houses under Mr. Andrews also require relaying. as in their present condition they are almost impassable, owing to Using flooded with sewage and other liquid, from which very foul odours are emitted. Many complaints are made with respect to bad smells arising from the untrapped inlets; and I , would suggest that traps be put in, more especially to those in- lets connected with the main sewer at the highest point. There is a pump and well which is intended to supply the whole of these honses, but the water is supposed to be impure; there- fore the whole of the population are dependent upon a running pipe situate in Water-street, which is not within reasonable distance, and not at all times of a reliable quality. Such being tt e case, I tv, uld rec,mmend that a sample of the water from pump and well be submitted for analysis, and if found to be unfit for domestic purposes, that the well be closed and another sunk in a better situation, at the joint expense of the various owners.

The INSPECTOR read paper upon thq sanitary condition of the water supply of Newtown and Frodsham, and he was instructed to serve notices for the requisite mains to be made, and also to obtain a sample of the water from the running pipe in Water-street and forward them for analysis. Nuisances arising from pigstyes and defective drainage up- on farm premises at Hatton were called attention to, and the Inspector was directed to ',communicate with the agent and forward him a copy of the Medical Officer of Health's re- port.
NOTICE BOARDS AT THE ouTrALL WORKS. It was reported that the notice boards had been printed and fixed at the outfall works at Frodsham in a ntisfactory manner. This was all the business.

div.head: WORKHOUSE MASTER'S DEPORT.
div.p: WORKHOUSE MASTER'S DEPORT.

The Master of the Workhouse (Mr. Birchall) reported that the number of inmates in the Workhouse during the past week was 422; the preceding week, 426; corresponding week of fast year, 494. The number of boys and girls in Kirkdale schools vras 133. There had b&en four deaths during the past week.

div.head: A. WAIIIIIN• TO TRAMPS.
div.p: A. WAIIIIIN• TO TRAMPS.

The Cx.aRIC (Mr. Hartley) said it was very probable that the `fragrancy Bill would soon become law, and he should recommend that they adopt a system of testing the accufacy of the statements of tramps who c tme to the Workhouse. For instance, if a tramp should sly he had come from War- rington or Liverpool, they could communicate with the masters of the Workhouses at those places, and if it were found tint the truth had not been told they could prosecute the tramp as a rogue and vagabond. He thought the Guar- dians would soon recoup the expenses of such a course, as tramps would begin to say that they must avoid Prescot, as they made enquiries into their characters.

div.head: TIIII DIRT OF WORKHOUSE_ OFFICERS,
div.p: TIIII DIRT OF WORKHOUSE_ OFFICERS,

A communication was read from the Local Government Board, stating that the district auditor had reported that the Guardians had not a proper scale of diet for the officers of the workhouse as was usual at other places. The CLEUx said that was the first intimation he had had that they had not a proper scale. Mr. FIDLER said he thought they had adopted one. The CLERK: Oh, certainly; I don't know where the auditor got his information from. If he had enquired I could have shown him a scale of diet.
RETURN OF PAUPERS.

The CLERX said there was a request frem the Local Government Board for a return of paupers receiving relief up to the let July. This return had been made out as fol- lows :—Outdoor, males, 200; females, 156; children under 16, 247; making a t(fal of 607. Indoor, males, 310; fe- males, 1,050; children under 16, 1,135; making a total of 2,545. The grand total was 3,172.

div.head: AN EFFECTIVE OBJECTION.
div.p: AN EFFECTIVE OBJECTION.

The Finance Committee recommended that the relief officer should receive £5 per annum extra on account of having to make out their returns in alphabetical order. Mr. Disavows said he should object to that proposal. There was no doubt that the present had made more work for the overseers by insisting:" on the names being put in alphabetical order in his books; but they all knew that the auditor had increased the work of the whole of the officers, Mr. Hartley as well the assistant overseers, and if the relief officers got an advance on account of the extra work, the salaries of the whole of the overseers would have to be increased. As a matter of fact one of the relieving officers got £l2O a year, which lie (Mr. Meadows) thought a very good salary. lie therefore meved that no additiona pay should be allowed them. Mr. BARNACLE said that perhaps Mr. Mead )wa wIS not aware that some of the relief officers did not get. £lOO a year, although he (Mr. Meadows) believed it was the will of the Givardians that they should be paid £lOO, but they had to pay out of their own pockets their travelling ex- penses. Mr. CHAMBERS said he was in favour of their officers being well paid, but at the last meeting of the Finance Com- mittee he thought it his duty to support the amendment made by Mr. Lae that £5 be not added to the officers' in- come. It seemed to him frivolous that a man should have £5 extra merely for making out an alphabetical list. He, therefore, seconded Mr. Meadows' amendment. Mr. FIDLER supported the Finance Committee's proposal. It was only right, he thought, that the officers should be remunerated for the extra work thrown upon them, and If they granted the £5 they would be doing no more than they would do by their own clerks under the same circumstances. Mr. TYRER did not think the Local Government Board would sanction this increase to the salary of officers most of whom had been only appointed within the last six months.

Mr. LEITHERBARROW : Are they compelled to make out an alphabetical list. The CHAIRMAN disputed the right of the aulitor to make the change. He thought if the nooks were presented as heretofore he would be bound to pass them. The CLERK explained that the books were made out at the commencement of the half year in alphabetical order, but it was afterwards dis-arranged by having to put, say, the name of " Abbot "at the end. The Loc 11 Government Board ordered that the list had to be in alphabetical order, and if the relief officers did not do it he would have to do it himself.
Mr. CHAMBERS said the instance mentioned by the Clerk could be surmounted by leaving about a dozen lines blank after each letter.
Mr. FIDLER : They would require to have a porter to carry their books.

Mr. CHAMBEUS : Oh, dear, no. Mr. MEADOWS was at a loss to understand why they should attempt to raise the salaries at such an unseasonable time, as they heard everywhere that trade was bad. As for the objection of Mr. Barnacle that the officers did not re- ceive £lOO a year, he (Mr. Meadows) could say that they received all they were told they would receive when en- gaged. Mr. Meadow's amendment was then put, and as 10 voted in its favour it was declared carried.

TRE PAYMENT OF ASSISTANT-OTERSEEns. CRAMBERs , in accordance with a previous resolution, moved that the assistant-overseers should in future be paid by results, that is so much per Ain the amount of rates• collected by them, as laid before the Guardians at their pre- vious meeting, instead of a fixed salary. In support of his motion he made a somewhat lengthy speech, in which he stated that the Local Government. Board were in favour of the system as it gave an incentive to the assistant-overseers to perform their duties promptly and efficiently. Mr. Mkanows, in seconding the proposd, said that the poundage had been so arranged that the salaries would amount to about the same as those which the assistant- overseers were at present receiving, or if there were an ad - vance in some instances it would be very trifling. The CHAIRMAN said he had received the following letter on the subject that morning : .‘ I am instructed by the Executive Committee of the Dis- trict of Widnes Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Association, to most respectfully invite your attention to the propos.,cl new scale of payment for the col'e:!tors of the poor rate. They do not so much object to the mode as they do to the rate of c)m - mission fivepence in the 2, in their judgment, being certainly too high, for according to the assessment, which is about £lOO,OOO, the present rate of 3s in thee will yitld the cAlector a salary of MOO, whilst a rate of 2s in the will yield a salary of upwards of £2OO per annum, which they consider would be too high a price to be paid. For it must be borne in mind that before Bold, Cronton, and Ditton were separated the rate was collected for a very much less salary. Further, the committee think, considering the great depression which hangs upon the town, the time most inopportune for such a conspicuous In crease of salary as contained in the proposed commission. They therefore trust your Board will give their request due considera- tion, with a view to a modified rate of commission to that already proposed.—SAMUEL OWENS, Secretary." The salaries seemed, the Clerk added, very large, that was of course if the figures were correct, but of course he knew nothing about the assessment of Widnes. Mr. FIDLER : They don't know dial they are writing about. Mr. SADLIR said that before the motion was put to the meeting he should like to propose that the portion referring to Widnes should be adjourned for a fortnight. He had taken some figures from the rate books which did not cor- respond with Mr. Hartley's. They covered the period from 1878 to 1882, and showed, after making allowances, that a rate of 4s. in the £ would raise a yearly salary of £l6B. This was not a time, he said, to raise salaries, as property owners could scarcely pay their way in Widnes, where there were about 000 houses empty, and for those which were occu- pied rent could scarcely be got. ' Mr. MEADOWS said they would not be raising the salaries._ _ .
Mr. CILLIMERS asked what the difference between the salaries would be ? Mr. SADLER : It Will be about £6O. Mr. MEADOWS: The question is whether your figures are correct,

Mr. SADLER : I got them from our rate book. The CLERK said the figures on which they had calculated their system of poundage were correct, as they had been taken from the official returns, and pointed out that the arrears were much greater than Mr. Sadler had allowed for. Mr. CHAMBERS said that if Mr. Sadler reflected for a moment he would see that there would more likely be a de- crease than an increase in the salary. Mr. SADLER said he was not speaking respecting an in- crease at all. What he contended for was that the rate over the past five years was something to go by, and he proposed that the matter should be adjourned for a fortnight to allow of further eviuiries being made. Mr. P. LONGTON seconded Mr. Sadler's amendment. He thought a fortnight's adjournment would not be a serious interference. Mr. CHAMBERS said as far as he was concerned he had not the slightest objection to the business being held over a fortnight. Mr. TYRER did not see any reason why the matter should be adjourned, as he did not think they could get any more facts than they had before them.

Mr. CHAMBERS said it was only because he did not want it to be afterwards said that there had been anything like unfairness, for he believed that Mr. Hartly had gone thoroughly into the matter. The CLERK said each guardian had got a printed notice of the btisiness and unless Mr. Meadows, as seconder-, was willing that the proposal should be withdrawn Mr. Cham- bers could not withdraw it.

Mr. MEADOWS said he should like to hear what advantage would be derived by postponement. Mr. SADLER said the clerk held his figures to be right and he held his own to be right, and they could settle the matter by adjourning it. The CLERK said he had taken his from Parliamentary re- turns, commencing in 1877. He was anxious that the new system should be brought into operation at the commence- ment of the next half-year, and it would take them a couple of months to get everything done. Mr. MEIDOWS said, as seconder, he did not think it would be wise to adjourn the matter under the circum- stances. The amendment was then put, when only 3 voted for it; 1 for the motion 10 voted, and it was carried accordingly, The Board then adjourned.

div.head: WARRINGION POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGION POLICE COURT.

BATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandlev. INEBRIATE.s.—WiIIiam Rogers, Michael K.arnes. and Par- k Ecabill, were each chirged with being drunk and dis- orderly. The two former were fined. ss. and costs, but the latter was dismissed.
MOXDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and tLe ExMkyor (Councillor Fairchiugh.)_

SMASHING A SHOP WINDOW.—John 'McManus, forge labourer, 5, Pocket-street, [IAA Patrick Mellor, forge labourer, 16. Stanley-street, were charged with being drunk and die- orderdly by fighting in Bridge-street, on Saturday; also with doing wilful damage to tlitt pla e-glass window of Richard Kilshall, i dge-street to the amount of 35s.—In amwer to the charge, McManus, sato Mellor gave him a shove" into the window; be was not guilty. Meitor p!eaded guilty.—The prise Der's were fighting lii Bridgo-street, opposite Mr. Kilshall's shop, and the assistant helring ;,tl.e noise went to the door. Just as be got there the window was smashed He pulled Mc (anus out of the window, and also Me'ior, was on the top of him." Be took them into the shop, and af erwards gave them into the custody of P.C. Co,coran.—The assistant, Martin, s aid the prisoner's relati vas or friends lied settle I with Mr. Kilshall about the window, and the second charge was thus withdrawn.—The prisonets were 'fined Sc. and costs each, total 10s. 6d.

MISCELLILNEOUS —Ann Nicholson, tramp, was committed in' seven days' imprisonment fr b-lag drunk and disorderly on Saturday night at the Police-sta:ion, where according to P.S. James, she entertained the offi ia's by giving " ex- presslon to her sentiments." Tha Chief Constable said the prismer was an "old roadster and on circuit." (Lsughter.) Prisoner: I don't deserve that seven days. The Mayor: 'I should have let you off if you had not been here before. You are an old hand.—Mary Flynn, a bad character, was charmed with being in possession of a meerschaum pipe, supposed to be stolen. She was sentenced to 14 days' impri- sonment, on the evidence of I' S. spinks.—Richard Holcroft, butcher, was fined 23. 6d. In--lading costs, for allowing his horse to stray on the 211 h June, at Latchford.—George Par- kinson and Joseph Leigh were summoned for allowing their two horiss to stray on Knutsford-road, Latchford, on the 30th June. They were each fine 2s. 61. including costs. Before Major Cartwright and the Ex-Mayor. KEEPING UNREGISTERnD LODGING KOUSES.—Ann Burke, 4, Chrimes' Yard, was summoned for having let her house in lodgings, the same not being registered for ledeing-house pur- poses.—lnspector Church deposed that he visited the house on Sunday morning, the 2nd inst., at 15 minutes past three, and , found six persons in the house, five being members of the family and one a lodger. The house was only adapted for three persons, and was not registered as a lodging-house.—She was , lined los. and costs, or 14 days' impr sonment.—Defendant : 103. and costs, Mr. Cartwrigh, ! I have not lfd !—John Col- lins, Morris's Yard, off Silver Square. was summoned for a liks offence, on the 18th inst. In defendant's house there were three of a family, and seven lodgers the latter being brother's and sisters-in-law of defendant.—Defendant's wife, who ap- peared for her husband, said she would look for a larger house, and the case was adjourned.—Owen O'Donnell, 36. Oliver - street. was summoned for keeping an unregistered lodging- house. There were eight persollS in the house, which was only adapted for four persons.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs, or seven days. TuEsnar.—Before Messrs. C. Broadbent and P. Monks. INEDRIATES.—The following were fined for drunkenness on the previous day :—Jas.llowarth, John Lyons, John Flannery, Luke Talley, Francis Lee, and John Fleming WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Alderman Chandley.

DRUNK IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. A respectab:e looking man, named George la iltiams, a French polis.her, residing at Bebbington-street, Liverpool, was charged with being intoxi- cated in a carriage on the Cheihite Lines Railway, whilst travelling between Manelinter and Warrington, on the pre- vious day. Prisoner arrived in Wart ington,by the 2.50 p m.train on Tuesday, and was lying on the seat of a second-class corn- part merit. When requested by the ticket collector to show his ticket he refused and used very abusive language. He also be- came very vio:eut and kicked the railway inspector. Prisoner was at once taken into custody, but when before the magis- trates be regrettod having been violent —He was ordered to pay 10s. and costs, or in di fauit to undergo 14 days' imprison- ment with hard labour. A DituznEEN MAN AND His FURNITURE.—Patrick Glynn. a labourer, resieing in Golborne-st, eet, was chsrged under a warrant with being drunk in Gaskell's-yard.—lt appeared from the evidence that the prison, r dashed his head through his own window, and bled very profusely. He also smashed all his furniture.—Prisoner said he had not been drunk for twelve months previous to this offeme.—He was fined lOs and costs,or the alternative of It days' imprisonment with hard labour. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.—A clerk named Thomas Wilson, of Peterbolou4b, was charged with riding in a third- class carriage, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, from Sheffield to Warrington, on Tuesday, the 11th instant, without having previously paid his tare, with intent to cheat and defraud the railway company.—Prisoner was ordered to pay the fare, ts Bd, and alio to pay a fine of les and costs, or to undergo ii days' imprisonment with hard labour. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—John Wilsen, alias Richard Jones, labourer, of Kensington, Liverpool, was charged with fraudulently enlisting in tho South Lancashire Regiment, on May list, 1882, by making false answers of attestation, having been discharged invanded from the Royal Welsh Fusilesrs Regiment. on Febru try 110. 1892,—Prisoner was sent to prison for 14 days, with hard labour.

THUP.SDAY.—Before Captain Litton and ilderm tn Burgess. ARREST ON SUSPICION.—Joseph Whiteley. of Batley, and G. Henry Gill, of Sheffield, were charged on suspicion with steal- ing a pair of men's cloth top b,:ots, and one sliver fruit knife, from some person unknown.—Police Constable Neil, said he was called to Mrs. Jackson's pawnshop in Church-street, where he saw the prisoner Gill attempting to p twn a pair of boots. He asked him what ace ,unt he could give of them, and prisoner replied that they beiomed to a yung man outside. He then took both prisoners into custody, and, when charged with stealing them, prisoner Whiteley said he had purchased them in Batley. lie then asl.ed prisoner to try the boots on, and he found that they were about three inches too long. Seeing the boots were too long for him be loked the prisoners up. That morning he again examined prisoner Whiteley, and found the knife about his person. He then said he had stolen it from a a lodging house, and the boots belonged to a train car con- ductor. The prisoner Gill knew nothing about the goodis stolen, and be was aceoringly discharged; but prisoner White- ley was remanded until Saturday for enquiries. COSTLY SALAD.--A young man named John Bibby, living at Prospect View, Win wick-road, was charged with stealing from the gaidens of Mr. David Faulkner and Alderman Holmes. Folly-lane, a quan,ity of lettuce and mint, value 4d.—P.O. Howbottom stated that he was on duty in plain clothes at an early hour that(Thursdav) morning, when he saw the prisoner and another boy enter Mr. Holmes and Mr. Faulknet's gardens and take the plant, produced. The other boy got away, but he succeeded in capturing the prisoner. He was fined 103. and costs.

FRlDAY.—Befote Alderman Holmes and Mr. John White. STEALING CIA:WEIL—Three respectably dressed young men named 6amuel Thonips.,n, Samuel Simcock, and John Gibson were charged with stea'ing a quantity of clover, value of 2s 6d. the property of Elizatseth Hall, farmer, Lat,hford, on the 12th inst.—lt appeared from the evidence of Mrs. Hall's representa- tive, tint the defendants filled a couple of bags with clover from a field near the canal, and afterwards began to knock down the c,ps of hay which had been cut, and were lying in the field.—Defendants were each fined 103. and costs, and were also ordered to pay 2s. 6d. damages, or in default to undergo 14 days' imprisonment. MiscELLAxxors.—George Delooze was charged with assault- ing a married womkn named Mary Bridge, in Buakley-street, on the Ist inst.—Complainant said that whilst she was speaking to a friend, defendant was quarrelling with his aged mother, and because he thought th.,t she (complainant) was talking about him, he came up to her and knocked her to the floor—Defendant was bound over in his own recog- vizaEc3 of £lO, to keep the peace for six months -- Mary Bridge, complainant in the last case, was then charged with assaulting Mary Delooze, wife of last defendant, at the same place.---Complainant stated that her husband was quar- relling with defendant, when defendant strack him with her clog several times. Not satisfied with Musing her husband, defendant struck complainant also —Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months.—A married woman. named Catherine Brannon, was summoned by Kate Hennessey for assaulting her in Scotland-road, on the Sth instant.—Com- plainant said that without the slightest provocation defendant called her very scurrilous names, and subsequently bit-a piece of flesh from underneath her eye, and dragged her to the ground by the hair of her head. Defendant then hit her on the head with a bowl, and raisedk very large lump; and, if a young man had not come up at the time and separated them, she declared defendant would have killed her.—Defendant stated that complainant also assaulted her ; and, after hearing the evidence, the magistrates dismissed the case.—Jane Gregson, for using obscene language to Wm. Thomas Terry, was ordered to pay the costs, 4s. 6d.

_ THEFT OF GARDEN PRODUCE.—A youth, named John James Kay, was charged with stealing a quantity of lettuce and mint from the garden of Mr. David Faulkner, Folly-lane, value 4d. or thereabouts, at an early hour on Thursday morning.—P.C. Rowbottom said that about 3.30 on the morning in question he saw prisoner, along with another man named Bibby, come along the railway, enter Mr. Faulkner's garden, and commenee to pull up the lettuce and mint above stated. He gave chase and sucneeded in capturing Bibby, and the prisoner Kay was apprehended auring the course of Thursday by P.S. Cox.—The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs for the offence, ss. for the loss of time sustained by Mr. Faulkner in appearing in court. and Is. for damage to the garden, or, in default, 14 days' im- prisomnent with hard labour. ABUSIVE LANGUAGE.—Sarah Wycherlev was charged with having, on the 10th inst., unlawfully made use of language to- wards Agnes Balmer, landlady of the Soldier's Return, Pinner's- brow, calculated to provoke a breach of the peace.—Complalrt- ant said that on Monday night, about 10 o'clock, defendant came into her house and asked her if there was a woman named Polly Grounds within. She replied that there was not, where- upon defendant used language of a most vile and filthy charac- ter to her, and only desisted when she called her husband to put defendant out of the house.—Defendant was bound over in her own recognizances to keep the peace for six months.

ALLY-GED ROBBERY AT WIDNES.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Catherine Larkin was charged with stealing five pounds scrap iron and a tame tortoise, the property of Michael Lancaster, 8, labnurer living in'Kent-street.—lt appeared that an officer found the articles In the possession of the prisoner about five o'clock that morning. It was:afterwards ascertained that the had been abstracted from the prosecutor's premises.—She was further charged with stealing, some time between the 10th and 11th instant, a bird cage, of the value of 25., sod a ' tame rabbit, value 6d., from the backyard of John Abbott, living in Milton-road, Widnes. The cage and rabbit had been found in the house where the prisoner resided.... Remanded to Monday.

div.p: FRIGHTFUL SCENES IN THE STREETS.

A Daily 7CICS telegram dated Alexandria, 10 a.m., yesterday, says :—Sir Garnet Wolsley is expected at Port Said on Sunday, but if Arabi makes a stand at Rosetta and Damanvour he will probably come on at once to Alexandria. The Marines and Blue Jackets, who landed in the morning, have spiked all the guns. They found one port with 15 10-inch Armstrong guns of the newest pattern. Some of these were lying on one side disabled; others were half buried, in the earth, with muzzle in the air lil:e frantic prancing horses, and although many gunners were buried, numbers were lying about mutilated in an undescribable manner. Seven men were seen dead under one gun. There are 180 marines strongly posted at the entrance to the gates, where on Monday last perhaps 1,500 Egyptian treops were stationed. At the Arsenal Gate, 150 men hold possession ; and at the Marini or Custom House Gate -190 Marines, with a Galling Gun, will remain all night. No Arab soldiers of any description were seen to-day in this quarter, but many looters were kiiled by our Marines in clearing the streets and in protecting the pro- perty in the neighbourhood of the Custom House. Some Italian refugees living near the harbour who escaped the massacre report that all Christian shops and stores along the shores were looted by the soldiers, who first killed their victims in a most horrible manner. The fires have reached the Arab quarter and Marina, where frigbtful scenes are ex- pected after dark. Empty carts are going to the Marina to fetch the dead bodies of soldiers. A crowd, with a green flag, passed down the principal Arab street, calling upon God and the Prophet. Native women and children are flying they know not whither, and soldiers in old uniforms, carry- ing bundles on rifles, are hurrying out of the town with their wives. There are neither sentinels nor police in the streets. The Governor tells the people not to leave, but they are so frightened, now that they know the truth about the bombardment and the certainty of the whole town being reduced to cinders, that every one is getting away as fast as possib:e. It is reported that six persons were massacred at the French Consulate. The Khedive is now arriving from Ras-el-Tin Palace, where he embarks on board the Charkich. The harem wing is still burning, and this is the only build- ing set on fire by shells during all the bombardment, but the damage done to the batteries at Ras-el-Tin is prodigious. Admiral Hoskyns has transferred his flag to the Penelope, and sailed for Port Said and Ismailia. He is anxious to have the Monarch with him, but as she draws too much water for the Canal she could only remain at Port Said. The wounded men in the English Fleet are going on well for the most part, and no deaths have supervened. At tile time of closing this message the fires in the town are still increasing, and men are seen running about with lighted torches completing the destruction of Alexandria. It is much feared that when the Egyptian army is driven to Cairo a repetition of the same fiendish work will be witnessed.
THE BRITISH LANDING.
BURNING OF THE ENGLISH AND FRENCH

div.head: CONSULATES
div.p: CONSULATES

The Standard correspondent telegraphed from Alexandria at 9-10 a.m. yesterday,—During the last twenty-four hours some very exciting events have come under my notice. It would appear the houses in the town were first plundered and then set on fire. The English church was first fired by one of our shells, but yesterday the mob completely des- troyed the sacred edifice. In the Eastern Telepraph Office I found a clerk who had been left behind murdered, like so many other Christians. At five o'clock last night our soldiers quitted the city and went in the direction of Rosetta. All the prisoners, including those captured during the riot a month ago, had been liberated; these continue the work of plunder and carnage, otherwise the city was entirely de- serted. We are informed that Arabi had spread a report to the effect that the English could only fight at sea, that he would withdraw until the British troops landed, and that then there would be a great battle. On returning to our own vessel we found a barge containing forty refugees, nine of whom are English. They had delayed their departure too long, and hidden themselves in the barge. The city is still burning. From the maintops of our vessels we can see Arab men and women still lurking in the streets. The Admiral had determined to land a force, but having been told by some refugees that nine thousand Egyptian troops occupied a position outside the city ready for attack, and as he could only land 300 men, he considered such a step unadvisable. Instedd, therefore, of sending men on shore, he ordered the city to be fired over, in order to frighten the rioters. Twenty armed Europeals soon. after- wards arrived. Tney had barricaded their houses, and thus escaped the general massacre. They confirmed in every particular all the information I have sent you. They passed through the streets this morning, the rioters appearing too busily engaged in their work of destruction to take any notice of them. They stated that with the exception of those engaged in the pillaging of the city, the place was utterly abandoned. The Egyptian losses during the engage- trit..nt of the fleet was very severe. They had been told by a pasha whom they met that the killed numbered over 600. The English and French Consulates have been burned to the ground, and the greater portion of the Grand-square is still in flatnes. A patty of bluejacke's were landed this morning at the Garbarrie Battery. They spiked and des- troyed nineteen guns which were in position. The Monarch opened fire at another battery, which was soon destroyed. The looting and burning of the city continuing to increase, the Admiral seemed to be much distressed that he could not afford a sufficient force of men to land, in consequence of the information respecting the large force of Egyptians ready to attack. Three officers have arrived in hot haste from Ratn- leh, where the Khedive is living in the utmost danger, and begged the protection of the English. The Admiral at once acceded to the request.
MESSAGE FROM TLIE ADMIRkL.-SAFETY OF
THE KHEDIVE.

The following has been received from the Admiralty:— A telegram from Sir Beauchamp Seymour, dated Alexan- dria, Friday, 7-10 a.m., says: Regret distance from cable ship impedes my telegraphing rapidly. Have occupied Ras-el-Tin :with marines of squadron, and spiked guns in six Batteries opposite. Alexandria still burning, but am clearing streets. Khedive safe in Palace, garrisoned by 700 marines. Conduct of officers and men beyond all praise. Officers and men send thanks for kind message from her Majesty. In reply to her Majesty's message, majority of wounded doing well, including Lieutenant Jackson, of In- flexible.

div.head: PROBA.BILITY OF A JOINT OCCUPATION
div.p: PROBA.BILITY OF A JOINT OCCUPATION
OF EGYPT.

The Daily _Yews says:—lt is expected the Conference will meet again to-day. The Powers here agreed to call upon Turkey to undertake the restoration of order in Egypt. A communication to that effect will be made to the Porte after the meeting of the Conference. In the event of Tur- key declining or hesitating we believe the Conference will call upon England and Francs to land a joint force with the object of reinstating the Khedive and restoring order. We believe that Sir Etlatard Malet will not return to Egypt.

Mr. MAME said so far as Warrington was concerned, Mr. Fulton came down three or four years ago, and he was quite familiar with the exigencies of the route, and he then saw no serious engineering difficulty in the way. Mr. MONKS believed it was a fact there were steeper gradients on the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway to-day than would be required on the London and North-Western Railway. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Adamson did not trust to the, re- port, but took the trouble to go over the ground hlmself, and he said he had come to the conclusion that the scheme could be made a commercial success. Mr. CARSON said that the scheme was perfectly feasible nobody could doubt. It was simply a question of money. He pointed out that they would have the opposition of the London and North-Western Railway Company, which had the strongest influence in the House of Commons, and that they would see everything the Warrington Chamber could do they were bound to do to assist the undertaking, which would be of immense importance to Warrington. Mr. BLECKLY said when the London and North-Western Railway Company began they were opposed by the Duke of Bridgewater, who secured two seats on the Board in London to protect his interests. The London and North-Western Railway Company had had to fight every inch of ground; but he pointed out that the public was a greater corporation than the London and North-Western Railway Company. The railways were becoming unable to manage their traffic, and he mentioned that there was a scheme for a plate rail- way along the road from Liverpool to Manchester, which Mr. Holt was promoting in a very energetic way, indeed, and no doubt if he could make out a case Parliament would never consider that the London and North-Western Railway Company might lose 1 per cent, of their dividend. While the work on the Tyne was a comparatively slight thing, on the Suez Canal they were getting interest which would very soon pay for another canal. Warrington did not get the full advantage of railways it might have done. If it had had the present corporation at the time the Liverpool and Man- chester Railway was made Warrington might have been in a diflerent position to-day than what it is. There was hardly any town in England better situated for water conveyance, yet there was hardly a town worse off for such conveyance. The scheme, if carried out, would be the making of Warrington, and there would be buildings from here down to Liverpool, when they got a really good navigation. He thought it was a matter of vital importance to Warrington. Mr. LONG: Even if it did not go beyond Warrington. (Laughter.) A proposition that a copy of the memorial be sdnt to Mr. Whitworth, the newly appointed secretary to the scheme, and suggesting that similar memorials should be sent from Manchester, Salford, and other local chambers, was agreed This was all the business.
THE WIRE GAUGE. The CHAIRMAN asked if the committee appointed to con- sider this question had any report to lay before the

Chamber. - Mr. MORRIS said the Masters' Association only arrived at a definite decision on the subject at the end of last week, and there had no: been time for the special committee to meet and consider the decision and suggestions of the Iron

and Steel Wire Manufacturers' Association. The PRESIDENT asked if it would be agreeable to them to have another meeting. Mr. MORRIS said he thought that would have to be done, because the special committee had on it gentlemen who did not belong to the Wire Manufacturers' Association, and who yet might have opinions on the subject of wire gauge. It was decided to hold another meeting to consider the subject.

THE PROPOSED TIDAL NANIGATION TO MANCHESTER. The PRESIDENT then proceeded to refer to a matter of vast importance to Warrington—the proposed tidal naviga- tion to Manchester. (Hear, hear.) He might tell them that at the inaugural meeting held at the house of Mr. Daniel Adatnson' at Didsbury, the preliminary proceedings were dismissed, and taken altogether, as an initiatory meeting, he thought be might venture to say it was a success. At that meeting, which was a meeting of what they might call pro- moters generally, a provisional committee was appointed with a view to seeing whether such a scheme was feasible, and whether it was desirable from a commercial aspect. That committee had had two meetings in Manchester, and he had to report to the Chamber, knowing there were many members who were very desirous of seeing something in the shape of navigation which would improve Warrington as this scheme would if carried out, that the
proceedings of these meetings had been such as led him to believe that the scheme was

practicable—[Mr. Broadbent: And will be done?]— and it was possible would be done. He confessed that up to the previous Friday be had considerable misgivings as to whether the object was attainable but lookinc, at the man- ner in which the Manchester Committee had acted, he began to believe that they were in earnest about the matter. When he looked at the representative character on the com- mittee which was acting in Manchester he was very much impressed with the feeling that it meant success; and look- ing at the matter altogether he believed the people of Warrington may yet see ships from 3,000 to 4,000 tons burden passing along the Mersey through Warrington up to Manchester. If such a thing came to pass he thought there could be no question that Warrington would very much benefit by such an undertaking. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he thought it behoved the Chamber to do everything they could to promote such an object. He had recorded on the

Iron, discussing the above scheme, says :—We never heard of any new undertaking that was not pronounced a mine of wealth by its promoters; but in this case, although estimates for works of this nature are generally below the actual cost, we believe that a fair dividend may be expected upon the outlay. At any rate the proposal deserves serious consideration, especially from the point of view of the im- mense advantages it would offer to Manchester.

minutes the following : The President informed the meting that a scheme for mak- ing a tidal navigatl'in up to Manchester was being promoted. that a guarantee fund was being subscribed, and that a cern- mittee was actively at work and would shortly issue a report determining whether the scheme was feasib'e aad likely to be a commercial success; and if favourable a company would be
formed, and possible, powers would be applied for in the next session of Parliament.

He would likewise bring before the notice of the Chamber the fact that the Liverpool Water Act of 1880 authorised the Board of Trade to determine at what depth the aqueduct from the Vyrnwy should pass under the river below Fidler's Ferry, and that such aqueduct should not interfere with the proposed improved navigation. He should like an indepen- dent member to move the following resolution :—" That this Chamber memorialize the Board of Trade to require the aqueduct to be fixed at a depth sufficient to accomplish that

object." Mr. BRoADBENT: Has not the depth already been fixed The PRESIDENT replied that it had not. He might te them that in 1880 he, not only as a memb3r of the Chamber, but as a member of the Town Council, in conjunction with the Mayor and Town Clerk, was very actively opposed to the Liverpool Water Bill, simply with a view to obtain a clause that would enable the Corporation, as far as possible, to preserve the existing navigation of the river, and like- wise to make some provision for any improvement in the navigation of the river. They drew up a clause in which they required that the aqueduct from the Vyrnwy to Liver- pool should pass under the Mersey at the point proposed— about a mile and a half from Fidler's Ferry—at a depth of not less than 15 feet below high water, when high water was 11 feet above Liverpool Old Dock sill. The clause was successfully opposed by the Liverpool Corporation, and it was perhaps a very happy thing for Warrington, or rather for the promoters of the scheme, that that was so, because they obtained a clause which he had read. It was as follows : " That notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, or in the deposited plans and sections, so much of the Vyrnwy aqueduct, by this Act authorised, as is situate below the bed of the Mersey shall be laid at such a depth under the bed of the river in the navigable channel thereof as ths Beard of Trade shall prescribe, and the sad aqueduct and all or any temporary or permanent works connected therewith shall be executed according to a plan and at a level and upon a site within the limits of lateral deviation, to be approved by the B,ard of Trade in writing, under the hand of one of their secretaries or assistant se,retaries, subject to such i estrictiens and regulations as the Board of Trade may from time to time require." He expected the Liverpool Corporation, who were now executing their works from Vyrnwy to Liverpool, were about applying to the Board of Trade for power to lay their pipes at such a depth as the Board of Trade should determine. If the Warrington Corporation had obtained the clause they prayed for, the pipes would not have been laid at a depth sufficient for the purpose of the proposed canal. Pfr. JOLLEY : Not by a long way.] He would therefore react a memorial he had drawn up on the subject ;- 1' To the Right Ron, Joseph Chamberlale, M.P. President of the Board of Tradd.--The respectful memorial of the War- rington Chamber of Otiinmerce, sheweth that your memorial- ists are deeply interested in the present and any proposed hilln"ovement of the navigation of the rivers Mersey and irwell. That we have heard with great satisfaction of a pro- posed inalroved tidal navigation of these rivers up to Man- chester that will enable the sailing of vessels of 3,000 or 4,000 tons burden up to that city, which is the commercial centre of a manufacturlrg population of six millions. That by the Liver- p3ol Water Act, 1880, your London Board are authotised to determine at what depth the aqueduct from the Vyrnwy to Liverpool shall cross the river Mersey, so that such aqueduct shall not interfere with the present or any proposed improve- ment of the navigation. Your memorialists therefore humbly pray that your London Board will be pleased to require that such alueduct, and any wo ks in connection therewith, shah be effected at such a depth, and in such a manner, as will not cause any obstruction to the carrying out of the proposed im- proved navigation.—Signed on behalf of the Warrington Chanl- her of Commerce." • Mr. MONKS said the Liverpool Corporation were going to I cut from Sir Richard Brooke's across the Mersey, but he thought the new navigation would be from Fidler's Ferry to Carter's House. Mr. BLECKLY said the memorial did not propose that the Chamber should have an opportunity of appearing before the Board of Trade. The PRESIDENT said if it had been a petition to Parlia- ment he would have put that in. Mr. RIGBY remarked that inasmuch as Warrington would be very largely involved in the scheme, he thought it would be very proper for them as a Chamber of Commerce to be heard. 1 Mr. BLECKLY stated that Manchester and Salford prayed to be heard. Mr. LONG asked whether it was not a matter more for the promoters of the scheme than for the Chamber of Com- merce. The PRESIDENT: We are looking after the interests of Warrington. Mr. RIGBY moved, and Mr. BeEckter seconded, the adop- tion of the memorial, which was carried. Mr. MoNks hoped those acting on behalf of Warring- ton would not consent to anything in the way of docks or dredging that would give them a 'less depth of water than they had now. The PRESIDENT said the committee might b 3 safely left to look at the matter from a Warrington point of view. Mr. LONG asked whether the Chamber would be within their province in asking the president why he had changed his opinion. The PRESIDENT said when he attended the meeting that took place on the previous Tuesday but one, at which Mr. Long was present, he was in a great measure under the im- pression that the engineer had not fully taken into account the difficulties that existed at Warrington and in the neigh- bourhood; but after an interview with that gentleman on the previous Tuesday week, at which he had the matter fully before him, and from what he said then from an en- gineer's point of view, he saw that the engineer was quite prepared to combat with the difficulty. It might not be generally known, but there were certain clauses affecting the railway companies in this neighbourhood, and requiring them to put up swing bridges so as not to interfere with the navigation of the river. It was a question, however, whether the Board of Trade would sanction swing bridges on a trunk line such as that from London to Scotland; still the very fact that such a clause existed would be of considerable assistance to the promoters in obtaining power requiring the railway companies to construct swing bridges. Mr. BLECRLY said what they had to consider was the in- tention that they had to regulate the canal in such a way that a vessel need not lower it masts to go right away to Manchester. They might say if they looked over the line of the London and North-Western Railway it would be a very difficult thing to raise the line to such an extent as to allow vessels of that sort to pass under, but the railway had fur- nished them themselves with a datum from which they could form an opinion. Take the line from Winsford. He found they climed right up to Runcorn Bridge and went rightedown straight to the line again ; and what could be done there could be done also in another part of the line. They would not want the line at a greater elevation than they had at Runcorn Bridge. Mr. Fulton, who had had the matter in hand for the last five or six years, had gone very carefully through it, and he had formed an opinion as tone practicability of it. It was put also in the hands of Mr. Leader- Williams, who was a practical engineer, and had been con- nected with canals all his lifetime, and his opinion was there was no insurmountable difficulty in the way. They were now taking it in hand. They were going to make a survey, and they would also submit it to a first-class gentle- man in London before the scheme came before the public;

for children's cribs. The committee d,' impos- sibilities, and they had no wish to • a not ask for t pressure upon the shoulders of the House Committ, but knowing that at the House there was steam appara' tor doing were surprised that the Ho. the work, they Committee should persistently say they would not hav,4 the washing done at the House. At the Barracks they. had no accommodation for drying the clothes. _

Major C/L<TWRlttitT : Oh my eye ! Mr. it:dows was not sorry the Major bad questioned that fact. The apparatus was on a limited scale at the ,Jarracks, atd as they were only there temporarily they had to do the best they could, and hitherto the Schools Com- mittee had done their very best to promote peace and con-
• cord throughout the establishment. The CLERK then read the following letter to the Master, dated 29th June :
The Guardians yesterday heard the matron's letter read; they also considered the remarks entered on the ss.tne subject in the
visitors' book. lam to point out to you that the 'Guardians have almost uuanimously directed that the washing referred to shall be done at their wash-houses at the workhouse, where the _ _ . .

most ample arrangements for washing exist, and that it is not competent for workhouse officers to put difficulties in the way of their directions being acted upon. With referexce to the duties of the matron, set forth in the regulations referred to In Mrs. Mackey's letter, at the schools, such duties are strictly re- quired to be performed on her part when the euardians direct washing to be done there, and they won't permit the matron to disobey their order, or act contrary to the rules • but the matron at the schools, who has also the duties of school mis- tress to perform, has not been directed to do the particular washing referred to. The Guardians approve of your obtaining any additional help that you may really require to enable obedience to their order, and they hope that in view of the great importance of the young children having a supply of clean apparel that no further discomfort hereon will arise.

Mrs. MACKEY wrote to the committee : In further reference to the washing of the Barracks clothes, I respectfully beg to state that, although I do not consider it any part of my duty, yet in deference to your wishos, and to relieve the Barracks staff from what appears to be a great diffi- culty, I will go down again by the directions of the House Committee, and do all the washing there as formerly. I can manage it on the spot much more conveniently than at the Wurkhouse; and I think you will then be convinced that the course I have taken hr the matter fully meets your approval. In reply to that the Clerk wrote the foilowing, dated 4th inst., addressed to the Matron : /kiadam,—l am directed by the Schools' Committee to ac- knowledge the receipt of your letter of this date, in reference to the washing of the sheets, blankets, and other heavy articles, and in reply to state that they insfst upon the resolution of the 29th September, 1180, being acted upon. The resolution duly approved by the Board is as follows :—" That the heavy wash- ing cloth.); be carted week'y to the Workhouse to be washed." The committee therefore cannot entertain your proposal. The MASTER reported that on the 4th inst. he received 15 children in the hospital from the Barracks (12 boys and 3 girls) with skin disease. On the 10th inst. he admitted to the hospital from the Barracks four boys, and on the following day two girls suffering from the same disease. Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded the confirmation of the School Committee's minutes. He regretted that the promise to the Board had not been carried out in respect to having the washing done at the Workhouse."lt had been done there since 1880 without much difficulty and without any unpleasant- ness, and he was sorry the Matron had ignored the resolution of the Board.—(hear, hear,)—and acted upon the instruction of the House Committee. The washing had been done at the House for the last two years and he did not see why it could not lee done there for a couple of months more with- out this unpleasantness. But the blame, if any, fell upon the House Committee who directed Mrs. Mackey not to pay attention to the resolution of the Board. Mr. GARNETT observed that it was uncourteous for three gentlemen to sign a minute in opposition of the resolution of the whole Board. There were appliances at that House which they had not at the Barracks, and he thought it would have been very much better to have worked harmoniously for a few months when there would have been an end of the question. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said when he found three gentlemen taking upon themselves to order the Matron not to do what the whole Board had ordered her to do he thought those gentlemen were taking upon themselves what they ought not to do; and he thought they would be lowering the dignity of the Board if they allow those gentlemen to dictate to them. (Hear. hear.) He for one should not submit to it, and he therefore should support the resolution of Mr. Brown. [Major Cartwright : Hear, hear.] Mr. GREENING said they had had a very eloquent address from Mr. Longshavr, but one in which he was sorry to say there was a good deal of feeling. In regard to the hose, he might remind Mr. Longshaw he had been a Guardian for sonie years, and had also been a member of the Visiting Com- mittee, and had allowed the disgraceful state of thingshe had alluded to to go on. Perhaps if they had asked Mr. Long- shaw he would have told them that there was such apparatus ; but it struck him that Mr. Longshaw even with his great foresight did not know it existed. (Laughter.) Mr. Garnett had expressed his surprise that his name was attached to the minutes. He did not know what sort of minutes that gentleman called them; but he called them sensible minutes. (Hear, hear.) In the regulations for the temporary schools was an order that the washing "shall be done" there, and that it should come up to the Workhouse was to him outrageous. They did not object to the washing being done at the House when they were able to do it ; but he believed the officers were better able to judge than he was as to what could be done by their staff. Mr. BURN again drew attention to the fact that 15 chil- dren had been brought from the Barracks, and asked if they had been properly attended to by those in authority at the Barracks. His heart really ached when he saw some of the children on Friday last. The CHAIRMAN stated that the doctor's reports had in- variably been that the health of the children was very good indeed. Dr. SPINES was called into the room, and, in reply to questions' said he had been informed that the children suffering from itch were told to keep out of his way, but he believed 'they did so because they wanted to go with the trip. Since the children had been at the Barracks there had not been a single case of zymotic disease. The CHAIRMAN asked whether they had lost one child during the time they had h2en at the Barracks. Dr. SPINES: Not that I remember. Major CARTWRIGHT : IS it as healthy as this place? Dr. SPINES: I do not see much difference. Mr. GREENING asked whether the cases sent to the ',House were cases of scabies or itch ? Dr. SPINKS : It is the same thing. (Laughter.) Mr. GREENING : You said on Friday last it was itch. Dr. SPINES: It is derived from the Greek word scab°, to scratch. , Mr. GREENING: You certainly said it was a case of com- mon itch before. Some said it was itch this morning, and others said "No, it is scabis." Mr. BnowN gave a word of warning respecting Mr. Burn. That gentleman had succeeded on two occasions in causing alarm—first in respect to the fire apparatus, and next in respect to the children. Mr. BURN rose amidst cries of "Vote," and said: Before I make a remark allow me one word! (Laughter.) I have the right to explain. ("No, no.") I think you have no right to put me down. (Cries of "Vote') I say now what I said before. You have no appliances to put a fire out in this Workhouse. The Schools Committee's minutes were unanimously passed, and a vote was taken on the minutes of the House Committee. For the minutes 7 members voted, and 15 in favour of the amendment, that the minutes be passad with the exception of that portion referring to the washing, which was carried. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: KILLING A NEIGHBOUR'S DUCK'S AT NEWTON.
div.p: KILLING A NEIGHBOUR'S DUCK'S AT NEWTON.

Before R. Houghton, T. Comber, and T. G. Gillespie, Esqrs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Emma Robinson, a married woman, residing at Newton, was charged by George Howard, a bookbinder, with maliciously killing, on the previous Tuesday, two tame ducks, kept for domestic purposes, of the value of 2s.—Mr. Moore, of War- rington, appeared for the defendant, and pleaded not guilty. The complainant stated that he owned a duck and five ducklings, and one morning when he came home two of the ducklings were dead. His wife told him that Mrs. Robinson had killed thein.—The Clerk : That is not eyidence. Did you see them ?—The complainant: I owned five ducks, and missed two of them. I have a witness here. Alice Tuustall, a girl, said she saw the defendant cut the ducks heads off with a knife, and she then ran to tell Mrs Howard. It was on Tuesday morning last, about twelve o'clock. Mrs. Robinson was in her own garden at the time, and Mrs. Howard's duck and ducklings had gone into her garden. She did not see her kill the second duck as she went to tell Mrs. Howard. When she came back two were killed.—Cross-examined by Mr. Moore : I am not certain whether it was Tuesday or Wednesday—Tuesday, I think, about twelve o'clock. I know a person named Mrs. Caton. I did not see her there. I knew the ducks belonged to Mrs. Howard. because I had seen them before. The ducklings were very little ones.—Mr. Moore : Do you mean to say that you saw this woman deliberately take a knife and kill this duck ?—The witness : Yes, sir. She had a potato in one hand and a knife in the other, and she killed the duck with the knife. I went and told Mrs. Howard, and she came to Mrs. Robinson's. I only saw her kill one duck. When I came back she had two dead ones in her hand. I did not see anyone else kill the other duck. The ducks were just on Mrs. Robinson's garden, and the old duck was with them. Between Mrs. Robinson's garden and that of the nekt door there is a hedge. I was about two yards away from Mrs. Robinson when she killed the duck. I told her that they were not our ducks, but that they were Ms, Howard's. She said," I don't care whose ducks they are, I'll kill them," and she thereupon struck one on the head. They were then in the garden. I then went and told Mrs. Howard, who lives next door but one to the defen- dant. I heard Mrs. Howard tell Mrs. Robinson that she had killed one of her ducks. I do not think the defendant made any reply to that. Mrs. Ann Howard, wife of the complainant, said the last witness knocked at her door, and from what she was told she went to Mrs. Robinson. She asked her what she had done it for, and she said she had not done it. She said she saw this girl (Alice Tunstall) do it. She (witness) said it was a cruel thing to do anything of the kind. As she was afterwards passing the defendant's house, the defendant called out "I'll kill more." She had also been round among the neighbours saying she would tear her (Mr. Howard) from limb to limb.—By Mr. Moore: I have never had any previous quarrel with Mrs. Robinson. I did not see who it was that killed the ducks. Mrs. Robinson said she did not. There were five of a hatch, and we have three "ow.—Mr. Moore: Do you know that your duck and ducklings are in the habit of trespassing on her garden? Witness: No.

4 'They are hot mine but knottier neighboiiii. It was on Wed- nesday that the ducks were killed. I nnot say who killed the second duck. They were prize eggs, and I had got them as a great favour. For the defence, Mr. Moom remarked that he would call a witness before the Bench who would swear the ducks were not killed by the defendant. There was one particular feature to which he would call the attention of the Bench. The plaintiff's wife said it occurred on the Wednesday, and that she did not see a person named Mrs. Caton there. On that day, Mrs. Caton was at the defendant's house, and Mrs. Robinson told her that the ducks of Mrs. Howard were again trespassing in the garden. They had 'seen in the habit of doing so and did a deal of damage there. Mrs. Caton and Mrs. Robinson saw them, and they did not touch or strike them in any way. All they did was to send them out of the garden. While Mrs. Howard had said it was on the Wednesday, the girl said it was Tuesday or Wednesday. There was some little discrepancy in the evidence. The de- fendant had not really killed the ducks, and she had no in- timation that she would be charged with it until she re- ceived the summons. When the complainant saw her, the defendant simply and emphatically said that she did not kill them. She simply drove them through the hedge. He must ask their worships to dismiss the case, and he felt cer- tain they would do if they could conscientiously do so. It was a pity that those two innocent little ducks should be the cause of creating a feud between persons who should live peaceably as neighbours. He then called Mary Caton, who stated that on Wednesday last she was in Mrs. Robinson's house. Mrs. Robinson was not " peeling" potatoes, and had not a knife in her hand. Mrs. Howard's ducks were in the garden, and Mrs. Robinson drove them out. They went through Tunstall's hedge. Tunstall's girl (the complainant's witness) said, "Don't send them here, they are not ours. If you do I'll kill them." She did not see Mrs. Robinson kill any of them. That was en the Wed- nesday. She did not see any of them killed. She was not related to any of the parties, and had spoken conscientiously the trnth. If Mrs. Robinson had had a knife in her hand, and had killed one of the ducks, she would have seen it. It was on the Wednesday. Mr. Moore: The complainant's wife says it was on the Wednesday. She must be wrong, or the summons, which says Tuesday, is wrong, and the case must fall through.— The Clerk said the summons was taken out on the Tuesday, and was dated for that day.—Mr. Moore said the defendant was summoned for having committed a certain offence on the 4th July—Tuesday. That was the day when the sum- mons was actually taken out and dated, but they could not convict the defendant for the simple reason that the com- plainant's wife said distinctly that it was on the Wednes- day, the sth of July. The prosecution must fall to the ground.—The Clerk observed that the little girl, the main witness, said it was Tuesday.—Mr. Moore : She :was not certain whether it was Tuesday or Wednesday.—The Clerk; She said Tuesday, but when you suggested Wednesday, she said she was not certain.—Mr. Moore said if there was a doubt about the case the defendant was entitled to the benefit of it. They did not kill the ducks; they were too young to kill. They would have wanted some green peas to them. (Laughter.) The Chairman: The defendant is fined ss. and costs, and 25., the value of the ducks. While another case was being proceeded with, the de- fendant exclaimed: What have I to do when the ducks come in our garden again ?—The Clerk: Just take that woman out of court if she is not silent.

At a subsequent period, Mr. Moore, addressing the Bench, slid he did not wish that be or anybody else should be de- ceived in that court by evidence given in any case. In the case of killing the ducks they heard one of the witnesses say they were killed with a knife, but they certainly did not present that appearance. They were in court for the inspection of the Bench if they desired to look at them. The Clerk: I think in the face of direct evidence- Mr. Moore: They are here, and if the witness says they have been killed with a knife-- The Clerk: She said they were hit on the head. The magistrates refused to accede to the request of Mr. Moore, who remarked: I have both ducks here to show that there are no marks of a knife at all.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Board held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday, Mr. G. Blackhurst presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Garnett, Greening, Cooper, Owen, Burn, Cartwright, Hall, Marsh, Wool fall, Wallington, Derbyshire, Taylor, Fairhurst, Houghton, Humphries, Longshaw, Greenall, Brown, Gib- son, Hunt, and Sutton (clerk). THE CLERK AND MAJOR CARTWRIGHT. Major CanTwetecierr was addressing the Board on the sub- ject of the removals, when The CLERK remarked upon the Major's complaints, stating that he was making all sorts of complaints when before the auditor. Major CAR'FWRIGHT: I did not go before the auditor in regard to you. The CLERK: You did. (Loud cries of "Chair, chair.") Major CARTWRIGHT: If you are the clerk—(" Chair.") If you are the clerk of this Board—(Renewed cries of "Chair.")—allow me— The CHAIRMAN: You must confine yourself to the busi- ness. Major CARTWRIGHT : Why should I be interrupted and not Mr. Sutton? Mr. BRower: If the clerk is not to make any remarks I think we ought not to hear the Major. Major CARTWRIGHT : If the clerk will be quiet until I give my explanation is reference to the removal I shall be satisfied. It is simply a question between the clerk and myself, and if I can prove it so and good. If Ido not prove it I shall be the first to apologise. Ido not say anything in regard to the clerk, but I do really want this case gone into. We have ho right to keep any pauper here that belongs to another Union. That is all. The matter then dropped. THE WASHING FOR THE BARRACKS.—THE CONDITION OF THE CHILDREN. At a meeting of the House Committee, held on the 7th inst., Mrs. Mackey again reported that she was unable to do the heavy washing for the Barracks here. The committee directed Mrs. Mackey to return the clothes sent up, and to inform the matron of the Barracks of this. Major CARTwmouT' in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that in .the meantime the matron had been down to the Barracks, and did the washing from Saturday morning to Monday at noon. The CHAIRMAN: And did sh I leave this House all day on cee y end half a day on Monday to do the washing theft ? Majer CARTwRICHI V: She is under the control of the House Committee. Don't forget that. The CHAIRMAN: I only asked the question. Major CARTWRIGHT: I have had no complaint since— not a word. I believe the work was done and properly done, and I verily believe the work can be done there. Mr. BURN seconded the motion, and stated he was quite willing to support his friend the Major when he was right. He thought that.morning, though the Clerk and the Major might differ, Major Cartwright's object was to save the rates, and he ought to he supported in that matter. He went on to say that in going round the house the committee found no less than 15 childten who had been sent up from the schools suffering frOm the itch, and a more disgraceful state of affairs he did not know. Mr. LteleiSHAW It is not true. The CHAIRMAN: Now, Mr. Burn, go on. what there was. Mr. BURN said they were told it was the itch, and there '-enst be something radically wrong at the school, as the children, when they were known to be afflicted with the disease, were told to keep out of the way of the doctor. Mr. GARNETT rose to a point of order, and asked had the discussion anything to do with the minutes. The CLERK: There is nothing on the minutes. Mr. GARNETT : Then if there is nothing on the minutes I think we ought to dispose of them first. Mr. GREENING said Mr. Burn and one or two other mem- bers made the wonderful discovery that there was no hose in connection with the outlet of the tank, and there was no connection so as to use the engine be case of are. The Board would see from the minutes that a resolution was passed that Messrs. Greening and Sons be asked to send in an estimate for making the necessary connection with the down pipe from the tank. That day week be came to the workhouse alone.to investigate the matter quietly, and see how it stood. In conjunction with Mr. Mackey he discovered that there was a valve in the down pipe from the tank all right, and a fire plug outside; and on further search they found a hydrant in the engine house, which they put all right, so that at the present time they did not need to spend a penny. They could put on the hose and supply water to almost any part of the house. Mr. LONGSHAW said everything was neglected, and a per- feet disgrace to the House Committee, the Master, and every one concerned. And yet the members of the House Committee interfered with other committees, and en- deavoured to upset the decisions of the Board and the School Committee. The state of things was a perfect disgrace to the Board, and the sooner the House Committee did their own work properly and said nothing about other people the better. (Laughter and applause.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that there was not much differ- ence between Mr. Burn's statement and that of Mr. Greening in regard to the fire apparatus. Mr. DArtisesnenE was in favour of the minutes of the House• Committee being passed, with the exception of that portion referring to the washing. (Hear, hear.) He wished to correct a statement en reference to the How& Committee having power over the officers of the Workhouse. The Board had power over those officers and not the committee, who were appointed to see that the officers discharged their duties in a proper manner, and to examine the state of the house, and the quality of the provisions. The House Com- mittee had no more power over the officers than any other committee. He moved art amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of that relating to the washing. Mr. LONGSHAW seconded. Mr. Bnowet then asked that the minutes of the Schools Committee should be read; and they were read by the Clerk—
Let us bear

The Schools Committee's book contained an entry, under d rte 4th inst., that there were 19 scabies cases, some of which were of a mild form. A letter was read from Mrs. Mackey referring to the question of washing of clothes from the schools, at the Workhouse. It was ordered that the superintendent hand the letter to the clerk to reply in accordance with the former reso- lutions of this committee and confirmed by the Board. At a meeting held on the 11th inst. it was reported that there were about 20 mild cases of scabies. The superintendent reported that he had called upon the clerk as per the committee's minutes of last week, and that Mrs. Mackey came to the schools to take charge of the washing of the sheets, which were directed by the committee and the Board to be done at the Workhouse. Mr. BROWN moved the confirmation of the minutes of this committee. Major CARTWRIGHT objected, and stated that it was very irregular to proceed in this way.
