div.head: GREAT STRIKE IN THE COAL TRADE.
div.p: GREAT STRIKE IN THE COAL TRADE.
3,000 MEN OUT ON STRIKE. The probabilities of a settlement of the dispute between
he firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. and their colliers

and day-wage-men, are as far removed as ever, and from to- day (Saturday) the strike assumes a far more serious and alarming aspect. Hitherto, since the notice of the firm ex- pired on last Tuesday week, about 700 men only have been out of employment, but the notices of about 2,500 others expired last (Friday) night, and as no agreement has been come to with the men, they were expected to stay away this morning. With this apparent unanimity on the part of the men to resist the reduction of tea per cent., and to oppose the system of fortnightly pays instead of weekly, there is an equally firm resolve and determination on the part of the firm to persist in the reduction, and the struggle is thus likely to become a very protracted one. As will be remembered, Messrs. Evans gave notice of a reduction of ten per cent. and fortnightly pays in the wages of their colliers at Pewfall and Downall Green collieries, which notice expired last Tuesday week. As the men had decided to resist the alterations, the colliers, who numbered about 590, came out on strike. They did not return on the morning of the day after the expiration of the notice, and the day-wage-men, numbering about 120, were told that if they intended to stay at work they woad have to go in the mine and get coal. As they refused to comply with this notice, nearly all the day-wage-men left, making a total of about 710 men out of employment. In the meantime, a mass meeting of the miners was held, and a deputation ap- pointed to wait on the masters. This deputation met Mr. B. B. Glover, the agent of the firm, on the Ist inst., and the men handed in their notice, which was dated that day. The colliers' notice was to the -effect that if the reduction was persisted in they would leave work in fourteen days, and the day-wage-men applied for an advance of ten per cent, the amount they had been reduced during the last few months. This notice expired yesterday (Friday), and it was expected that the men would brir.g out their tools, and stop working from this morning. The Peufall and Downall Green pits—three in number—were entirely closed last Wednesday week, and the whole of the 14 pits will probably be stopped from to-day. The firm employed about 3,000 colliers and under-ground hands, while with top-hands, foundry men, dsc. the number is increa-ed to about 4,000. During the week rumours have been rife to the effect that the firm had offered to concede five per cent. if the men would return to work, but we have the authority of Mr. Glover for stating that the statement is entirely without foundation, The firm, he said, were as determined as ever to carry out the reduction, and they intended to' continue the struggle till the men submitted. The firm has been working at such a great loss for some time past, that they had no other course to adopt but reduce the wages of the meu, aad that they fully intended to do. Mr. Glover told our representative on Wednesday after- noon last, that the reasons for the reduction taking place (and such as he told to the deputation of the men) were that owing to the bad trade and the low selling prices of coal, the firm foun.d themselves in such a position that they were compelled to do so. This was also done in accordance with an agreement with the men last year. On the let November, a deputation of the men waited upon him (Mr. Glover) and applied for an advance of ten per cent in their wages. Upon the strength of the markets, and the fact that the selling prices of coal had advanced, they gave the men ten per cent. upon the distinct, understanding that if their prices in the markets were not maintained, the ten per cent. would have to come off again. He said that the men should not blame him for the disturbance, but should candidly tell the public that it was they who were causing it by not keeping the bargain of last Novem- ber. With respect to fortnightly pays, Mr. Glover said the firm wished the system to be brought into operation owing to the increased expense the trouble, and annoyance put upon the firm by weekly payments. He (Mr. Glover) believed that if the men's wives were canvassed, nine out of every ten would be in favour of the proposed alteration. Mr. Glover said he distinctly told the deputation that if they submitted to the reduction the men would certainly have it given back to them as soon as they could afford to give it, by the prices in the markets being advanced. The reduction was not to go through all the pits, as had been stated, for the firm had some pits where the collier's were working for wages 10 per cent. less that what they were really entitled to, but owing to the very bad state of trade and considering that they were selling that coal is, per ton less in the market, the firm could not afford to give them any advance. Alluding to the statement that he had "twitted " the colliers and day-wagemen, Mr. Glover said he told the depu- tation that he had every sympathy with them, for he believed that their wages at the present time were quite little enough, in fact, as had been stated, could hardly keep body and soul together. He told the deputation that, and also remarked to them that it was a strange thing the colliers would quietly stand by and see the day-wage-men's wages reduced from 3s. Bd. to 3s. 4d. per day right through the pits without a single word of opposition. Directly the colliers wages were touched they sought the sympathy of the day-wage-men, and promised that if they would help them the colliers would also assist them in return. Mr. Glover also informed the deputation that he had been told by one of the day- wage-men that morning that they did not intend to help the colliers, as the latter had not helped them. Referring to other matters Mr. Glover said that with respect to the notice served by the men, he had informed Mr. Dix,who introduced the deputation,that he did not take their notice as a legal one, because he thought it should be given from the " making-up " day they could not give him a notice from any day they liked. He thought that in all fairness to the firm, the men should work up to the Tuesday, when " making-up " was reached. Mr. Dix said he wopld lay the matter before the men, and he thought they would work up to the Tuesday night. Mr. Glover told him not to misunderstand him. He did not say that to get two more days' work from the men, but simply that each side should deal fairly with the other and take no mean ad- vantage in any shape. Referring to the composition of the deputation, Mr. Glover said it was not true that each pit was represented by two men. The men at their two Parr pits had not attended a single meeting, nor had he (Mr. Glover) received any communication from them in any way. If the Parr men stopped on the Saturday he had decided upon a certain course, select one or two men to take before the magistrates as test cases of the legality of the notice. The proceedings would be taken without any ill- feeling, and simply as a test case. Mr. Dix said it would be all right,and they would try it. Mr. Glover also said it was

not true that they had men working 40 per cent. below gIY other. It is stated that the masters are willing to meet 3 O% tation of the men at any time, and they are as anTO ;ibue to be as lenient with them as they possibly can be. by they have been willing to avert and preventa stri,lc.a notice of anything reasonable, they cannot withdravr theheo _el with the reduction after the bargain that was made masters do not wish a strike to ensue on behalf of the. t„ themselves. The firm appear to be determined in theirsq. the firm have expressed their intention to pressed intention to carry on the struggle until the men L last November. The reduction must take place, though 4: mit, and not the slightest hope can be held out that the aolor will be withdrawn. Though the bit banks are well stockme_ without reducing thens to any great extent. It is an the stood that they are being supported in the struggle 1/ ..,. colliery proprietors of Lancashire, and not the slightere difficulty has been experienced in getting coals to meet tm., their reqairements of the firm and to enable them to suPPIY customers. la ancl several meetings of the men have recently been he—, i at each a resolution was passed that they should contine the struggle with the masters. The prospect is, therefeore; a very gloomy and dispiriting one, and only a deteralni _e: and persistent struggle as to who can hold out the lo geP is what can be expected. ; i fight " the Ter!

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL B.)ARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL B.)ARD.

Mr. F. H. Gossage presided at the monthly meeting of this Board, held on Tuesday at the Board's offices. The other members present were Messrs. Kershaw, Carey, Pank- burst, Handley, Booth, Wright, Midwood, Johnson, Martley, Forster, Shuttleworth, Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Roberts kengineer), and Dickson kinspector). THE SURCHARGES REMITTED. A communication was read from the Local Government Board informing the Board that they had considered their appeal against disallowances and surcharges of sums amount- ing to £460 16s. Bd. which were made by Mr. Darlington, district auditor, together with his reasons for such disal- owances and surcharges, and the correspondence which had aken place in reference to the appeal. As regarded the sum f £403 las. Bd., the Board directed the writer to refer them o the letter which they had addressed to Mr. Heyes, con- veying their decision upon his appeal against the disal- lowance and surcharge of a sum of £64 6s. 10d. As in the case of that disallowance and surcharge the Board in the present iastance upheld the legality of the auditor's decision with respect to the disallowance and surcharge of the sum of £4O 16s. Bd., and the four sums of £l5 which were paid to Mr. W. Cooper as salary for his services as medical officer of health. It appeared that on the 12th February, 1873, Mr. Cooper was appointed to the office referred to for a period of one year, ard that in the month of March. 1874, he was reappointed for a period of 12 months, from the termination of his former engagement. But upon the expiration of the 12 months he was not reappointed, although, on the 3rd June, 1879, the Local Board purported to authorise the payment of an increase of salary to him, and he had no legal appointment as medical officer during the period in respect to the four sums of £l5 which were paid to him. The Board were therefore of opinion that the auditor's decision in respect to the dis- allowance and surcharge of those sums was lawful for the last reason he had assigned, namely, that there was no legal authority for the payment. The Board were prepared, how- ever, under the present circumstances, to remit the several disallowances and surcharges in question, in the exercise of the equitable jurisdiction conferred upon them by 11 and 12 Viet., cap. 91, sect., 4; and 33 and 39 Vict., cap. 55, sect. 247. The CLERIC said there were three letters like that, all re- mitting surcharges. Mr. liAtimmy But since then the appointment of Mr. Cooper had been put right. The CLERK: Yes.

A letter was read from the Woolton Local Government Board complaining of the emmission of dense smoke from the Netherley works, and asking that steps would be taken to abate it.

Dr. Boon' : They should come to Widnes. The CHAIRMAN : If there is an emission of smoke it is through gross negligence on the part of our stokers, at Netherley. HIGHWAY, &C. CO3INIITTEE—WATERLOOHOAD CROSSING—

div.head: DESTRUCTION TO PROPERTY.
div.p: THE DESTRUCTION TO PROPERTY.

At a special, meeting of the above committee, held on the 26th June, letters dated 13th and 19th June were read from Mr. H. Mather, in reference to claiming £303 as compensation for breach of contract. It was recommended that the Board repudiate Mr. Mather's claim. The surveyor was instructed to write to Mr. Mather for any account he may have for extras. At an ordinary meeting held on the 19th June, a letter was read from Mr. H. Mather asking for a further payment on account of the Moss Brook Bridge approaches. It was recom- mended that the Finance Committee make a payment of £l6O on surveyor's certificate. Mr. Aathei's account, £l2 Is. 9d. for alterations at sewer in Bank-street, was presented, and it was recommended that it be referred to the Finance Committee. A letter dated 12th June was read from Mr. Hitch!n on bahalf of Mr. B. White, complaining of the damage done by surface water from Viaduct, Parsonage, and Bank-streets. The sur- veyor was instructed to reply denying liability. In reference to Waterloo-road crossing, letters dated 20th and 22nd June were read from L. and N.-W. Ry. Co. stating that the altera- tions which they c snsidered necessary were completed, and that the shunting had been so much reduced that it might be said there was no ground for complaint. Recommended that the Company's engineer be asked to meet the Highway Committee, on the spot, at an early date. A letter from Mr. James Taylor, dated 26th June, was read a-king for the dtain in Peel House-lane to be deepened, and as to laud to be given up for road improvements. Recommended that Mr. Taylor be in- formed that this Board was willing to carry out its former minute as to rand, and that th 3 survey ,r was instructed to report to a future meeting about the drain. A letter was read dated 12th June, from B. and M. R. Co., statlng that they pro- posed raising the wall in Moss Bank-road three feet. This was considered satisfactory. On the sth July, Mr. Beasley's account was submitted and referred to the Finance Committee. The surveyor submitted his schema on public lighting for dividing the district into four divisions of about six miles, and about the same number of lamps in each division. It was re- Commended he be instructed to obtain estimates for the light- ing, extinguishing, and cleaning in each division or the whole of the district ; also estimate for glazing. A letter was read, dated Ist July, from the Runcorn Property Company, asking for the footwalk in front of the houses in Lower House-lane to be curbed and :nicked as per agreement. It was recommended that the surveyor be instructed to proceed with the same. It was recommended that the clerk be instructed to write to the Inspector of police, calting his attention to the wanton destruc- tion of property in this township, and suggesting that an example should be made of a few of the i-ffenders.

Mr. KERSHAW moved the adoption of the minutes, and, referring to the letter from the London and North-Western Railway Co., said the steps taken the committee did not con- sider satisfactory, and they thought it well to ask the com- pany to meet them on the ground so that the committee might have an explanation from them as to whether they intended to do anything further. He thought there was less shunting than there was formerly, but the committee were inclined to press upon the company the necessity of afford- ing better facilities for crossing the road. Mr. Mtuwoon, in seconding, asked if the surveyor had received the bill of extras from Mr. Mather. The SURVEYOR: No, I have not.

Mr. MARTLEY remarked that he did not think there was anyone who suffered more from destruction to the property than he did, and he hoped some good would result from the• letter that had been written in reference to the subject. The minutes were agreed ta. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

On the motion of Mr. PAI.4KHURST, seconded by Dr. BOOTH, I the minutes of this committee, which were as follows, were Ad3pted :- 4. meeting of the Gas and Water Committee was held on the oth nit., The engineer's report was read. It stated that the Pp, " Cross," at lc. eihericy, had worked satisfactorily since sg Leiser' over on the sth June for the month's trial wor Several letters received from Messrs. Daglish during the month were submitted. One of the 27th June referred to their pro- posed mode of reducing the noise made by the working of the large valves. Pumping had been carried on continually at the station since the sth, exceping a stoppage for 16 hours on the 12th, by Messrs. Daglish, to put in additional weight, and other matters, and auother by the Board for three hours on the 27th, to rectify matters in the pumping main. In conse- quence of the pedestal bolt and cap, attached to the gearing for working the air pump, breaking at midnight on the 28th June the engine lead been stored.from that time, waiting the repairs to be made, A etch Coal been prepared for a proposed tackle L°7 Winov.ing the ends or covers of the surface condenser, when requisite, for the purpose of cleaning or replacing any of the tubes. The ccst of the tackle shown was estimated at a4;4 this Including the cast and Wrought ironwork, the base stone 3 for columns, and erection. Consequent on matters at Netherley,. Cemparatlyely little work had been done at Stocks Well. Water In stock, 22rt June, 1882, 10,218,529 gallons. The rainfeill for the month had been—Per Gas-yard guage 5 150 leer", per Pex-hill gauge 5'565 inches; mean 5'457 inches. Water puenp-d during the four weeks ending 21st June, 1882, 35,737,143 gals; corresponding period 1881, 39;014,702 gals.; decrease percent.. B'4o. Water delivered during the four weeks ending 21st June, 1882, 36,289,220 gals ; corresponding period 1881, 38,814,36 gals.; decrease per cent., 6•30. Gm made during the four weeks ending 21st June. 1882, 2,963,000 cubic feet; corresponding period 1881, 3,184,000 cuble feet; decrease per cent.. 6•94. Gas delivered during the four weeks ending 21st June, 1832, 2.810,000 cubic feet; corresponding period 1831, 3,114,000 cubic feet; decrease per cent. 976. The illuminating power of the gas during the month has averaged 16.51 candles. The letter from 11. Daglish & Co., dated 27th inst., was read, explaining the propcsed mode of preventing the noise now made by the main steam valves; and it was recommended that it be referred to the engineer to have the necessary alterations made. A letter from the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Co., re hire of in- struments, was held over for further consideration. Mr. Deacon, engineer to the Liverpool Corporation, wrote with reference to a branch being put on the Vyrnwy main for the Board's supply, stating that the matter had attention. A letter was read from Messrs. T. Lea & Son, in reply to the engineer's complaint of the quality of slack supplied, and the engineer was instructed to insist upon a quality equal to the sample being supplied. It was recommended that the tackle for removing condenser ends at Netherley be obtained at an esti- mated cost of £ll complete A letter was read from Mr. Oppenheim as to exchange of land with the Sheffield and Mid- land -Railway Company at the Ditton-road Gasworks, the com- pany now having the whole of the'frontage on Ditton-road. Recommended, that Mr. Oppenheim be instructed to insist upon the clause inserted by him in the agreement requiring the company to take over the full liability of making, sewering, &C., Ditton-road, opposite such frontage.
THE NEW BYE LAWS.-MR! _KERSHAW AND TILE CHAIRMAN.

- At a meeting of the Health Committee, held on the 17th June, the annual inspection of the district was reported, the committee having visited the following places: Promenade, near to the river; No. 104, Hurst-street; property in Bank- street, Beamont-street, Parsonage-road, North-street, Barn- street, Elizabeth-street, Travis-street, George-street, Edmund- street, and Derby-road (No. 4, d:c.), excavation on Dr. Robin- son's land, Church-street; closet, No. 69, Waterloo-road ; Mr. Lee's stable, Victoria-road; Mr. Bentley's cellar, Lugs- dale-road; and Mr. Urquhart's backyard, Charlotte-street; stagnant water, at and near Moor-lane, Lugsdale-road, behind Oxford-street, and off Albert-road. also the following unadopted streets: Wellington, Marsh, Elizabeth, Margaret, George, and Victoria streets. The Travis-street property was occupied, but had neither a water supply or closets. The alterations which had been made at some of the properties were approved. In other cases the Surveyor and Inspector were instructed to serve the requiste notices to abate nuis- ances, and to close houses unfit for human habitation. The committee considered that if the unadopted streets, with the exception of Victoria-street, were- well cindered, clothing more might be required for a time.—At a meeting on the 4th inst.., the Medical Officer reported for June as follows : Births 110, 52.8 per 1,000; death (total) 36, 11.28 per 1,000; including children under one year 9 4'32 per 1,000; children between one and five years 10, 4 8 per 1,000; zymotic diseases 3, 1.4 per 1,000; inquests 2. The Nuisance Inspector's report for June stated that the three deaths classified as zymotic were from scarlet fever, typhoid, and diarrhcea. Scarlet fever had been reported Porn three houses, Bridge-street, West Bank. Children were affected; one died and the others were convalescent. The Medical Officer and he had inspected the houses, disinfec- tion and isolation were being carried out as far as possible, and the children were kept from school. The Surveyor had had the ditch between Moor-lane and Cheshire Lines Rail- way thoroughly cleaned, and Messrs. W. and M. Taylor had effectually abated the nuisance at their property in Moor-

lane. As to meat inspection 181bs. ham, and 371bs. beef had I been destroyed.—The Clerk was instructed to write to the Local Government Board, suggesting certain improvements which might be made in the Canal Boats Act, 1877, Amend- ment Bill.—The new bye-laws, as approved at the special Board meeting, on the 28th February, 1882, having now been laid on the table for two months, as suggesteel by Mr. Kershaw, it was recommended that they be printed, and for- warded to the Local Government Board for confirmation.— It was recommended that Mr. Beasley's account be referred to the Finance Committee, and the Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for June were £2l 16s. Bd., an in- crease compared with last year of £8 9s. 11d. Five shops were still let, and the stalls are doing better.—lt was recom- mended that the fair be not advertised, in accordance with the wish of the Board. _ _ _

Mr. CAREY proposed the adoption of the minutcs of the committee, and said it had been the custom of the Board to grant the use of the Market Hall for the annual exhibition of the Window Plant Association, and he asked the Board to permit the use of the building for that purpose this year. Mr. WRIGHT seconded.

Mr. JOHNSON adverted to the report on the annual inspection, and asked whether the streets were sewered at the expense of the Board or the property owners. Mr. KERSHAW thought the chairman of the committee must have forgotten himself when he made the recommenda- tion on the new bye-laws. It was a matter for the joint committee to whom it was referred, but now it was brought up by the Health Committee. He would like to know whether the new members had seen the bye-laws. He had looked for them, but had never seen them; and if they had not been presented to the new members he thought it would be altogether consistent to ask them to pass the recommenda- tion. It was necessary the new members should know what they had to deal with. Mr. HANDLEY asked what improvements had been suggested to the Local Government Board in connection with the Canal Boats Act -Amendment Bill.

Mr. JOHNSON adverted to the shopsin the market-and said it would be advantageous to reduce the rents and get all the shops let. The market had been a great loss to the Board, and it was no use having the market doing nothing, or next to nothing. Mr. CAREY, replying to Mr. Johnson, said be thought his suggestion was an extremely good one, and it was one on which the committee had acted on one or two former occasions. The committee would be very glad indeed to take the suggestion into consideration at their next meeting, and see if it was possible to reduce the rents any further. they quite agreed with Mr. Johnson that it was better to let the shops at some price than no price; but Mr. Dixon re- minded him that the shops were all let and occupied on Saturdays at about is. 6d. a day as stalls, instead of as shops at 2e. 61 a week, so that there was not the loss there appeared to be at first sight. Mr. JOHNSON: We have before us here only five shops, and that was the reason I mentioned the matter.

Mr. C.&REY said the shops were not let as shops. On Saturday afternoon they let them as stalls, and as to reduc- ing the weekly rent they would certainly consider the matter at the next meeting. Referring to the bye-laws, he said he did not know why Mr. Kershaw had such determined opposition to these unfortunate bye-laws. A great many months ago when he came to the Board for the second time, he objected to the bye-laws, and the committee delayed them for many months:in order to satisfy him on certain points. They had two or three meetings at which the bye-laws were properly thrashed out, and he understood Mr. Kershaw personally was fairly satisfied with the result. Of course none of them were absolutely satisfied, because they did not get ab3olutely their own way. Still, they arrived at a sort of compromise upon some matters, and he thought all the members who went through them at the time were fairly satisfied with the result. But Mr. Kershaw recommended in February last that, as they were so near the election they should allow the bye-laws to remain on the table for two or three months that they might be read over by the new mem- bers. The bye-laws had been what was technically under- stood asbeing on the table. They had been open to the inspection of the new members, who had had a full opportunity of reading them over. The reason why the com- mittee were pressing the bye-laws forward was because they feel it highly implrtant that the bye-laws should be passed without delay. Of course, if any member had any sugges- tion to make by which the bye-laws could be improved it would be perfectly absurd for them not to acknowledge the improvement, and they would be very clad to accept it. But in the absence of any such suggestiou the committee must press for the bye-laws to be submitted to the Local Government Board forthwith. As to sewering streets, all private streets were to be done at the expense of the pro- perty owners. Victoria-street he thought ought to be made, but all that they were doing woald be done at the expense, in the case of all private streets, of the property owners. Mr. JOHNSON Victoria-street included. I presume?

Mr. CAREY : Yes; unless they could prevail upon the committee to do what they ought to do—insist upon the making of tt e streets. He had been through the Canal Boats bill with Mr. Dickson, and the Canal Boats Inspec- tion, and found there were one or two clauses which they thought would press very hardly upon some Of the poorer owners of boats, and which in that district at all events were unnecessary. He thought it was quite right they should be applied to the boats called narrow boats of the midland counties; but they did not apply to the boats on the Mersey, and he thought it ought to be pointed out to the defendant responsible for the Bill that the boats at Widnes differed in a great many respects from the ordinary canal boats of the country:

Mr. •Minwoon thought Mr. Carey was wrong as to the bye-laws. He had been very anxious to see them, but had never seen a scrap of paper. The CHAIRMAN : Have you applied to Mr. Allen ? Mr. Marwoon : No, sir, I have not. The statement made was that they had been oa the table, but I am sure I have never seen them.
The CHAIRMAN : I have al ways understood the papers were in the office so that any member could apply to see them.

Mr. MthwooD : How could I get to know that these bye- laws were there ? They are very important indeed, and I think it should be the duty of every member to read them carefully through before supporting them in any way. Mr. KERSHAW : My remark was that this matter is not in the bands of the Health Committee at all. Mr. CAREY : The bye-laws have been out of the hands of the joint committee a long time. Mr. KERSHAW : Not at all.
nANDLEY The Board decided that they should oir.be left over for two m0;,...4.1.41: and it is a question for the Board. _ _ _
_ The CHAIRMAN : I think every paution has been taken in this matter. _ _ _ _
Mr. KERSHAW : I most certainly sly that is not so. The new members do not know about them.
Mr. MIDWOOD : I have been waiting to hear about tbem.
The CHAIRMAN said it was quite within the province of any member to move that the recommendation be referred back to the committee.
Mr. KERSUA.IV, who remained seated? said; I think it is wror24---, The CuAimiAN: Then get on your legs, and we shall hear what you bare to say. Mr. KERSILIW : Perhaps you will Hit file up

The CHAIRMAN : If you do not speak in a proper way to the Board you will excuse me if I leave the chair. We have rules to which everybody ought to conform, and after this expression of opinion I shall certainly resign the chair unless you support me. Mr. WRIGHT : I think we have a right to support the Chairman, and I think Mr. Kershaw has spoken too strongly —stronger than becomes him or any other member. I have read the bye-laws relating to Health Department, but I have not seen the bye-laws relating to the highway. The CAMILUAN : Excuse me, that is not the question. I have asked the Board to support me. Mr. WRIGHT: I beg to propose that the Board support the chairman.
Mr. FORSTER seconded the proposition, which was carried, all voting in favour of it except Mr. Kershaw. Mr. KErtsuaw then rose to move an amendment to the minutes_._ He suposed he might do so.

The CHAIRMAN, interrupting, said at a previous meeting the Board passed some rules, and one of these rules was, in addressing the chairman each member should stand on his feet, and should not speak more than once on any subject. At the time these ru!es were passed everybody agreed to them, and as long as he sat in that chair he should expect the members of the Board to treat him with due respect, and to keep to the rules. He got no advantage from being chair- man of the Board. He had been a servant of Widnes for a dozen years now, and this was the first time he had been asked to take tbe chair. No, it was not the first time. He hid been asked several times, but had always refused before, because he thought his temper was not sufficient. He thanked the Board for supporting him, and he thought Mr. Kershaw would also support him. Mr. KERSHAW remarked that in the heat of the discussion he might have been disrespectful to the Chairman, and if he had be begged to apologise. The CHAIRMAN: I quite accept your apology, Mr. Ker- shaw.

Mr. KERSRAW then went on to observe that he did not want to make an amendment to the minutes. He wished the chairman of the committee could see his way to with- draw the recommendation. He did not wish to say an angry word in reference to it; but they had heard members say they had not read the highway bye-laws, and it was only justice that they should have time to consider them. Mr. CARET did not wish to be obstinate and pi ess the bye- laws at the present moment if members had not seen them. He considered, however, that it was entirely the fault of those members if they bad not seen the bye-laws. He thought instead of being unjust to them they had been very unjust to the committee, b2cau92 all this time the bye-laws had been on the table in order that they might have an oppor- tunity of seeing them. His object was to get the bye-laws passed so that the Board might be able to combat with some of the tendencies in that neighbourhood to unsanitary con- ditions, and so long as the bye-laws were not passed the Board would not be able to grapple with the state of things that now existed. No one had delayed them more than Mr. Kershaw,—he did not say he had done it pur- posely—but still he would consent to the bye-laws being de- layed another month if it was clearly understood that the new members would have the goodness to spend a few hours on the bye-laws during that period, so that at the next meeting the Board would be able to pass them. The CHAIRMAN : I have spoken to Mr. Allen on the sub- ject, and he says he will be able to supply each member with a copy of the bye-laws. MT. FINANCE. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on sth I inst., it was recommended that Mr. Mather's account, £l2 7s 9d, for lengthening dra'n in Bank-street, be referred to the Board. Several baying failed to keep up their pay- ments as agreed upon, it was recommended that unless pay- ment be made within one month, legal proceedings be taken for recovery of the same. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 24th June, sanctioning the keep- ing of one current account instead of three as at present. The month's collections amounted to £1,597 7s lid. Mr. MIDWOOD drew attention to the account of £ll 7s 9.1 for work done at West Bank, which it was understood was completed some years ago. The work had been charged to the property owners and paid for, but now the Board were expecting the ratepayers to pay a sum that the property owners had paid for a supposed completed sewage scheme. In his opinion it was not justice to call upon the ratepayers to pay for private work. The CHAIRMAN: What do you recommend on the sub- ject?

Mr. MIDWOOD recommended that the gentlemen who gave orders for the private work to be done out of public money should pay for it. The CHAIRMAN said that could not be put to the Board. Mr. HIGGINSON said it was Mr. Mather's property. The CHAIRMAN said the question was—could the Board make the property owners make the extra length, or was it not much better to do the work at a small expense and give the public the benefit of it. Mr. HANDLEY proposed, and Mr. FORSTER seconded, that the account be referred back to the committee.
Mr. MIDIVOOD moved, and it was seconded, that the bill be not paid. The amendment was lost, and the proposition having been passed, the minutes were confirmed.

occupied the large room on tkn ground floor, and the scene it presented on entering was a very pretty one. Arranged round the room were the stalls, seven in number, laden with a great variety of beautiful articles, affording many striking contrasts in cplour. Each stall was surmounted with a peak, bearing a trophy of flags, while in the centre of the room was what may be best described as an imitation fountain, almost hidden by an encircling cluster of hot house flower- ing plants. and ferns. Add to this the moving throng of charmingly attired stallholders and visitors, and the picture is complete.

No. 1 stall was presided over by Lady Brooke and the Misses Brooke. It would be tedious to describe the many beautiful articles to be seen on this stall, but the fine selec- tion of Venetian glass ornaments and Valeure pottery can- not pass unnoticed. Handsome hand painted ornaments and painted hani screens, executed by Lady Brooke and the Misses Brooke, were very numerous. A painted screen given by Lady Brooke was much admired, and quickly sold for £lB 18s. There were also three water-coloured draw- ings, the work of Major Orred; China plaques given and painted by Mrs. Higson; pin cushions painted with repre- sentations of horses by Mr. Egerton Warburton, M.P. ; a beautiful banner screen worked in beads, lace tea tablecloths, and a large variety of other goods. No. 2 stall presided over by Airs. Barclay, Mrs. Brundrit, and Mrs. Bryant. Here was a splendid large sofa blanket of double Berlin wool in crewel work, and a handsome easy chair made of walnut wood and upholstered in silk. A beautiful stool in ebony and gold, attracted much attention. Those visitors not in search of the ornamental, had here the opportunity of purchasing a sewing machine, and there was also a quantity of useful wearing apparel. The men at Mr. Brundrit's shipyard had exercised their ingenuity in making a number of wood-work goods and also a model ship. A number of Queen Anne tables, cushions, antimacassars, tea cosies, drc., completed the stock. No 3 stall, presided over by Mrs. Crosby, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. White, Mrs. Summerfield, and Miss Booth, contained some exceedingly pretty specimens of Mintons, Turners, and Old English pottery, one set of the former in the willow pattern, being especially good. A well executed oil painting of Endor,Wales, by Thorley, occu- pied a prominent place. There were also a handsome electro- plated tea and coffee service, and a beautiful silver tea kettle; pretty banner and fire screens in crewel work and beads; Queen Anne tables; a fender, stool, and buffets, in crewel work, sic.

No. 4 stall was under the superintendence of Mrs. Wigg and Mrs. Steele, and possessed an attraction in the shape ot an automatum. This was a negress, attired in gorgeous finery, and holding a basket of flowers. When the mechan- ism was wound up, a "melody of sweet sounds" was heard, and a flower opened disclosing a monkey grinning as only a monkey can. On this closing another opened, and a small fairy was discovered dancing, while last of all appeared a white mouse, twirling round and round. An Indian cabinet of exquisite workmanship was for sale ; also a miniature horse and cart, excellently made by Mr. Barrow, of Haltrm ; a model brig made by the joiners at Weston Works, a charmingly worked devotional chair, a lounge chair in old gold, and several large dolls. No, 5 stall, presided over by Mrs. Charles Hazlehurst and Mrs. G. Lloyd Wigg, pcssessed among numerous other desi- rable objects, several pretty water-coloured drawings, a great variety of beautifully worked chairs in velvet and beads, a number of skilfully painted large plaques, banner screens, cushions, antimacassars, iikc. A large doll's cot, with crimson curtains, was very pretty, and attracted some atten- tion. No. 6 stall was in charge of Mrs. Claudet, Mrs. Fitzsimons, and Miss Imison, and in addition to the usual articles found at bazaars, contained a pretty carved birdcage of no mean workmanship, while a handsome skin cu.., from Australia, occupied a prominent place. Not the least valuable article was an excellent wringing and mangling, machine. A nnmber of artistically printed terracotta orna- ments and fans, and several water-coloured drawings were tastefully disposed on the stall. There was a seventh stall, named the "Newtown," pre- sided over by Mrs: Meadowcroft, Mrs. Mather, Mrs. Pownall, Mrs. Cropper, Mrs. Roberts, and Mrs. Carr. It was crowded with a miscellaneous assortment of goods of all kinds, in- cluding a model brig made by Captain Smith. The articles we have thus briefly alluded to were only a very small proportion of the goods displayed, which were of great variety, and their tasteful arrangement showed the ladies were no novices in the art of decoration.

An adjoining schoolroom had been adapted as a refresh- ment room, where public luncheon and tea was provided on luesday and Wednesday. The decorations were very effec- tive. The windows were draped with red and white cur- tains; trophies of figs adorned the wall ; and in one corner a flower stall, constructed after the style of a fernery, pleased the eye with the bright colours of its contents, which soothed the. senses with their delightful fragrance. Miss Hunt, Miss Johnson, and Miss Rowlands were the ladies entrusted with the oversight of this stall, and who, with the aid of Mr. Wright, had so artistically arranged the flowers and plants. The refreshment stall was presided over by Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Joule' Mrs. P. Wright, Mrs. C. Pownall, Mrs. Wm. Bankes, and Miss Wilson. The conformation of the building made it especially adapted fOr the multifarious uses of a bazaar, and the many rooms it contained were fully utilized. In one room, Mdlle. De Lara, the wonderful child pianist, delighted her hearers with her performances on the piano at stated intervals. In another part the Runcorn Parish Church Band under the leadership of Mr. Evans, played the'following selection of music :—Overture "Fair maid of Perth," Widdel ; grand slow march " Appollo," Little; valse 'Light and shade," H. Round; fantasia " Elmere," E, Mullott romanza, "The wanderer; "serenade " The evening Star," H. Round; fan- tasia "On guard," L. Bousquier ; national anthem. No bqaar would be complete without its "Fine art gallery," and there Wa6 one possessing more than ordinary attrac- tions, in "The fasting cat" warranted to" a-mews," and not to scratch. "Reminiscences of childhood" were quickly brought to remembrance by the sight of a birch rod, and an Al cock's porous plaster was the true representative of "A bosom friend." Doubts may be felt as to a wedding ring being a "Pitfall for the unwary," but it will be generally :,d...;ed that the poker is "a popular agitator." "Our church wardens" were represented by two long clay pipes, and 24 sheets of note Diner were shown without fear as "The Runcorn choir;" while a contemplation of "a study of fish, in oil" was afforded by a tin of sardines. A marionette show was a source of pleasure to those who entered, and of profit to the bazaar, being largely patronised. On the second floor, a room had been admirably fitted up for dramatic per- formances, and concerts, and on Tuesday evening half hour concerts were held. The following programme was capitally gone through : March "Russian Parade" F Godfrey. The Runcorn Orchestral Society. Song "The better land" F. H. Cowen. Miss Pierpoint. So'o (pianoforte) "Pas Redouble", Sydney Smith. Miss Heald. Sang Mr. C. Pownall (pianoforte) " Balmoral " Miss Harrison. Trio & Finale "7th Symphony" Haydn The Runcorn Orchestral Society.

The bazaar was also largely attended on IVednesday and Thursday, when numerous entertainments were again held. On the latter day Lady Brooke presented the " Child Pianistc," Mdlle. De Lara, with a beautiful bouquet of flowers, and expresed herself very much pleased with her performances. The dramatic representation, " Ruth's Romance,".was performed each night, and attracted crowded audiences. The parts were taken by Miss Houghton, Mr. Peat, and Mr. Vandal. The Orchestral Society's band gave an enjoyable concert, under the conductorship of Mr. W. I. Argent, each evening, and the bands of the Parish Church, and 2nd C.R.V., played selections. As many goods re- mained unsold, it was decided to hold the bazaar last even- ing, and again to-day (Saturday). The following is a list of the subscriptions promised :

at the'end of that period, became a student of Westminster College, London. He creditably paned through the two years' course of study there, and, at its conclusion, the head mastership of the Brunswick Wesleyan Day Schools, Run- corn, being vacant, he applied for the post, and was appointed. Since that time, a period of about 12 years, he has retained the position, and under his able and energetic management the school has made great progress, and is now in a flourishing condition. But it was by his connection with the Sunday school that he was most widely known. From his advent into the town he had taken great interest in Sunday school work, commencing his labours as librarian to Brunswick school. Three years ago he was appointed superintendent, and he held that office at the time of his death. In his power of attracting the attention and awaken- ing the sympathies of•children he was equalled by few men. His addresses to the scholars on Sundays were invariably listened to with rapt attention; a Bible story told by him possessed a new interest ; and his influence over the young vas consequently powerful. His cheerful temperament, which alone made him capable of bearing his long and pain- ful illness; his general urbanity and his straightforward character, made him very popular and highly esteemed beyond his own circle of acquaintances, and when the news of his death was received on Wednesday, expressions of regret were universal.

At a meeting of the above committee, held on the 7th inst., letters dated 30th June were read from the surveyor, giiing notice to the contractor for the main sewer, and his sureties, that unless the work be proceeded with within two days he would act under the powers conferred upon him by the specification and contract. Correspondence between the clerk and Mr. Jeffries, dated 4th July, was read. Recom- mended, that the tender of Mr. Jeffries be accepted, upon satisfactory sureties being given, and subject to his signing the coitract to be prepared by Messrs. R. Davies and Co. It was recommended that the trustees of the late Mr. Hut- chinson be asked if they will agree to leave the question of compensation, if any, to an arbitrator to be appointed by the Local Government Board.
The minutes were submitted to the Board, who thee went into committee, and the reporters retired.

div.head: GRAND BAZAAR AT RUNCON.
div.p: GRAND BAZAAR AT RUNCON.

With the object of raising funds for the erection of a new church in Greenway-road, Runcorn, a three days' bazaar, en a most extensive and elaborate scale, was commenced in the National Infant School, on Tuesday. Surrounding the spot where it is intended to erect the building, a fresh population of more than 3,000 people has arisen since 1871, and though uot left entirely without religious instruction, the fact could not longer be disguised that more church accommodation was needed. From a concise account published by the Bazaar Committee, we learn that "to provide for the educa- tional and spiritual wants of this newly settled population, a school chapel was erected in 1866, which has ever since been used as a public elementary school on week days, with an average attendance of 110 children; on the Lord's Day as a Sunday school attended by 130 scholars; and as a Mission Church, where divine service is performed morning; and evenin. The time, however, has come when a perma- nent church is urgently required, for which an eligible and valuable site has been presented by Major Orred ; and plans have been prepared for a church capable of accommodating about 600 worshippers. At present, how- ever, it is proposed only to erect the nave, at an estimated expense of £3,000, leaving the transept, tower, and chancel— in other words the more ornamental, and therefore the more expensive portions of a building, to a future time, when ad- ditional funds may be forthcoming." As four-fifths of the population for whose benefit the church is intended belong to the working classes, it is not surprising that in these days of monstre bazaars, that that method of procuring the required sum should be resorted to by the Building Com- mittee, which consists of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. John Brundrit, S. Beckett Chad- wick, E. A. Chorlton, C. Whiteway Hazlehurst, F. A. Lake, Matthew Steele, William Whittaker, Chas. Wigg, G. Lloyd Wigg. And that determination arrived at, the members of the Parish Church, with the Vicar at their heal, left no stone unturned to secure its successful accomplishment, and no encomium is too high to bestow upon the result of their labours.

The bazaar was under the patronage of His Grace the Duke of Westminster. K.G., the Right Hon. Lord Delamere, the Right Hon. Lord De Tahley, Hen. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P.' Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Piers Egerton Warburton, Esq. M.P. and the gentry of the neighbourhood. As the time for the performance of the opening ceremony ap- proached the bells of the Parish Church rang out a merry peal, and a large number of people gathered round the school door to " watch the arrivals." The street was rendered gay by a display of bunting, while erected at the entrance to the bazaar was a temporary verandah, covered with green leaves and decorated with trophies of digs. The opening ceremony was performed by Major J. Cavendish Orred, of Maidwell Hall, and amongst the brilliant assemblage present were the Revs., Canon Barclay, M.A., J. J. Bryant, M.A., F. M. Arm- son, M.A., 0. B. 13!,?gi (vicar 9! Frodsbam): A. Anderson, Robert F/..1. ' wards Dr. Steele, Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. B. Chad- wick, J.P., Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst, J.P., Mr. John Simpson, Mr. C. Wigg, Mr. E. A. Chorlton, Mr. & Mrs. Geo. Hazlehurst, Mr. and Mrs. F. G. Claudet, Mr. and Mrs. John Brundrit, Mrs. John Hazlehurst, Mr. G. L. Wigg, Mr. W. F. Salkeld and Miss Salkeld, Mr. W. Hayes, Mr. and Mrs. J. R. Frith, Mr. B. Lascelles, Mrs. J. Johnson, Mrs. Garrett, Mrs. Day, Mr. Peter Briscoe, Mr. M. Barker, Mr. R. 11. and Mrs. D. Brundrit, Mrs. Fitzsimons, Miss Turner, Miss Houghton, Mrs. Bryant, Miss Barclay, Miss Savage, Miss Itnison, the Misses Haztehurst, Miss Rougier, the Misses Brundrit, Miss Mouritz, Mr. and Mrs. Lightliurn. . . -

The Rev. Canon BARCLAY, in introducing Major Orred, said it was a very pleasant duty he had to perform in intro- 'clueing a gentleman whose name was known to most of those present, and who himself was personally known to many of there. Ever since he (the Vicar) had been connepted with A„ncfarn, which was more than 36 yeass, the name of Orred had been a z7s, familiar one. An ancestor of Major Orred's, v a very dear old lady', who livel near to him was well known in the annals of Runcorn for her valuable donations to every good work. She was a very large donor to the Parish Church, and one of her last donations WAS giYea to that school in which they were assembled. He need hardly soy she was an honoured contributor to every parochial institu- tion, and she showed her goodwill to her native place 17 , leaving legacies to it, from one of whicll that school no— de ived a certain and another which ben'efited the J poorer inhagkants of Runcorn. In tirr., of course, the good'old lady was translated to her rest, and although the father of Major Orred did not succeed to her accumulated wealth he did succeed to her landed property in that neighbourhood, and. found that property brought its duties and responsibilities as well as its privileges and advantages. He was the first gentleman tt•at started Weston Mission by suggesting that a school- chapel should be built there, where the inhabitants might attend divine service on a Sunday. He, however, not only gave valuable suggestions, but showed practical proof of his support by giving a piece of land for, and a handsome dona- tion towards, the building of the place. His was the first liberal donation given towards Newtown Mission Church,and they hoped by means of that, and by the kindness of their friends, to exchange that mission for a permanent church. The time for such an exchange had now arrived. He need hardly say that the good qualities of the sire bad descended to the son. (Applause.) Major Orred had not made a single change in the subscriptions his father had been in the habit of giving, but had more than once increased them. (Ap- plause.) When he saw tbe necessity for a permanent church instead of the temporary schoolroom in Newtown, he gave a valuable piece of land in a part of Runcorn, which was much coveted for building purposes, in order that a new church might be built there. (Applause.) He thought he had said enough to show that he was justified in inviting Major Orred to open that bazaar, and that they would agree with him that he was the right man in the right place. He would take that opportunity, however, of returning his thanks, as vicar of the parish, to those ladies who bad taken so much pains to produce that magnificent result they now saw before them. He was sure they had succeeded in one part, and that was in producing a very good and excellent bazaar, but whether they succeeded or not in the main feature—selling their articles, or in procuring stich a sum of money as would give them a good lift in the work in which they 'were engaged, he thought all present would agree with him that they had done their best to deserve success, which no man could command. (App'ause.). He then introduced Major ORRED, who said he was very much obliged to the Rev. Canon for the kind references to himself and family, and although it was not in their power to live in Runcorn, they would do what they could for the town in every way. He; personally, wished they had found a better spokesman to open the bazaar, because he could tell them he was no orator. (Laughter.) He could remember coming to Run- corn for the first time some 25 or 26 years ago. He travelled by train to a place called Ditton, on the other side of the river, and walked down to the ferry and crossed the river by boat. At that time he did not think there was a single house on that side of the canal where they proposed to erect the new church. It was now desirable there should be a church there. At present a curate in charge ministered there. They wished to convert it into a regular district, but until they had a building capable of accommodating 600 people the Ecclesiastical Commissioners would not allow this. No definite plans had yet been decided upon. To- wards the estimated cost of the building £l,OOO had been promised and partly paid, but the committee dare not begin work until tbey had over £2,000 in hand. , Looking at the stalls around him, laden with many beautiful things, and so ably presided over by Lady Brooke, and other ladies of Runcorn, he was convinced that before the end of the week their hopes would be somewhat realised. He now declared the bazaar open. (Applause.) Mr. C. WIGG proposed a vote of thanks to Major Orred for opening the bazaar, remarking that his presence amongst them would be welcomed by all. Major ORRED briefly responded. The sales were then proceeded with. The bazaar proper

DEA'fil OF MR, C. SOULBY, OF RUNCORN. Our readers will hear with profound regret of the death of Mr. Charles Soulby, of Runcorn, which occurred at Shanklin, Isle of Wight, on Tuesday night. Mr. Soulby had suffered greatly from a constitutional weakness which first afflicted him about five years ago. At that time he was attacked with rheumatism, which eventually developed into consumption. Notwithstanding every precaution was taken, the disease gained upon him, and he put himself under the care of Dr. McDougall. About twelve months ago his medical adviser ordered him to leave the town as the only means of saving his life, and he took up his residence at Frodsham. No beneficial result, however, followed. Gradually growing worse he consulted Mr. Waters, physician, of Chester, who, as a last resource, advised him to visit the south of France. He, therefore, obtained six months' leave of absence from his scholastic duties, and with the intention of ultimately acting upon the advice of the physician, he departed for London early in May of this year. After spending a short time with his friends there, he went to Hastings. This change appeared to have further enfeebled him, and he remained there but a short time, next taking up his abode at Shanklin, in the Isle of Wight. The pure atmosphere of that charming spot, however, in no de- gree restored him, and becoming weaker and weaker he died, as previously stated, at 10 o'clock on Tuesday night. He had only attained the age of 33. He leaves a widow and one child, a girl about seven years of age, to mourn his loss. Mr. Soulby was a native of Bingley, in Yorkshire, where he received five years' training as a pupil teacher Successful in passing the Government examintions, he,

div.head: ALTERATIONS Or -THE TOWNSHIPS.
div.p: ALTERATIONS Or -THE TOWNSHIPS.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board adverting to their orders of the 27th December last, making certain alterations in the townships of Antrobus, Seven Oaks, Norley, and Kingsley in the Runcorn Union, and in- quiring what arrangements had been made by the Guardians for the administration of medical and general relief in the townships as altered. The CLERK stated that there were no arrangements to be made.
THE DAINTY DINNER AT DUTTON.-THE @LEEK AND THE
REPORTS.

The CLERK said that he found in the report of the last meeting in three or four different papers, including the Runcorn Examiner, that he (the clerk) was reported to have said that "it was a very good dinner and they made a very good job of it." He was not present at the dinner, nor did lie make any remarks of that kind. If they were to have reports at all they should have them correct, because it might be offensive to some gentlemen to have words put into their mouths that they never used. He could not say that such words were not made use of, but they were certainly not made use of by him. The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD observed that on going to Liver- pool early the next morning his eyes were attracted by a very large poster at a newspaper office, bearing the words "Economical epicures." He found that it had reference to the Guardians' meeting which he attended the day be- fore, and he went into the office, saw one of the papers, read the account,and found that his opinion was correct. He saw the remark made with reference to the clerk, and he at one time thought of sending a little postscript to the editor stating that it was-a wrong report of the man's statement. He knew who did make the remarks, but they were certainly not made by the clerk.'

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

A letter was submitted by the Clerk from P. E. Warbur- ton, Esq., M.P., dated June 30tb, which stated that he should have great pleasure in presenting the petition in favour of closing public houses on Sundays from the Run- corn Union.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Committee recommended that the sum of £595 ss. 10d. for the salaries of officers, for articles supplied, and for work done be paid. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE moved, and the Rev. J. LOCKWOOD seconded, that Mr. Handley be added to the Finance Com- mittee, and that Mr. Handley and Mr. Fisher be added to the Relief Supervision Committee. This was agreed to.

SPECIAL ELECTION OF GUARDIANS. The CLERK stated that the following gentlemen had been, without opposition, elected as Guardians for the township of Runcorn :—Wm. Fisher, Highfield House, gentleman; Wm. Handley, Church-street, boot manufacturer, Wm. Whittaker, Castle View, Moughlands-road, gentleman. On the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. JACK- SON, it was agreed that the sum of £5 be allowed to the clerk for the expenses of the special election.

MEDICAL ATTENDANCE AT THE INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL. The CLERK read a letter from Dr; McDougall as follows On the 14th June I received an order to attend John Cress- well, aged 17 years, who was alleged to be ill of smallpox on a narrow boat, moored against Stonecroft, Top Locks. The case proved to be smallpox, and was removed to the Infectious Hospital, and was discharged cured on the sth of July. I beg to call the attention of the Authority to the want of provision for medical attendance in such cases at the Infectious Hospital. In the case referred to I attended it in order to obviate any dif- ficultv.—l am, yours truly, J. hi cDotrout.L. The CLERK: We have an agreement with the Runcorn Commissioners with respect to th 3 Infectious Hospital. Mr. HANDLEY : Dr. McDougall says that this is an extra duty, for which be ought to have a salary or pay- ment.
After some further discussion it was decided that the Clerk should prepare a report of the matter,to be presented at the next meeting for consideration.
THE LOCAL 09yEHNMENT BOARD AND THE MASTER'S 1,47,11 LY.

The following letter h,i.d been received from the Local Government Board, dated July Ist : I am directed by the Local Government Boarl to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the Ist ult. respecting the proposal thit certain of the children of Mr. R. Jones, master of the workhouse of the Runcorn Union, should be allowed to continue to reside in the workhoure. The Board observe with satisfaction that the master's son, aged 20 years, no longer re- sides in the workhowe, and they pxisume that the Guardians will in pursuance of the power conferred upon them by the general order of the 19th August, 1857, appoint as an assistant the con' aged 17 year., whose services are it appears required for the discharge of the duties of master's clerk. The Board, with the view to meet so far as possible the wishes of the Guardians, will raise no further objection to the arrangements under which the master's daughter comes to the workhouse on Saturday evening. The Board would have been glad to hear the views of the Guardians with respect to the boys, aged respectively 14 and 15 years, but feel that having regard to the invariable rule on the subject, they cannot properly con- sent to the continuance of the arrangements. The Board further, In order to avoid unnecessary inconvenience to the master, are willing that-he should be allowed six months during which to arrange for their residence elsewhere than in the workhouse. This was all the public business.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The first meeting of this Board, after the election, was hel4l at the Cemetery .oilices on Welnesday. There were present Messrs. Coleburn (retiring chairman), Jas. Handley, Moss. Mellor, and Salkeld (secretary.) The first business was the election of chairmln, and Mr. Selkald presided pro tent.

div.head: THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.

Mr. HANDLEY said before proceeding to the election of chairman for the ensuing year he thought it was their duty to accord a vote of thanks to Mr. Coleburn, who vacated the chair that day, for the very great attention he had paid to the business of the Board during the period of his office. He evidently believed in the well known maxim 'Example is better than precept," ind he could safely say that as re- garded punctuality of attendance at the meetings of the Board he had had no equal. That influence seemed to have been exerted on the attendance generally, for if the secretary would refer to the record of attendances for several years past he would find that the attendances during the past year had been more regular than at any other time. (Hear, hear.) He thought he was quite right in attributing this to the excellent example set by the late chairman, and it was with sincere pleasure that he asked the Board to unite with him in his pioposition.

Mr. Moss seconded the motion. The SECRETARY put the motion to the meeting, and it was unanimously carried. Mr. COLEBURN, in acknowledging the compliment, said his duties as chairman had been very light during the year. This resulted from the manner in which the business had been carried out by all the members. He did not remember a single year that had been more agreeable or pleasant. No questions of importance had been brought under their notice, and no questions involving serious differences of opinion had occupied their attention. He thought this was ewing to the appointment of a Finance and General Committee. Al- though he was a member of that committee, he must say that he had had very little to do, for under the excellent chair- manship of Mr. Handley, with the able assistance of Mr. Moss, the business of the Board had been carried out in an admirable manner without causing any loss of time to the Board. The financial business was the most important part only of their affairs' and if that was carried out efficiently there was little left for the chairman to do.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Moss proposed that Mr. Whittaker should he appointed chairman for the ensuing year. He was hivhly respected by everybody, and his appointment would give the greatest pleasure. Mr. COLEBURN seconded the proposition. It had been understood that the oldest member of the Board should suc- ceed to the office of chairman, and Mr. Whittaker would fill the chair with ability. He was closely connected with church matters, which sometimes were identified with the business of the Board. The motion was carried. Mr. HANDLEY proposed, and Mr. MELLort seconded a motion that, in accordance with the custom of the Board, the deputy chair be filled by Mr. Coleburn. The proposition was adopted. THE INTERMENTS.

It was reported that there had been 70 interments during the month ending June 25th; corresponding period last year, 78; decrease, 8. The fees received for the same period amounted to £6B 18s. Bd.; corresponding Month last year, £73 18s. 10d. ; decrease, .£5 Os. 2d.

div.head: FINANCES.
div.p: THE FINANCES.

Mr. HANDLEY read the report of the Finance Committee, which stated the income of the Board for the past month was £24 Bs. 6d., and the expenditure £ll 10s. Gd., the balance £l2 18s. Od, having been paid into the bank to the credit of the Board. Accounts amounting to £9 16s. 6d. were recommended for payment. Mr. Handley had also to report that this month the coroner had paid 7s. 6d. for the use of the mortuary and office, on the occasion of an inquest held on a man unknown on the 27th ult. It would be some

satisfaction to the public to know that the outlay on the mortuary, was in Some measure being re-couped, and that it was a useful building to the town. He proposed the adoption of the report. Mr. Moss seconded, and the motion was carried. Mr. MELLOR proposed, and Mr. HANDLEY seconded, that the following members should constitute the Finance Com- mittee :--Messrs. James Handley, Coleburn, Moss, Littler, and the chairman (Mr. Whittaker). Carried.

THE DEBT UPON THE CEMETERY. Mr. Moss said he wished to call the attention of the Board to the manner in which they were repaying the mortgage debt on the cemetery. The members would be aware that in this matter they were not carrying out the provisions of the law, which required that the annual contribution of the ratepayers towards the extinction of the debt should be in- vested so as to form a sinking fund which should accumu- late from year to year until such a sum was realised that the debt could be paid off. Instead of this the Board had adopted a system of paying off the debt by instalments,which was clearly illegal. It had been argued with great plausi- bility that it was more economical to pay off the debt by instalments which bear four per cent. interest than by a sinking fund. This was a mistake. The fact seemed to have been overlooked that if money was sunk for a long period of time, it accumulated at compound interest, which produced a result very different from simple interest. Ile had calculated the results obtained from the two systems.of dealing with the debt, and assuming that one- fiftieth portion was contributed every year by the legal method, the Board would be in a position to pay off the debt in 30 years, whereas by the system of paying adopted 50 years would be required, and the cost to the ratepayers would be :£2OO more for every £l,OOO of debt. It conse- quently seemed to him rather unfortunate that the law had not been adhered to, as they would then have been in a much better position with regard to the debt at the present time than they were. However, "It is never too late to mend," and he thought they had better at once proceed to adopt the legal system, as it would effect a saving to the ratepayers of about £l,lOO. He, therefore, begged to move that the Finance Committee be requested to take into con- sideration the desirability of providing a sinking fund for the extinction of the mortgage debt on the cemetery in ac- cordance with the Burial Act, 1857. Mr. HANDLEY remarked that it was a very proper ques- tion for the committee to consider, and he should be very glad to second the motion.

- The CHAIRMAN observed that when the cemetery was opened it was thought the method of paying the money at present in force would effect a saving to the ratepayers. The proposition was carried. This was all the basiness.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Bibby and George Pilkington. DRUNKENNESS.-Hugh Moran and Charles Matthews were charged with being drunk and disorderly at Widnes, on the 10th inst., and the former was fined 76. 6cl. and the latter as., and costs.

THEFT FROM THE RAILWAY.—A boy named Jas. McCor- mick (10) was charged on remand from Tuesday with steal- ing 10 empty sacks from a waggon on the railway at a place called Carterhouse Shunt, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Thomas Waldron, shunter, said on Monday he saw the prisoner and another boy in a waggon emptying scrap iron from a number of sacks. He jumped in the waggon and the boys ran away, but he succeeded in capturing the prisoner. Ten empty sacks were lying in a corner of the waggon, the iron being scattered on the bottom.—lnspector Carter stated the sacks were worth 2s.—ln answer to Mr. Bibby, the prisoner said he and the other boy intended to sell the bags, and he was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

DEFRAUDING THE CHESHIRE LINES COMPANY.—Patrick Connolley and Hugh McDonald, of Liverpool, were brought up in custody charged with travelling in a third-class carriage on the Sheffield and Midland Railway without having previously paid their fare with intent to avoid pay- ment thereof.— On the arrival at Widnes of the five minutes to one train from Liverpool on Tuesday, the prisoners alighted. Enoch Pitt, a porter at the station, asked them for their tickets, but they had got neither tickets nor money. They stated they had entered the train at Liverpool with the intention of getting out at Garston, bat the train did not stop there. The prisoners were intoxicated.—The chief clerk gave confirmatory evidence.—P.C. Thompson deposed to apprehending the prisoners, who informed him they had got some drink at Liverpool, and had not sufficient money to purchase a ticket. He searched the prisoners, and found 7P. upon McDonald and a penny upon Connolley.—Prisoners were each fined ss. and costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment.

THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK. Mr. Danby, on behalf of the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for not regularly sending their children to school, and tho usual fine was inflicted in each case :—Jas. Welsh, Jno. Sproston, Catherine Tomlinson, David Dickens (adjourned for a week), Martin Canovan, Henry Whitfield, and Richard Glassey. AN UNSUCCESSFUL APPLICANT.—Mr. Husband appeared on behalf of Wm. Ince,contractor,to apply for the temporary transfer to him of the licensed premises in John-street, Wid- nes, at present held by Thomas Golding. Mr. Inspector Barnett objected to the transfer on the ground that the ap- plicant was not of sufficiently good character, and called P.S. Clarkson to prove that he had been charged with steal- ing timber to the value of £2 103. in May, 1874, when he was released on entering into sureties to appear when called upon.—Mr. Husband contended his client was not convicted, and saki in the name of all that was fair and just this un- convicted offence ought not to be brought against him now. The Bench told the applicant to apply at the transfer sessions.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campb.2ll, and Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst.

EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A Boy. Richard Collingswood, 16 years of age, was brought up on remand charged with stealing £1 is. the monies of Joseph B.alphs. The prosecutor is a seaman on board the schooner Jane, of Preston, on which the prisoner is also cook. On Thursday morning the prosecutor's trousers containing the money named were safe in the locker in the forecastle, but the money was subsequently abstracted by the prisoner who was apprehended at Runcorn railway station by P.C. Price.—ln cross-examination by the prisoner, the prosecutor admitted that he had skown the prisoner the money and purse which held it, and spoken of it in such a way as to lead him to con- clude it was his wages. This, he stated, was the only way to get the prisoner to work.—The Bench dismisssed the case. —Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the boy had told him one tale all the time he had been in the cells, that he be- lieved the money was his wages, and no doubt he did. TUB SAILOR AND His MONEY.—WM. Jack, seaman on the schooner Margaret Edwards, lying at Weston Point, charged Margaret Smith with stealing 63. 81. from him on the previous night. After hearinti the evidence, which showed that proceedings of a disreputable character had oc- curred, the Bench dismissed the case. QUARRELSOME RELATIVES.—Mary Alice Walkey, a young woman, was summoned by John Walkey for using defama- tory language to him on the sth, inst., and also with assault. ing him on the night following.—Mr. W. H. Linaker ap- peared for the complainant.—A number of witnesses were called to give evidence as to the language used by the de- fendant, who is wife to the complainant's brother, and a man named Hitchmough stated the defendant walked across the street and spat in the face of the complainant.—The de- fendant had issued a cross summons against John Walkey for using threatening language to her of the sth inst. stated that when she saw him in the street she was about to ask him a question when the defendant shook his clenched fist in her face, and, using a foul expression, said he.would knock her brains out. She totally denied using defamatory language to him, or spitting in his face.—Mr. Linaker re- plied, and called the defendant, who denied using the threatening language.—The summons against John Walkey was dismissed, and Mary Alice was bound over to keep the peace for six months in one surety of £lO. The costs amounted to £1 6s.

ASSAULT ON A CHILD.--James Aston, a rather queer looking young man, was charged with unlawfully and in- decently assaulting Mary Ann McDonald, a child seven years of age. It appeared that the prisoner lodged with the father of the girl in Alcock-street, and on Sunday night about about half past eight, he went to the house. 'I he girl was in charge of the house alone. The prisoner left the house, but again returned in a short time. He then took hold of the girl in an indecent manner, and she screamed loidly. A neighbour named Mrs. Mulhearn hear- ing the screams went into the house, and found the prisoner sitting on a chair and the girl standing besides him crying. The girl subsequently made a statement to her.—The Bench reduced the charge to a common assault. The prisoner denied the charge totally. He was fined 10s. and costs, 14s. 6d. A DisonnEras CHARACTER.—Mary Oneil, a had character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mill-street on the 2nd inst., and she was fined 10s. and Os. 6d. costs, or in default 14 days' hard labour. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brundrit, and Mr. C. W. _
Hazleburst.

A DISORDERLY WARRINGIONIAN.—MichaeI Conn, of Warrington, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Church-street, on Tuesday evening, and on the evidence of P.C. Wallace, he was fined ss. and costs, 5. 4d. ASSAULT ON A WlFE.—James Clare, of Sewell-street, Run- corn, was charged with assaulting his wife Alice. The evid- ence went to show that on Saturday last the prisoner Went home' slightly the "worse for liquor." He gave his wife 305., but she apparently not satisfied with the amount "threw it at him." She then left the house and went to her mother's, and the prisoner followed her. Ile brought her from the house, and she alleged he dragged her back home. On arriving there he blackened her eye with s fist, and kicked her. The Bench bound the prisoner over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and two sureties of each, and pay the costs 14s. fid.

"I am astonished at your Honour's decision," said a young lawyer to a judge who had decreed against him. "This re- mark cannot be permitted," said the judge," aLd an apology will be necessary on your part." " Permit me," said the senior counsel, " to offer an excuse for my younß friend; he is new in these matters, and when he has practised as long before your Honour as I have, he will be astonished at nothing."

MO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- coaraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Purchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best makers for ec3nomy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed ou the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, ll,nager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.
